title: Remember the frontier AI pause? Chip companies don’t either
abstract: AI Tech Remember the frontier AI pause? Chip companies don’t either Nvidia and AMD earnings show booming demand. This is why a frontier slowdown might not derail it. Nvidia and AMD earnings show booming demand. This is why a frontier slowdown might not derail it. by Rani Molla Nov 18, 2026, 3:44 PM UTC If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. Nvidia began shipping its most advanced AI computing system, the Vera Rubin NVL72, calling it the “fastest product ramp in the company’s history.” Image: Nvidia Part Of Fall 2026 earnings watch see all Rani Molla is a journalist with 15 years of experience covering how Big Tech companies are reshaping society. This summer, OpenAI paused its largest planned frontier training run after its AI agents accidentally hacked Hugging Face and early evidence suggested that its next model could independently find and exploit security flaws. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing advances in the most powerful AI models , warning that they could be used to launch cyberattacks or become harder for their own creators to control. It was a strange moment for the AI boom. The people building the most powerful models were warning about what those models might be capable of, and investors were suddenly wondering what would happen to chip demand if the labs eased up on new models. US chip stocks bore the brunt of the sell-off . “Pumping the brakes on frontier training won’t shrink the AI chip market but it will simply reallocate the spend.” Despite the hubbub it created, whatever slowdown there was appears to have been short-lived. OpenAI had announced only a two-week pause; it restarted the run 10 days later, at the end of August, though it continued to “temporarily hold back some smaller experimental training runs.” Anthropic released upgraded versions of its Fable and Mythos frontier models in November, touting improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision. And the companies selling the chips powering those advances are doing better than ever. Nvidia on Tuesday posted a blockbuster quarter , with data center revenue rising 110 percent from a year ago to $107.6 billion in the three months ended October 25. The chip designer began shipping its most advanced AI computing system, the Vera Rubin NVL72, calling it the “fastest product ramp in the company’s history.” The Rubin platform generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments alone. The racks are already running at CoreWeave, Google, Microsoft, and Oracle. Meta plans to expand Vera Rubin deployments to train and run AI models and agents. Nvidia name-dropped Anthropic and OpenAI, too. Anthropic has expanded access to Vera Rubin capacity through cloud providers and continues to work with Nvidia on future chip designs tailored to its workloads. OpenAI is among the companies adopting Nvidia’s new Vera CPUs. “Proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic continue to advance the frontier,” Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress said on the earnings call. She said the company expects major frontier labs to account for approximately 15 percent of its data center revenue this fiscal year. Nvidia also raised its revenue growth forecast for next fiscal year from 70 percent to 75 percent. Chipmaker AMD, meanwhile, reported its biggest quarter ever earlier this month, with revenue up 45 percent to $13.4 billion . Data center sales drove that growth, nearly doubling to $8.5 billion. OpenAI and Anthropic were among the first customers running workloads on AMD’s new high-end Helios systems, which use its latest MI450 GPUs. Broadcom, which helps many of the biggest AI companies design their own custom chips, has yet to report earnings. But so far, there’s little sign of a frontier slowdown hurting chip sales. Of course, even if AI labs were to significantly scale back their training ambitions, it would take a while to show up in chipmakers’ earnings. Neil Shah, vice president of research at Counterpoint Research, told The Verge in September that it would take about six months to see the financial effects of a slowdown, owing to existing computing and memory procurement agreements. The impact could show up sooner in orders placed with chip manufacturers like TSMC. So far, there’s little evidence of that, either: TSMC’s latest sales figures also show continued strength . But there’s another reason a frontier slowdown might not be particularly bad for the chip industry: growing demand for inference, the process of running the AI models we already have. “While one might argue the need for top-end GPUs will reduce with this shift toward inferencing, these workloads will collectively require more compute infrastructure than training,” Shah said. “Overall, it means a net increase in demand for all types of accelerators.” There’s another reason a frontier slowdown might not be particularly bad for the chip industry: growing demand for inference, the process of running the AI models we already have. According to our analysis of the latest data from corporate spending platform Ramp, frontier model families accounted for about 60 percent of token usage among businesses using Ramp in early November — a record high and about three times their share at the start of the year. That includes OpenAI’s Astra and Sol models and Anthropic’s Opus and Fable models. But even as businesses use more AI, their spending is only growing modestly . “It’s not really a demand issue though,” Ara Kharazian, lead economist at Ramp, tells The Verge . “By all measures, companies are using more AI.” Rather, competition among AI model providers is driving down token prices so rapidly that it’s calling OpenAI and Anthropic’s revenue projections into question, Kharazian says. That could prove beneficial for the companies supplying computing power. On Nvidia’s earnings call, Kress said token prices had fallen nearly 60 percent since May, spurring more usage. Meanwhile, rental prices for Nvidia GPUs across generations have gone up. Nvidia and AMD are positioning their most powerful chips for both training and inference, including the demanding workloads created by AI agents. That doesn’t necessarily mean Nvidia will maintain its dominance. As AI companies get more serious about the economics of serving their models to millions of people, they’re increasingly turning to custom chips that can do so more cheaply than general-purpose GPUs. Counterpoint expects shipments of custom AI server processors to surpass those of data center GPUs by 2028 . “Pumping the brakes on frontier training won’t shrink the AI chip market but it will simply reallocate the spend,” Shah said. Indeed, on Nvidia’s earnings call, UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri asked Kress whether the company would be willing to sacrifice some of its hefty profit margins as frontier labs increasingly invest in custom chips and prioritize computing efficiency. Kress maintained that Nvidia’s systems justify their pricing and reiterated the company’s gross margin outlook. For companies like Nvidia, the bigger threat may not be that AI companies slow down, but that they find cheaper chips on which to keep going. title: Will Wright’s next game uses AI to map your memories
abstract: Gaming AI Entertainment Will Wright’s next game uses AI to map your memories MyMems, from the creator of SimCity and The Sims, is a new social simulator powered by AI. MyMems, from the creator of SimCity and The Sims, is a new social simulator powered by AI. by Jay Peters Nov 18, 2026, 2:00 PM UTC Image: Gallium Studios Jay Peters is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme. Will Wright, the creator of legendary franchises like SimCity and The Sims , is working on a new game — and it’s built around AI. The new title, focused on your memories, is called MyMems . Like Wright’s other titles, it sounds extremely ambitious, giving players a new way to explore worlds they create on their own. “We want to take your autobiography and turn it into a toy world,” he tells The Verge . The MyMems website describes the mobile game as a “social simulation” with worlds “built from your memories and the people who shaped you.” You can add “memories” to your game, like speaking a short story to your phone, and those memories are generated into pieces you can place on the game’s map. Your worlds can also include AI-powered avatars, which can represent people you know in your life. Ideally, as you play, the planet starts to become a “map of your psyche,” kind of like Inside Out , Wright says. Worlds can be private, but you can also share them with others. Here’s another way to think of it, from Virginia McArthur, executive producer and GM at MyMems developer Gallium Studios: “It’s a cozy world builder with a really deep social simulation underneath.” Image: Gallium Studios I’ll admit that I don’t totally get it, and it seems like a tricky idea to grasp without playing it. Still, as heady of a concept as it might be — turning your memories into a game world — Wright and team still want it to be fun. “This isn’t meant to be your legacy diary necessarily,” says Anthony Maitz, a product manager at Gallium Studios. “It’s meant to just be something you kind of play around with.” However, Maitz notes that what you’re working toward is a “proxy” of you — a word that seems to be the inspiration of the game’s earlier title, Proxi: Yesterday’s You Tomorrow . The game will use the “Behavior Engine” from a company called Artificial Agency , which makes AI tech for video games, as a “foundational technology.” Like other industries, gaming is starting to reckon with generative AI. Early AI virtual worlds created with models from a startup backed by a Pixar cofounder and Google’s Project Genie weren’t experiences you’d actually want to spend dedicated time with, and indie developers I spoke to in March were largely opposed to the technology . But AI technology has taken some big leaps this year with companies like Google , Meta , and Roblox now letting users make games with AI right from their phone, and retro gaming becoming overrun with AI-powered ports of classic titles. Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said earlier this year that generative AI has “zero part in what Rockstar Games is building” with GTA VI . But even as a recent industry survey indicated that more game developers are starting to use generative AI as part of their job , workers are pushing back against generative AI use , and the technology is at the center of fierce debates over indie game awards . Many players are rejecting AI outright, and I wondered if the Gallium Studios team was worried about opposition toward MyMems ’ use of AI. Wright says he has three boys at home and that they are all “pretty negative” on AI. He attributes negativity over AI to be toward the meaning of art and authorship and credit, a concern he calls “well-founded.” But he also calls AI an “amazing tool.” Image: Gallium Studios “We’re not making slop,” says McArthur. But Maitz notes that while the team has “been concerned” about a negative response to the generative AI use, they’ve learned that people don’t mind when they use AI in a “ Scribblenauts -y style” for things like having the game make a high school. The team also found that people got “addicted” to a test app with a character creator, including Maitz’s own daughter, who he says “hates” AI. “By making it so that the player is authoring it over and over, bit by bit, it doesn’t really feel like you cheated,” Maitz says. “We’re not making slop.” MyMems , which is set to launch in 2027, will join a growing field of other social simulations, like Krafton’s Inzoi and Nintendo’s smash hit Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream . But none quite have the pull of The Sims , which remains one of EA’s most important franchises. With The Sims , Wright says that many people tried making their real families in the game. “It was interesting how people really were naturally trying to map this game, which was like a little toy, onto their real life,” he says. With MyMems , that’s what the team is trying to do the “follow-through” on — what if they made the whole game focused on you? Imagine opening a family scrapbook and the way people and things jump out, Wright explains. “As you go through more and more pages, pretty soon you have this whole little circus of people and events and things from your life.” It’s chaos, he says. “I want something that feels kind of like that.” Update, November 18th : Added context about Artificial Agency. title: Nvidia isn’t selling any more AI chips to China
abstract: Tech AI News Nvidia isn’t selling any more AI chips to China After former CEO Jensen Huang fought for US approval to sell H200 chips in China, Nvidia is now walking away.﻿ After former CEO Jensen Huang fought for US approval to sell H200 chips in China, Nvidia is now walking away.﻿ by Jess Weatherbed Nov 18, 2026, 1:01 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge Part Of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned. What happens next? see all updates Jess Weatherbed is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews. Nvidia has stopped sending its advanced AI chips to China despite the approval it received from the White House to do so in December last year . The announcement was made by interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress during an earnings call on Tuesday , marking a notable shift for the company that, under former CEO Jensen Huang, fought for the right to ship its powerful Hopper architecture H200 chips to China. “Our guidance ⁠does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping ​licenced Hopper data center products to China,” Kress said . She did not explain why Nvidia was ceasing its H200 processor shipments or clarify whether Nvidia would pursue other business with China in the future. The pivot comes after Huang stepped down from his position as Nvidia CEO last week following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, one with a woman who was suspected by US intelligence to be a Chinese spy . Nvidia already faced difficulties around offloading the AI chips prior to this scandal, however. Concerns were raised about failings to properly vet Chinese companies that were approved to handle the H200 AI chips. Reuters also reported earlier this month that around 600,000 ⁠H200 chips ​were stuck in Hong Kong after Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports, with China seeking to reduce its dependency on US technology. title: Suno now lets you make AI videos for your AI music
abstract: AI News Tech Suno now lets you make AI videos for your AI music The new Visuals feature generates images and 15-second videos that automatically sync with Suno songs.﻿ The new Visuals feature generates images and 15-second videos that automatically sync with Suno songs.﻿ by Jess Weatherbed Nov 18, 2026, 11:16 AM UTC Here are some of the examples that Suno provided to show what Visuals is capable of. Image: Suno Jess Weatherbed is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews. Suno has introduced image and video generation in its latest effort to expand beyond being an AI music platform. The new feature, called “Visuals,” allows users to turn Suno songs into AI-generated video clips that automatically lipsync to lyrics, or make images via prompt descriptions that can be used as thumbnails and album artwork. Visuals is available on web, iOS, and Android. The exact layout differs across Suno’s desktop and mobile interfaces, but users will find a new Visuals tab under Create mode on each version. Web users can also access Visuals by selecting the three dot menu on a song in their library. From there, users can select which section of the track to use, up to a maximum of 15 seconds, and select a reference image to build the generated video clip. There are three options available for the starting image reference: selecting one of the original character presets provided by Suno, uploading your own photo or artwork, or generating the image directly on Suno using descriptive prompts. The image generation capabilities also allow users to select specific aspect ratios, optimizing results for landscape or portrait modes and online platforms. For video generation, users can select whether the reference image is used as the start or end frame, making it easier to edit the 15-second clips together. There’s a toggle to automatically lipsync vocals to the generated video, and tools for adjusting aspect ratio and clip length. Visuals also includes a dedicated video editing timeline for assembling clips into longer videos, and adding customizable song lyric text. The H3 Move AI model is being used to power Visuals, based on H3 from MiniMax. Suno says the AI has been “optimized for our community including adding additional protections and safeguards,” which include a “suite of new text and visual filters” designed to block people from using or generating the likeness of specific artists, public figures, copyrighted works and IP. Visuals also uses its own “Visuals credits” to generate videos and images, which are distinct from the song credits used to make AI music, meaning Suno users will have additional expenses to pay in order to use this new feature. The Visuals launch follows Suno introducing a Speech feature in October for generating spoken words and voiceovers. Adding video capabilities is another attempt to diversify the platform after Suno’s music generator attracted a number of high-profile lawsuits , though it seems some users would rather the company focus on improving those song-generating capabilities . In the YouTube video for the Visuals launch, one user says “FIX AUDIO BEFORE ADDING CRAP NOBODY ASKED FOR” — a sentiment that other commenters are echoing. title: The Gemini app is now available on lower-memory Android devices.
abstract: The Gemini app is now available on lower-memory Android devices. Angus Logan Builder, Gemini App Nov 18, 2026 For hundreds of millions of people globally, a lower-memory Android device is their everyday connection to the internet, education, and business. Until recently, hardware limits meant those phones only had basic voice commands. Now, we’re bringing the Gemini app to eligible Android (Go edition) devices , putting Google’s personal AI assistant in the hands of hundreds of millions more people. We re-architected the app so the core Gemini experience runs smoothly on hardware with less memory. Instead of typing out long prompts, you can talk things through or practice for an interview out loud in more than 45 languages with Gemini Live , point your camera at notes or forms to learn and translate, or create custom images with Nano Banana — like a flyer for a weekend bakery sale. To get started, download the Gemini app on Google Play, press and hold the power button on supported phones, or look for it preloaded on upcoming devices from partners like Transsion.

We’ve built it for anyone who has tasks piling up during all the classes, meetings, and school drop-offs that fill the day. Our goal is for Gemini to save you time and money. Starting now, this update is rolling out free of charge for hundreds of millions of people across the U.S., Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India, using our new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. We’re also rolling out a set of advanced features, starting in the U.S. How it’s changing my daily routine If your emails, calendar, passwords, photos, files, and payment cards are already in the Google ecosystem, Gemini is your best choice as a personal assistant because this sensitive data already lives at Google securely, and you don’t have to send it elsewhere. Here’s how I’m using it. Recently, our minivan’s check-engine light came on. Ugh. I pulled out Gemini and told it, "Our minivan is overdue for a service appointment. Please call the two nearest dealerships and figure out how to get an appointment early Friday morning over the next month or so." Because Gemini already knows we drive a 2019 Honda Odyssey and where we live through Personal Intelligence , it found the nearest shops on Google Maps and called both at once 1 . Thankfully, I didn’t have to suffer through any hold music. Gemini did the job, found a time in my Google Calendar when I was free, and added the Friday early morning appointment in less than five minutes. Done. (On the dealership's end, Gemini disclosed right away that it's an AI. Businesses can opt out whenever they want, and Gemini won’t give out my payment or private account info unless I say so.) In the background, Gemini called both dealerships at once, sat through the hold music for me, booked an appointment at the shop that accepts appointments vs. walk-ins only, and put Friday's appointment on my calendar without me having to check it. Last month it saved us real money after we got hit with a surprise $389 electric bill. I gave Gemini permission to access our utility portal with the new Google Password Manager integration and asked for it to analyze our past billing statements in my email. Gemini worked for a few minutes, and then nailed it. The primary culprit was our heat pump, which it turns out was kicking on around 4 p.m., right in the middle of peak pricing. My wife and I never would have caught that digging through the PDFs and emails ourselves. I use it for smaller stuff, too. For our upcoming holiday trip back to Oklahoma, I recently asked Gemini to give me the best options for a USB-C charger. Gemini quickly compared chargers thanks to Google’s Shopping Graph, asked me follow-up questions about the wattage and color, and then helped me check out using the new Google Pay integration. The best part: it also found a discount code so I saved an extra $10. Done. Gemini now uses the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) to make purchases like this. We’re working with American Express (coming soon), Mastercard, and Visa to keep your purchases secure with digital tokens on supported cards. And when you shop with Gemini, you still earn your card's points, cashback, or purchase protections during checkout. You can also set a hard spending cap upfront, and Gemini is designed to stay within your budget. All of your receipts and tracking info land straight in Google Wallet, which is expanding to iOS starting today . Up next, we’ll integrate the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) into Gemini so everyone can expect an even faster and more reliable shopping experience from discovery to checkout. Gemini lets you set the spending limit and still earn every airline mile, cashback point, and perk on your card. Gemini helps with weeknight dinners, too. I recently stared down a nearly empty fridge rushing out the door in the morning, and I texted Gemini with the new RCS integration 2 : “Add lasagna, strawberries, cucumbers, and vanilla ice cream to our Instacart order.” On the walk out, I saw an empty Cheerios box in the pantry, so I snapped a photo and sent a quick follow-up: “Add this too.” Gemini added it, and then handed me off to Instacart to complete the order. Groceries were on the doorstep when we got home. Done. Today, Gemini connects with more than 60 popular apps and, as a developer, you can apply to join our Connected Apps Platform . My wife and I also use Gemini to sort out medical bills, keep track of insurance renewals, and stay on top of our kids' schedules. Earlier this week, I forwarded a batch of school emails from Gmail to gemini@google.com. In less than a minute, every date was on my calendar with my wife invited. Better yet, it noticed a conflict during basketball practice and asked if I wanted to text one of the other parents to trade carpool duty. How we protect your data As Gemini becomes more capable, we continually advance our security defenses. When you assign Gemini a task, it uses Google Cloud’s Agent Compute Engine to work in a hardware-isolated virtual machine that’s dedicated to your account and never shared with other users. Each virtual machine is sandboxed, so Gemini works in a separate, isolated environment that’s regularly tested by our security red teams. This sandbox is just one of multiple layers of defense, including prompt-injection filters that scan search results, webpages, and more alongside Google Safe Browsing to limit which links Gemini can open. As Gemini works on a task, you can jump in to give it more instructions at any point, and it’s also designed to pause and check with you before critical steps. For example, Gemini is designed to ask for your confirmation or pre-approval before clicking "Buy," and will ask clarifying questions if an instruction is ambiguous.

title: DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency
Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say
abstract: Back to Articles Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say Team Article Published November 18, 2026 Upvote 6 Bruno Duarte brunoduarte01 Follow Dharma-AI Gabriel Pimenta de Freitas Cardoso GabrielPimenta99 Follow Dharma-AI Isis F Carvalho isisfc Follow Dharma-AI Breno de Almeida Beleza BrenoBeleza Follow Dharma-AI Felipe Lima limafelipe Follow Dharma-AI Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs. A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models . The full version will be on arXiv soon. GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move. Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon. We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors. The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs. The estimate everyone uses is compute-only For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time: T_theoretical = (6 · P · D) / (N_GPU · FLOPS_peak · MFU) Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance. This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O. These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart. To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range. What we built We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded. Two design choices shaped the work: Everything is known before dispatch. Every input comes from the submitted configuration: hyperparameters, dataset sizes, model identifiers, GPU allocation. No runtime logs, no partial progress. That is what makes the prediction usable for scheduling. Features that expose the overheads. On top of the raw configuration we derive quantities such as num_eval_data (samples processed across all evaluation cycles), num_saves and num_params_saved (checkpoint I/O), and per-GPU token volumes. The FLOP estimate itself, with MFU fixed at 0.45, goes in as one more feature ( baseline_time ), so the model starts from the compute-only number and learns the corrections. We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features. The data 272 SFT runs from the operational logs of a corporate production environment, covering several model families up to 15 billion parameters, both LoRA and full fine-tuning, and a wide range of dataset sizes and hyperparameters. Shared infrastructure. Jobs ran on 1, 2 or 4 GPUs drawn from a pool of 8 to 32 H200s across 1 to 4 nodes, alongside other training and inference workloads. The measured times include real contention. Durations from 1.6 to 172.4 hours , with a mean of 23.43 h and a median of 15.29 h. Stack: Hugging Face Transformers and Unsloth. We model the stack as a categorical feature and make no assumption about a fixed speedup between the two. Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h. Results All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting. Model R² RMSE (h) MAE (h) FLOP baseline (MFU 30%) 0.31 20.45 12.41 FLOP baseline (MFU 45%) 0.18 22.38 13.01 FLOP baseline (MFU 60%) 0.01 24.56 14.62 Calculon −0.51 30.40 20.36 Linear Regression 0.69 ± 0.14 13.52 ± 4.23 7.52 ± 0.49 Ridge 0.73 ± 0.09 12.72 ± 3.70 7.23 ± 0.68 XGBoost 0.97 ± 0.01 4.18 ± 1.17 1.95 ± 0.32 CatBoost 0.98 ± 0.01 3.52 ± 0.78 1.71 ± 0.33 A few things stand out. No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average. A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It shows how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step. Linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model. Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board. What the predictor relies on CatBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data , the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params , batch_eval_size_percent , num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent , with num_params_saved close behind.

title: Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases
abstract: Back to Articles Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases Enterprise Article Published November 18, 2026 Upvote 18 +12 Nicholas Fuller nfuller Follow ibm-research Sean Falconer thefalc Follow ibm-research Ayhan Sebin ayhansebin Follow ibm-research Pankaj Dayama pankajdayama Follow ibm-research Roman Vaculin vaculin Follow ibm-research Bilge Zeren Aksu bzeren Follow ibm-research Julian Payne Pyjamacardinal Follow ibm-research Mountu Jinwala mjinwala Follow ibm-research Wesley M. Gifford wmgifford Follow ibm-research Chandra Reddy creddyhf Follow ibm-research Vijay Ekambaram vijaye12 Follow ibm-research Arindam Jati ajati Follow ibm-research Robert Metzger rmetzger0 Follow ibm-research Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs. Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next. The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome. IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action. Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic. Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy ( documentation ). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.( documentation ). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs. The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made. See how time series and real-time context come together to create value: Streamhouse: real-time data and intelligence for agentic era Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening. A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state. Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere. Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate. Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them. This approach can help teams in four ways: - Scale model development . A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one. - Refresh predictions as data changes . Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration. - Put signals closer to decisions . Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment. - Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment. Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent Mission-critical use cases across real-enterprises The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic. Use Case 1 | Production optimization: every tub in spec An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result. To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range. When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails. The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills. Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment. Use Case 2 | Anomaly detection: from a flag to the right action A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus. AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store. When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock.

title: 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers
abstract:
Back to Articles 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers Published November 18, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 5 Tarek Ziadé tarekziade Follow Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation. I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally.
At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound
of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory. Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a
dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two
terabytes of disk. I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen
sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop
tower is not for me. My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use
it from my laptop through pi . That model does the coding tasks, an online
model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for
auto-completion in Neovim. When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next . What is Strata? Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts
stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE
model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less
memory. Like my RTX 4090! It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing
exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp , at
13.5 tok/s. That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to
scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and
could run at a decent speed. How do other engines offload? Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts
live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token? llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the
CPU ( --cpu-moe , --n-cpu-moe N , -ot "exps=CPU" , or --fit on to pick for
you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations
cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they
don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache ( --moe-cache-mib ) just
landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses
~10% even when everything fits. vLLM 's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels
read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts,
but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and
there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers,
read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big
batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU. Transformers offloads through Accelerate ( device_map="auto" , offload_folder ), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU
before forward . For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so
every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them.
No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory,
so "offload to CPU" frees nothing. I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM,
and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags: Engine Decode (tok/s) Strata, Q8_0 82 - 88 llama.cpp, Q8_0, --fit on 63 - 64 llama.cpp, BF16, --fit on 35 - 36 vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 --cpu-offload-params experts 20.1 vLLM, FP8, same flags, --enforce-eager 14.7 vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 9.7 vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 --cpu-offload-params experts 7.3 vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 3.3 Transformers + Accelerate 0.16 Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half
the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload
backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s. If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to
stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the
SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert
kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do
it out of the box. Making Qwen3.8-Flash-Next work on my 32 GB Mac with Transformers Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going
to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to
try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as
the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work. All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific
package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the
profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming . Start small I started with OLMoE-1B-7B , which fits in memory, so I could compare every token
with vanilla Transformers. First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop
running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1
tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm , which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel. The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot
pool : one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer
table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the
pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No
custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for
vanilla. experts_offload I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained , in huggingface/transformers#50717 .
To try it, install Transformers from that PR: pip install "git+https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.git@refs/pull/50717/head" Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: path = snapshot_download( "tarekziade/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-expert-streaming" ) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( f" {path} /dense" , dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map={ "" : "mps" , "experts.*" : "disk" }, quantization_config=MetalConfig(bits= 8 ), experts_offload={ "cache_bytes" : 12 << 30 , "quantized_experts" : f" {path} /experts-q3" , },
) That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script :
the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table. Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's
offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded
implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per
expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to
guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are
smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout. The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go
through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than
their own option. Running 121 GB of experts on a 32 GB Mac Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8.
Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding
table that needs its own disk path. So: experts quantized to 3 bits: 49 GB on disk, 12 GiB cached on the device dense layers in 8 bits (~5.4 GB, +0.2% perplexity vs BF16) the n-gram table stays on disk, rows read when needed The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt
peaks at 25.4 GiB.

title: Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages
abstract:
Back to Articles Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages Published November 18, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 10 +4 Reson8 reson8-thomas Follow Reson8 Mark 't Hart MarktHart Follow Reson8 Eustache Le Bihan eustlb Follow Eric Bezzam bezzam Follow Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size. Runs anywhere : native support in 🤗 Transformers and vLLM, no custom code 40+ languages : automatic language detection Output control : numbers as digits or words, fillers, verbatim repeats, forced language Extremely fast : an hour of audio in about half a second, with over 7,000 RTFx on full batches Holds up on real phone calls : on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) on a 302-hour call-centre benchmark Quickstart Transcribe with 🤗 Transformers uv pip install torch transformers accelerate from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM model_id = "Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map= "auto" ) inputs = processor.apply_transcription_request( audio= "https://hf.co/datasets/hf-internal-testing/dummy-audio-samples/resolve/main/bcn_weather.mp3" , language= "English" , # omit to detect automatically ).to(model.device, dtype=model.dtype) output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 512 )
generated = output[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ]:] print (processor.decode(generated, return_format= "transcription_only" )[ 0 ]) # return_format="parsed" if detecting language audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these. How it's built Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code . To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip. On-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities. On-policy distillation with GOLD Results Accuracy for its size On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER . The best score for its size Speed Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx . That's an hour of audio in about half a second. Real phone calls Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER , on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better. Real phone calls, 14 English accents Try it The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash . It's also available through our API . We're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version.

title: New LoRA Adapter Lifts Qwen3.8 Coding Success From 39% to 65%
abstract: Hugging Face’s harness-hub team has released Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted , a LoRA adapter for Qwen3.8-27B . It was trained with reinforcement learning to work inside the pi coding agent . The Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted LoRA adapter targets one harness instead of general chat. For developers running local coding agents, that is the point. You keep the open base model and swap in a small, harness-specific adapter. Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted is a PEFT LoRA adapter that turns Qwen3.8-27B into a model tuned for pi. pi is an MIT-licensed agent toolkit with a coding agent CLI. The adapter is released under Apache-2.0 . It applies to the q, k, v, o, gate, up and down projections. It only works on Qwen3.8-27B. The base model is a dense hybrid . It alternates Gated DeltaNet linear-attention blocks with Gated Attention blocks across 64 layers. The method comes from Hugging Face’s harness adapters post from November 6. The idea is 1 LoRA adapter per model and harness. Training runs inside the unmodified harness on verifiable tasks. For this checkpoint, the model card lists these details: Every tool call passes through safeagents , a rule-based proxy. It blocks calls such as fetching benchmark answers from the Hub. Blocked rollouts score 0, so RL pushes the model away from reward hacking. All numbers below are self-reported. They use the pi harness, 1 attempt per task. The adapter solved 15 new SWE-bench Pro tasks and lost 2. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, it gained 16 and lost 2. Efficiency is the larger story. On tasks both models solved, median turns fell from 59 to 23 on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, they fell from 18 to 8. The adapter also generates about 4.5x fewer tokens than the base model with thinking. With thinking on, the base model already scores 64.7% on SWE-bench Pro and 54.2% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. So the adapter matches thinking-level accuracy without paying for long reasoning traces. With thinking on, the adapter reaches 66.7% and 56.6%. OpenCode adapter numbers use a different harness and are not directly comparable. The model card gives 4 routes: Because adapters share 1 base model, a single server can host pi and OpenCode adapters side by side. title: SID AI Releases SID-2 Agentic Search Model With 0.720 NDCG Swarm Mode
abstract: SID AI has released SID-2 , its second-generation agentic search model, alongside SID-2 Swarm. SID-2 is an agentic search model from SID AI that searches your data, reads results and returns ranked document IDs. It replaces fixed RAG pipelines with a model that decides what to search next. SID-2 is a small search specialist, not a general chat model. A static pipeline runs rewrite, embed, search and rerank in a fixed order. SID-2 instead searches, reads results, adapts and searches again . Developers implement the search tools against their own backend. A text_search tool covers keyword search and a search tool covers vector search. The model ends each episode by calling report_helpful_ids with a ranked list. No reindexing or data movement is required , since SID-2 only sees what your tools return. SID-2 Swarm runs several agents that message each other and fork their context into new agents. Each agent explores a separate slice of the corpus. SID argues search gains more from reading more documents than from reasoning harder about each one. SID-2 offers low, medium and high reasoning effort. Each level was trained as a separate expert, then merged with multi-teacher on-policy distillation. Metric Steering lets users target NDCG, F1 or Recall@k, with k from 1 to 50. On SID’s 506-question validation set, SID-2 at high effort scores 0.14 to 0.22 higher per metric than the base model. Training used 2-stage reinforcement learning. Stage 1 optimizes retrieval quality only. Stage 2 adds a multiplicative latency penalty that applies only to positive rewards. A proposer-solver self-play loop generated hard queries against a frozen SID-1 solver. SID reports a 6x training-throughput gain over SLIME’s default setup. SID built a 506-question benchmark across 19 corpora. These include HotpotQA, Enron emails, SEC filings, PubMed and BrowseComp-Plus. All numbers below are self-reported from Tables 2 to 4 of the report . Swarm leads on 11 of 19 corpora. On WixQA, a single high-effort agent matches Astra at about 232x lower cost. At its lowest effort, SID-2 beats 4 parallel SID-1 runs with 13x fewer FLOPs. NDCG, time and cost rows are measured by SID on its own benchmark. Retrieval backend time is excluded. SID-2 is available through SID’s API and on Baseten . SDKs exist for Python ( sid-sdk ), TypeScript ( @sid-ai/sid-sdk ) and Go ( github.com/sidhq/sid-go ). A SageMaker helper covers AWS deployments. The reference implementation uses the OpenAI client format. SID-2 costs $0.25 per million input tokens and $1.00 per million output tokens . Swarm costs $0.50 and $2.00. Cached input is 10% of the input price. Check out the SID-2 technical report , the docs and the model page . title: Anthropic Adds Code Mode to Claude Code: Claude Now Chains Tool Calls in JavaScript
abstract: Anthropic has added Code Mode to Claude Code as an experimental, opt-in feature. Claude Code Code Mode is a mode in which Claude writes JavaScript that makes several tool calls in 1 step. It shipped in Claude Code v2.1.323 last week . For developers, it changes how the agent spends round-trips on multi-step work. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Without Code Mode, Claude requests each Bash, Read or Edit call directly. It reads every result before choosing the next step. With Code Mode, Claude writes a piece of JavaScript, and Claude Code runs it in your session. According to the docs , one piece of code can run commands in parallel. It can feed one result into the next call. It can also return only the output Claude needs to read. Anthropic’s example raises a retry limit. The code finds the file, edits it and runs the tests: In the conversation, you see the tool calls, such as the diff. You do not see the code by default. Press Ctrl+O to open the transcript viewer and expand a collapsed Code row. Set CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 in your shell, or in the env block of ~/.claude/settings.json . Before the first session, Claude Code asks you to confirm. Select “Yes, turn on Code Mode”. Claude Code then restarts and shows ‘Code Mode (experimental) is on’. A Code Mode session resumes only with the variable still set to 1. Setting 0 anywhere turns it off, even if 1 is set elsewhere. Admins can block it org-wide with a 0 in managed settings . They cannot force it on. Anthropic recommends it for tasks with many related tool calls: Each tool call inside the code still passes your deny and ask rules. It also passes PreToolUse hooks under the tool’s usual name, such as Bash. Review differs by permission mode: Hook authors should check each part of a command. A git push can arrive as cd 'app' && git push . To inspect the code itself, match the REPL tool and read tool_input.code . If Claude waits, the code stops after 10 minutes, including time at permission prompts. In the background, it can run for up to 2 hours while you keep chatting. Background runs need a session started in auto or bypassPermissions mode. Cloudflare coined ‘Code Mode’ on September 26, 2025 . Its Agents SDK turns MCP schemas into a TypeScript API that runs in V8 isolates. Anthropic then published code execution with MCP . In one example, token use fell from 150,000 to 2,000, a 98.7% saving. Its API feature, Programmatic Tool Calling , uses Python. It cut average usage from 43,588 to 27,297 tokens on complex research tasks. Claude Code’s version applies the pattern to the CLI’s own tools. The docs give no token figure. One independent test reported system-tool context of 11.1k tokens with Code Mode versus 24.6k without. Treat that as a single third-party measurement. title: Perplexity Computer Adds Multiagent: Up to 16 AI Agents That Cross-Check Work
abstract: Perplexity has added Multiagent to Computer , its agent platform for research and multistep work. Perplexity Computer Multiagent is a new effort level that sits above Ultra. A lead agent runs a team of agents on different frontier models. Those agents work in parallel, share findings directly and check each other’s work. For developers and analysts, the change is structural. Supporting agents no longer report only to a single lead. Multiagent is the highest effort level in Perplexity Computer. It coordinates AI models to analyze complex tasks and cross-check their work, per Perplexity’s announcement . It builds on effort controls launched on September 17, 2026 . That release added 4 settings: Light, Standard, High and Ultra. Each setting picks the orchestrator model and its reasoning depth. Lower settings use less expensive models. The lead agent plans the task and assigns parts to supporting agents. It can assign up to 16 agents and also does part of the work itself. In Perplexity’s example, Claude Fable 5.2 plans the task. It splits work among agents running Claude Opus 5.5, GPT 6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Carbon. Those 3 models form the default team. Fable 5.2 and GPT 6 Astra join as supporting agents only when requested or needed. Key mechanics from the launch post : Perplexity now offers 3 ways to put several models on 1 problem: Perplexity positions Multiagent for large, interconnected work that can run in parallel. Its examples include deal data room diligence, multi-scenario forecasts, annual report review, competing-hypothesis research and year-end tax preparation. The clearest difference is model diversity. Perplexity mixes Anthropic, OpenAI and Google models in 1 team. Kimi and Grok run their own model families. Kimi trades depth of debate for scale, with up to 300 sub-agents. Multiagent is available to all Perplexity Max subscribers. It runs on the web only. Users select Multiagent in Computer’s effort slider when starting a new task. Perplexity’s pricing page lists Max at $167 per month billed annually. Max includes 10,000 Computer credits per month. The launch post does not state credit cost per Multiagent task. title: OpenAI Releases GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol With a 20% Cheaper Astra API
abstract: OpenAI has released GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol , twp closed models aimed at professional and agentic work. The GPT-6.2 Astra model is the new frontier tier for hard, long-horizon tasks. GPT-6.2 Sol is the efficient everyday tier. For developers, the key point is cost per task. Astra’s token prices fall 20%, and OpenAI says both models finish tasks with fewer output tokens. Both are live in the OpenAI API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol . GPT-6.2 Astra is OpenAI’s frontier reasoning model for complex professional work. It succeeds GPT-6 Astra. OpenAI says it produces cleaner slides, spreadsheets and documents that follow templates and field conventions. It also builds better frontends, games and 3D scenes. GPT-6.2 Sol replaces GPT-6.1 Sol as the everyday model. Both accept text and image input and return text. Both share the same context limits . The split is cost and depth. Neither model accepts reasoning effort none . OpenAI recommends keeping prompt prefixes unchanged and appending new instructions. That improves cache reuse and preserves reasoning across turns. OpenAI’s own claims focus on cost-adjusted gains: Independent results from Artificial Analysis mostly hold up. Astra scores 62 at max effort, with a $4.00 cost per Intelligence Index task. Fable 5.2 scores 65, Gemini 4 Carbon 60, Claude Opus 5.5 59 and Sol 57 . Sol matches GPT-6 Astra’s score at about 15% of its cost per task. On Harvey LAB-AA , Astra passes 15.0% of legal assignments. The Astra for Law configuration passes 20.8%. Epoch’s Capabilities Index puts Astra at 174, tied with Fable 5.2. Astra’s input and output prices are 20% below GPT-6 Astra. Cached input is 60% cheaper. Sol keeps GPT-6.1 Sol’s rates. Requests over 272K input tokens double input and cache rates, and output costs 1.5x. Batch is 50% of standard. Ultrafast is 3x standard through February 28, 2027, then 6x. Index, AA-3D and robotics figures for competitors come from Artificial Analysis as reported by The Decoder . Astra is also OpenAI’s first released model to meet the High threshold for AI self-improvement. Check out the OpenAI announcement , the GPT-6.2 Astra model page and the GPT-6.2 Sol model page . title: Clearing Up the Confusion on AI Data Retention: Two Standard Designs Explained
abstract: Data retention has become one of the most misunderstood terms in AI infrastructure. After a wave of AI security headlines, many dev teams now ask a simple question. Does my AI provider keep my data? The honest answer depends on how you send it. Send a prompt to an inference API, and it is processed and returned without being kept. That design is called zero data retention (ZDR). Upload a dataset for a batch job, and it stays stored until you delete it. Both are standard designs, and in both the customer is in control. What changes is who manages the data lifecycle, and where. Fireworks AI cofounder and CEO Lin Qiao set out a clear way to think about this. In a November 13, 2026 post on X , she described two standard API designs. Each one decides where control of the data lifecycle sits. The same split has shaped data processing systems for decades. In this article, we will go through that framework with examples from public API documentation. An AI data retention policy defines what a platform stores from your requests, and for how long. OpenAI’s data controls describe two layers. Application state is data a feature must keep, such as uploaded files. Abuse-monitoring logs are copies held for safety review. A platform can be at zero on one layer and not the other. AI inference and training APIs follow two lifecycle designs. The difference is who manages the data, and where. You create a file or dataset, run jobs against it, then delete it. The platform keeps the data stored and available until you ask for deletion. It cannot know when you are finished unless you define it. So deletion is your job, done through the platform’s APIs. Batch APIs with uploaded datasets are the standard example: Once you delete the data, it is gone. According to Fireworks CEO, it keeps nothing after a deletion request . OpenAI non-batch files persist until you delete them. Fireworks AI managed training datasets have no time limit, and the customer deletes them. Amazon Bedrock and Google batch jobs read and write your own cloud storage. OpenAI batch files last 30 days by default, and Anthropic batch data 29 days. Treat expiry as the exception, and confirm it per feature. You send data, the platform computes, and the result comes back. No application state stays behind. Your application owns the conversation history, so no platform cleanup step is needed. This is the pattern ZDR applies to. A synchronous response alone does not establish ZDR. Think of saving a spreadsheet to a cloud drive versus passing its numbers to a calculator. The drive keeps the file for later. The calculator computes the answer, returns it and keeps nothing. In both designs, customers fully control how their data is handled. What differs is where the lifecycle is managed. In pattern 1, it is explicit dataset creation and deletion. In pattern 2, it lives entirely in your application. The answer is No. ZDR is scoped per endpoint, and defaults differ by platform. OpenAI keeps abuse-monitoring logs for up to 30 days by default. The Amazon Bedrock none mode writes no request or response data to durable storage. Fireworks AI documents ZDR by default for open models. Its ephemeral inference APIs, Training SDK and Nexus carry ZDR guarantees. Prompts and generations are not persisted at rest. For the Batch API , Fireworks document states that no data is retained after deletion . A single parameter can also flip the pattern. On Google’s Interactions API , store defaults to true. At OpenAI , setting store to false is not ZDR, which needs approval. Documentation checked November 15, 2026. Policies change, so confirm against the linked pages. OpenAI and AWS note that content flagged as CSAM can be retained even under zero retention. Every retained copy must be protected, tracked and eventually deleted. Data that never reaches disk cannot be taken from disk later. Regulation points the same way, with one important thing to note. Under GDPR Article 5 , ephemeral processing supports storage limitation. Data minimisation still depends on what your application sends. “Ephemeral processing is preferable whenever the workflow allows it.” Lin Qiao, cofounder and CEO, Fireworks AI ( post on X ) The reasoning is about human error. Ephemeral processing leaves no forgotten datasets and no missed delete calls. It also means fewer retained copies to protect and eventually delete. Stored features still have a place: dataset-based fine-tuning needs data at rest. Further reading: Lin Qiao Post , OpenAI data controls , Amazon Bedrock data retention , Google zero data retention , Anthropic API data retention and Fireworks AI zero data retention . Thanks to the Fireworks team for the thought leadership / resources for this article. This article is sponsored. title: NVIDIA Open-Sources NVKE and NVKR for Managed Kubernetes on GPU Infrastructure
abstract: NVIDIA has released 2 open-source projects for running managed Kubernetes on GPU infrastructure: NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE) and NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR) . Both were recently announced as components of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform . NVKE is the control plane for a managed Kubernetes service. NVKR builds the OS images, container images and packages those clusters depend on. Both ship under Apache 2.0 and are in public preview. NVKE is open-source software that an AI factory installs to run a managed Kubernetes service on its own NVIDIA GPU infrastructure . The repo calls it ‘a self-hosting factory for Kubernetes clusters,’ not a distribution. It exposes a REST API and controllers on a management cluster. Customers get standard clusters and use kubectl . The operator manages them through the NVKE API or the nvkectl CLI. NVKE uses upstream Kubernetes, kubeadm and Cluster API . It is written in Go and has no runtime dependency on NVKR. NVKR is a build system with declarative Definitions . It produces executables, container images, Helm charts and node images for amd64 and arm64. ‘Recipes’ define validated combinations of software versions and GPU generations. Hosted workflows attach signatures, SBOMs and provenance to digest-pinned OCI references. NVKR can also build artifacts for other Kubernetes management systems. The NVIDIA technical blog walkthrough describes 5 stages: A node must present an attested SPIFFE identity before it gets join credentials. The README says SPIRE uses TPM for this. Per-cluster etcd encryption is available. An OpenTelemetry-based Helm chart exports logs, metrics and traces over OTLP. Inside workload clusters, 3 companion projects plug in: AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) for the GPU runtime, NodeWright for node packages and NVSentinel for break-fix automation. NVIDIA Cloud Partners Firmus and SK Telecom are integrating both projects into AI factories. Mirantis, Rafay, Spectro Cloud, OpenNebula Systems and vCluster are adding components to managed Kubernetes offerings. Netris is enabling NVKE for its network automation. A local quickstart runs on 1 Linux host or VM, amd64 or arm64. It needs at least 6 CPUs, 12 GiB free memory, 100 GiB free disk, Docker and virtual TPM support. No GPU or NVIDIA account is required. A real install needs a NICo deployment with enrolled capacity, a build host with KVM, an HTTP server and a registry. NVKR has no qualified Release yet . title: Sarvam Launches Sarvam Token Factory: Bringing India-Hosted Inference to 8 Open Models
abstract: Sarvam has opened Sarvam Token Factory to everyone. Sarvam Token Factory is an inference platform from Sarvam that serves its own models and open-weight models from GPU clusters in India. Developers reach every model through one OpenAI-compatible API . For India-based teams, this means low-latency tokens without sending traffic to overseas clouds. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . It is a managed inference stack, not a single model. Sarvam first previewed it as Sarvam Inference at its Epoch event. The launch post lists 8 models: Sarvam 105B, GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1 Pro and Gemma 4 31B. The docs split them into 2 groups. Pay-as-you-go models run on shared endpoints. DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3.1 Pro, Qwen 3.8 27B, Clef and EmbeddingGemma 2 need Provisioned Throughput, enabled per organisation. The stack has 3 layers around a shared cache: It builds on vLLM, SGLang, Dynamo, Mooncake, NIXL, DeepEP, DeepGEMM and FlashInfer. An orchestrator agent proposes experiments, and an engineer approves each deployment. Caching drives most of the gains. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash serves 450B+ tokens per day, with 95.7% of prompt tokens served from cache. On GLM 5.3, the planner cut prefill GPU-hours from 32.3 to 17.1 under the same replayed load. For Sarvam 105B, MXFP8 weights plus speculative decoding raised output throughput about 2.2x. That cut each replica from 2 B200s to 1. Sarvam says none of these changes reduced accuracy. All numbers below come from Sarvam’s launch post . They are self-reported. The results are not a clean sweep. On DeepSeek V4.1 Flash with a 10K prompt, Together posts 0.71 s first token vs Sarvam’s 0.90 s. Together also streams faster, at 278 tokens/s vs 130 on Sarvam Standard. Prices are in Indian rupees per 1M tokens, per the docs : Introductory pricing runs through the end of 2026. A faster DeepSeek Interactive endpoint costs ₹25 input and ₹105 output. Provisioned model rates are not published on the docs page. Check out the technical blog , the API docs and the launch post on X . title: Liquid AI Releases d1.2 and d1.2-ultra: Omnimodal Decision Models That Top the AA Decision Index
abstract: Liquid AI just released d1.2 and d1.2-ultra . A decision model does not write text. It returns calibrated probabilities over a fixed set of answers. The Liquid AI d1.2 decision model family now accepts text, images and audio. It also adds 5 new answer types. d1.2-ultra scores 75 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1 , the top score among decision models on the index. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . d1.2 is a hosted decision model from Liquid AI that answers typed questions about text, images or audio in 1 call. It returns a probability per option and generates zero output tokens , so only input is billed. d1.2-ultra targets harder decisions. d1.2 is faster and costs less than half as much. The model IDs are d1.2 (default) and d1.2-ultra . Earlier d1 , d1.1 and d1-ultra are now deprecated and do not support audio or the new tasks. d1.2 adds 5 typed answers on the same endpoint and request format: Audio can be the subject of a question, such as which language is spoken or whether a siren is audible. The question can also be spoken. The API takes 16-bit PCM WAV and counts 10 tokens per second of audio. On held-out ESC-50 and FLEURS (43 languages) recordings, both models answer 95% to 97% of questions correctly. The index combines 6 evaluations. AA-Paperclip carries 30% of the weight. EvalSafe-O*NET-AA, AA-Omniscience-Decision v1.1, HLE-MultiChoice v1.1 and AA-Symmetry v1.1 carry 15% each. When2Call carries 10%. Its Decision Score penalizes confident wrong answers. On the AA chart shared by Liquid AI, d1.2-ultra scores 75. Drex Max v1.1, SubQ Snap 1.2 and GLiDE v1.2 follow at 73. d1.2 scores 69. That is 2 points below the deprecated d1-ultra at 71. Liquid AI argues no model scores higher than d1.2 for less money. A calibrated model that says 80% is right about 80% of the time, so teams can route low-confidence cases to humans. Across 13 benchmarks and 22,505 questions, Liquid AI reports these calibration errors: Note: These figures come from Liquid AI’s own test. Liquid AI used held-out splits of public datasets; no public benchmark exists yet. d1.2 beats d1.2-ultra on multi-label picks, 90% to 87%. Pricing is $0.02 per 1M input tokens for d1.2 and $0.042 for d1.2-ultra . New organizations get $2 in free credit on Liquid Console . Images cost 1.5 tokens per 32×32 patch, so a 1024×1024 image is 1,536 tokens. Shared state and media are billed once; each extra question adds only its own tokens. The endpoint is https://api.liquid.ai/decisions/v1/systemone . Check out the launch blog , the d1 API docs and the AA Decision Index .
