title: Introducing Gemini Decision 1: A Model That Picks Answers Instead of Writing Them
abstract: Introducing Gemini Decision 1: A Model That Picks Answers Instead of Writing Them Google's newest model has one job, and it never writes a word doing it. Decision 1 reads text, images, video, audio and PDFs in a single forward pass, up to 262,144 input tokens per request. By Shittu Olumide , Technical Content Specialist on November 18, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence Google's newest model has one job, and it never writes a word doing it. Gemini Decision 1 , launched last week with the new Gemini Decisions API , takes an input and a list of closed questions and returns probabilities instead of prose: yes or no, option A, B or C, a score on a rubric. That sounds small, but it isn't. Every agent stack runs on dozens of these quiet calls: which model gets this query, which tool fires, whether this message breaks a policy. Most teams handle them with a full generative model and a JSON parser, paying for output tokens they throw away. Google now sells that layer on its own, at \$0.10 per million input tokens and nothing for output. What Gemini Decision 1 Does Decision 1 reads text, images, video, audio and PDFs in a single forward pass, up to 262,144 input tokens per request. Against that one input, you can ask up to 1,000 independent questions of three kinds: Yes/no ( noul in the API) returns a probability between 0.01 and 0.99 Choice picks from 2 to 255 options and returns a probability for each Score grades against an ordered rubric and returns a weighted score plus a probability per level Every answer carries a confidence value, so your code can send uncertain cases to a fallback or a person. The pricing is the pitch. You pay \$0.10 per million input tokens , the shared input is billed once no matter how many questions you ask, and output costs nothing because there is none. A no-cost tier in Google AI Studio covers prototyping. The capability table shows what this model is not. Text generation, thinking, function calling, structured outputs, batch and caching are all listed as unsupported. It's a scoring engine, not a chatbot. What Happened When We Ran It? We installed Google's google-genai SDK, created a free API key in AI Studio and ran three tests: Google's quickstart, Google's image example from the launch post , and an ambiguous support message of our own. Latency was timed from our machine, so it includes the network round trip. The quickstart asks two questions about one customer message: from google import genai client = genai.Client(http_options={"api_version": "v1beta"}) result = client.decisions.create( model="gemini-decision-1", input="The blue mug I ordered on Monday arrived cracked on Wednesday.", questions={ "is_damaged": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Did the item arrive damaged?"}, "queue": { "type": "choice", "instructions": "Which support queue should handle this message?", "criteria": { "billing": "Payment, invoice, or refund questions.", "replacements": "Damaged, missing, or wrong items.", "general": "Product questions and account updates.", }, }, }, ) print(result.answers["queue"].choice, result.answers["queue"].confidence) For the image test, input becomes a list holding an image URL and a text note. Here's what came back: Test Input Answer Median latency Input tokens Quickstart "Mug arrived cracked" Damaged: 0.99. Queue: replacements (0.98) 407 ms 173 Ambiguous "Charged twice, handle chipped" Damaged: 0.99. Queue: replacements 0.50, billing 0.48 574 ms 181 Image + text Breakroom counter photo Spill: 0.95. Action: wipe with cloth (0.98). Severity: 1.19 of 2 1,343 ms 1,326 Medians exclude each test's first call. Accuracy was clean: both of Google's examples came back right, and the image result matched Google's own screenshot . Every call billed zero output tokens. In dollars, the text query costs about \$0.000017 per call, roughly 58,000 calls for a dollar. The image query costs about \$0.00013 . Google Is Already Running on It Google says four of its own products use the Decisions API: Gemini Notebook routes each query to a model tier and thinking level, which Google says cuts latency on everyday queries by up to 40% Stitch uses it in its rapid canvas experiment to build playable wireframes and apply voice or tap edits CC from Google Labs picks an emoji reaction from more than 200 options without adding visible delay Google Search uses it as a safety layer that checks Model Context Protocol tools for adversarial behavior Our Take 1. The Confidence Score Is the Real Product Our ambiguous message is the test that matters. It fit two queues, and the model said so: 50.2% replacements, 48.4% billing, confidence 0.50. It didn't fake certainty on a coin flip, and in the same call it still rated the chipped handle as damage at 0.99. One example doesn't prove calibration, which is measured across thousands of cases. But it's the behavior Google is selling, and it showed up when we went looking for it. 2. Read Confidence, Not Just Choice Here's the trap. On that coin-flip message, the choice field still returned replacements , with no flag attached. Code that reads only the winner routes it as confidently as the clear case. The calibration is only worth something if you set a threshold on confidence and send everything below it elsewhere. Google's quickstart prints the winner. Your production code shouldn't stop there. 3. The Speed Claim Didn't Hold for Images Google quotes 150 to 250 ms end to end. After the first call, our text calls landed between 339 and 577 ms, a gap network distance can plausibly explain. Our image calls took 1.1 to 1.4 seconds, a median five to nine times the claim, though Google says its figures hold across multimodal inputs. Some of that may be Google fetching the image from a URL and processing 1,064 image tokens. We can't separate the causes from outside. Two more details: Google's latency figure covers contexts up to 16K tokens, not the full 256K, and identical calls in our runs varied by more than 300 ms. Benchmark it on your own media before it goes anywhere near a real-time path. 4. The Benchmarks Are Google's Own The "nearly 5x cheaper" figure compares Decision 1 with Google's own Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, on a benchmark suite Google chose . That's useful if you already run Gemini. It says nothing about how Decision 1 compares with a small fine-tuned classifier you already have. 5. Check the Small Print The model page pitches classification over live media streams, while the same page lists the Live API as unsupported. And the model is Gemini-only for now. It's on OpenRouter , LangChain , Vercel's AI SDK , LiteLLM and others, but Google Cloud support is still marked as coming soon . Wrapping Up Decision 1 does one narrow job well. It's cheap, it was accurate on everything we gave it, and it admitted doubt when we pushed it. Use it for routing and policy checks now. Wire your code to confidence from the first day, and time it on your own images before you promise anyone 200 ms. Resources Gemini Decision 1 model page Decisions API documentation Google's launch post Decisions API playground in AI Studio Pricing Shittu Olumide is a software engineer and technical writer passionate about leveraging cutting-edge technologies to craft compelling narratives, with a keen eye for detail and a knack for simplifying complex concepts. You can also find Shittu on Twitter . <= Previous post

title: Jagged Intelligence: Why AI Is Brilliant One Minute and Clueless the Next
abstract: Jagged Intelligence: Why AI Is Brilliant One Minute and Clueless the Next Why models ace Olympiad math and still fumble simple everyday tasks. By Nate Rosidi , KDnuggets Market Trends & SQL Content Specialist on November 18, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence AI systems from Google and OpenAI solved five of six problems at the International Mathematical Olympiad . Months later, chatbots told a user to walk his car to a repair shop 50 meters away. A person who can do the first would never make the second mistake, which is why the gap is so hard to anticipate. Researchers call this pattern jagged intelligence . It matters to anyone who evaluates models, builds AI features, or decides whether to trust an output, because one benchmark score or one impressive demo says little about the next task. What Jagged Intelligence Means Andrej Karpathy , an OpenAI co-founder and former head of AI at Tesla, coined the term in July 2024 . Models do some things extremely well and fail badly at others, and it is hard to tell in advance which is which. Human abilities tend to be correlated and improve together from childhood to adulthood. Someone who solves Olympiad problems will not be confused by a 50-meter walk. In models, capabilities often don't move together. People use one demonstrated skill to guess at others. A model that writes a working function looks like it can also count the words in a paragraph. That inference fails, which is why a demo predicts so little. Some researchers frame the pattern as many separate skills with no general intelligence behind them. Four Proposed Explanations for the Pattern None is settled, and they may overlap. Verifiable Rewards Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) became a major training stage in 2025. It works where answers are clearly right or wrong, such as math and code that passes tests. Karpathy argues that models spike near verifiable domains. Creative writing, philosophy, and parts of science have no automatic checker, so in this account progress is slower. Data Coverage The internet holds only a fraction of human knowledge and very little about the physical world. A model trained on digital patterns struggles with planning, new ideas, and unseen tasks. Pattern Replication The authors of Apple's GSM-Symbolic paper hypothesize that large language models (LLMs) replicate reasoning steps from training data instead of reasoning logically. A problem that matches a familiar template gets solved, and a small change to the template breaks the chain. Incoherent Concepts A separate "Potemkin understanding" paper from MIT, Harvard, and the University of Chicago traces failures to internally incoherent concept representations. A model can hold a correct definition and a faulty working version of the same concept, and nothing forces the two to agree. Verifiable rewards may explain why models excel at certain tasks, while the other three theories offer possible explanations for their weaknesses. For example, difficulties with clock-related tasks (e.g. reading the time from an analog clock image) might reflect gaps in training data. Failures caused by adding irrelevant information to a problem could suggest that models rely on familiar patterns rather than logical reasoning. And cases where a model correctly defines a concept but fails to apply it could indicate inconsistent internal representations. These connections are plausible, but none has been established as a direct causal explanation. Six Failures Documented by the Scientific Community We use "jagged" broadly here: unevenness across tasks, across difficulty levels, and between test conditions and real use. A Distractor Clause Breaks Grade-School Math In Apple's GSM-NoOp test , researchers added an irrelevant sentence to grade-school word problems, such as "five of the kiwis were smaller than average." Models subtracted those kiwis from the total. One extra clause that looked relevant cut performance by up to 65% across state-of-the-art models. A student would read the sentence and ignore it. Defining a Concept Versus Applying It GPT-4o correctly defined an ABAB rhyme scheme, then wrote a poem that used a word that didn't rhyme. The Potemkin study tested seven models on concepts from poetry, game theory, and psychology. Models defined the concepts correctly about 94% of the time and failed classification tasks on the same concepts about 55% of the time. If a model can recite a definition and still misapply it, a correct definition tells us little about understanding. Reading an Analog Clock On ClockBench (September 2025), humans read analog clocks with 89.1% accuracy. The best model then, Gemini 2.5 Pro, reached 13.3%. Reading a clock means finding the hands, judging their angles, and mapping them to numbers. When a model read the time correctly, follow-up arithmetic was fine, so perception failed and the math held. ClockBench is a single-author benchmark and has not been peer reviewed, so we read the numbers as indicative. Strong Medical Scores, Poor Results for Real Users In a Nature Medicine trial from Oxford , 1,298 participants tried to identify medical conditions. LLMs alone identified them in 94.9% of cases. People using the same LLMs identified them in at most 34.5% of cases, below the 47% of a control group that did its own research. On choosing the right next step, LLM users did no better than that control group. The valley here sits in the model and user together, and we count it because any product built on the model inherits it. A model's solo score and its value to a real user can sit this far apart, and standard benchmarks did not show it. Logic Puzzles and a Contested Result Apple's Illusion of Thinking study tested Tower of Hanoi, River Crossing, and Blocks World at rising difficulty. Standard models beat reasoning models on easy puzzles, reasoning models won at medium difficulty, and both collapsed on hard ones, even when given the solution algorithm. Which model was better changed with difficulty, so the unevenness showed up inside a single task family. A rebuttal argued that part of the collapse comes from the test setup, so we treat this result as open. A New Benchmark Version Drops Scores Below 1% ARC-AGI-3 is a benchmark launched on March 25, 2026, designed to evaluate how well artificial intelligence can learn, reason, and adapt to completely unfamiliar situations, rather than simply answer questions based on previously learned patterns. Every frontier model scored below 1%, while humans solved all of its environments. Gemini 3.1 Pro had already reached 77.1% on ARC-AGI-2, so a high score on one version did not carry over to the next. The new version also switched to interactive environments, so the drop mixes format and difficulty. Scores are moving quickly, so check the current leaderboard before quoting a number. Why One Benchmark Score Misleads Karpathy has said he lost trust in benchmarks in 2025. Benchmarks are verifiable environments by construction, which is where RLVR works, so labs can train directly on tasks like them. The score can rise without general ability rising with it. Benchmarks also assume that a few correct answers signal understanding, because human errors follow predictable patterns. A student who defines an ABAB rhyme scheme correctly will almost always apply it correctly, so an exam can sample a few questions and infer the rest. The Potemkin authors argue that a model's misunderstandings don't follow those patterns, so it can pass the test without understanding the concept. Benchmarks such as GSM8K are vulnerable to contamination and don't measure sensitivity to small changes in wording. In the Oxford study , neither standard medical benchmarks nor simulated patients predicted what happened with real users. The authors recommend systematic human user testing before deployment.

title: AI and Data Science Salaries in 2026: What Practitioners Are Actually Earning
abstract: AI and Data Science Salaries in 2026: What Practitioners Are Actually Earning A data-backed breakdown of compensation across roles, experience levels, industries, and geographies, so you know where you stand and where the premium opportunities are. By Vinod Chugani on November 18, 2026 in Career Advice Data science remains one of the best-compensated fields in tech, and 2026 has brought both clarity and complexity to compensation conversations. Salaries vary so dramatically across sources, roles, and regions that a single headline number like "data scientists earn \$125K" can either discourage practitioners earning far more or mislead those just starting out. The honest picture is more nuanced. A junior analyst in a mid-market city earns something entirely different from a senior machine learning engineer at a frontier AI lab. A generative AI (GenAI) specialist commands a premium that simply didn't exist three years ago. Remote work has reshuffled the geographic salary map in ways that still aren't settled. This guide draws on data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), Levels.fyi , Glassdoor , Indeed , Built In , and job-posting analyses. The goal: give practitioners at every stage an accurate, role-specific picture of what the market is paying in 2026, whether you're evaluating an offer, preparing for a negotiation, or planning your next move. Understanding the Data Science Salary Range Before getting into specific figures, it helps to understand why salary sources often seem to contradict each other. Platforms differ in who they survey, whether they capture base pay only or total compensation (including bonuses and equity), and whether their data skews toward self-reported tech-hub salaries or broader national samples. With that in mind, here's where the major sources land for data scientists in the United States in 2026: BLS (national median): \$112,590–\$120,230 Indeed (average base salary): \$130,239 Glassdoor (average total pay): approximately \$156,000 Levels.fyi (median total compensation): \$185,000 The spread reflects the difference between all data scientists nationally versus those at companies that participate in high-transparency compensation platforms. For practitioners at established tech companies or in finance, Levels.fyi figures are more representative. For those in healthcare, government, or smaller organizations, BLS and Indeed provide a more grounded baseline. A useful working range for most practitioners: \$120,000–\$160,000 in base salary , with total compensation reaching well above that at larger companies. Salary by Experience Level Experience is the single largest predictor of compensation in data science. The market has matured enough that the gap between entry-level and senior roles is now substantial and well-documented. Entry Level (0–2 Years) Base salaries typically run from \$84,000 to \$105,000. At big tech companies, entry-level total compensation can already clear \$130,000 once equity is included. The entry-level market is also more competitive than it was in 2021–2022, with more candidates chasing each opening. Early Career (2–5 Years) This is where practitioners see the most significant jumps. Base salaries move into the \$100,000–\$135,000 range. Those who've built expertise in production machine learning or GenAI implementation can reach the upper end quickly. Mid-Level (5–8 Years) Experienced practitioners with a track record of shipping models and influencing business decisions earn \$130,000–\$160,000 in base salary. At large tech companies, total compensation at this level often exceeds \$200,000. Senior and Staff (8–12 Years) Senior data scientists and staff-level practitioners at well-funded organizations earn \$160,000–\$230,000 in base pay. Senior machine learning engineers at FAANG companies regularly see total compensation of \$300,000–\$400,000 when stock vesting is factored in. Principal, Director, and VP (15+ Years) Directors of data science earn \$180,000–\$250,000+ in base salary, with total compensation at top-tier companies ranging from \$350,000 to \$500,000+. Quantitative finance roles at hedge funds can exceed \$400,000 in total compensation at this level. Salary by Role: The AI Premium Is Real The data science job family has expanded significantly. In 2026, practitioners aren't all competing in the same compensation band. Your specific role and skill set determine which band you're in. Data Analyst The most accessible entry point into the data field. Average base salary runs \$84,000–\$112,000, with tech-sector analysts reaching the upper range. Adding Python to a SQL and business intelligence foundation adds meaningful compensation lift. Data Scientist The broadest category. Base salaries average \$120,000–\$130,000 nationally, with significant upside based on industry and company type. Data Engineer Data engineers earn slightly more than generalist data scientists on average, around \$136,000 in base salary. That reflects demand for the people who build the pipelines data scientists depend on. Machine Learning Engineer One of the highest-paying roles in the data field. Base salary ranges from \$128,000 to \$186,000 across major salary sources, with Levels.fyi reporting median total compensation of approximately \$261,000. Senior machine learning engineers at FAANG companies regularly clear \$350,000+ in total pay. AI/Machine Learning Engineer Glassdoor reports median total compensation of \$180,837 for this title, with a typical range of \$148,000–\$225,000. Top earners hit \$271,000 at the 90th percentile. GenAI and Large Language Model Engineer The highest-ceiling specialization in 2026. Compensation for dedicated GenAI roles ranges from \$200,000 to \$400,000+, driven by a talent pool that's still shallow relative to demand. The role only emerged as a distinct category in late 2022, so the supply of experienced practitioners remains limited. AI Research Scientist Research scientists, typically requiring a PhD, earn \$180,000–\$280,000 in base salary. Total compensation at frontier AI labs can reach \$350,000–\$700,000 when equity is included. Salary by Industry: Where You Work Matters as Much as What You Do Two data scientists with identical skills can earn very different incomes depending on their employer's industry. The gap isn't small. Quantitative finance and hedge funds: \$140,000–\$300,000 base, with significant bonus potential on top. This is the highest-paying industry for data scientists because a better model translates directly into trading profit. Big tech (FAANG and frontier AI labs): \$150,000–\$200,000 base, with total compensation frequently exceeding \$300,000 when restricted stock units are included. The AI and machine learning sector is seeing salary growth of roughly 12% year-over-year, the highest of any technology discipline. Healthcare and biotech: \$100,000–\$160,000. A growing sector for data science hiring, with demand accelerating as healthcare organizations build AI-powered diagnostics and clinical analytics tools. Finance and banking (traditional): \$120,000–\$160,000. Stable compensation with consistent demand for practitioners who can work within regulatory constraints. Retail and e-commerce: Data science salaries average around \$140,000, reflecting strong demand for demand forecasting and personalization work. Energy: Around \$150,000 on average, driven by grid optimization and predictive maintenance applications. Government: Lower base salaries than private-sector peers, but with strong benefits, pensions, and job stability. Salary by Geography: Where Location Still Matters Despite the expansion of remote work, geography still shapes data science compensation significantly. San Francisco Bay Area / San Jose: The highest-paying metro in the country for data science. BLS data puts San Jose's location quotient at roughly 3.5, meaning data scientist employment is far more concentrated there than in the average U.S. labor market.

title: How to Calibrate Your Classifier’s Probabilities in Scikit-learn
abstract: How to Calibrate Your Classifier’s Probabilities in Scikit-learn In this tutorial, you will train two scikit-learn classifiers on a real dataset, expose their miscalibration with a reliability diagram and a Brier score, and fix it with Platt scaling and isotonic regression By Shittu Olumide , Technical Content Specialist on November 17, 2026 in Machine Learning Your model says 0.9. You treat it as a 90% chance, set a threshold, and build a decision on top of it. Then you check the predictions the model scored near 0.9 and find that noticeably fewer of them were right. Nothing is broken. The model ranks cases well, and it is still a poor judge of how sure it should be. That gap between a score and a real probability is what calibration closes. In this tutorial, you will train two scikit-learn classifiers on a real dataset, expose their miscalibration with a reliability diagram and a Brier score, and fix it with Platt scaling and isotonic regression. By the end, you will know how to calibrate classifier probabilities in scikit-learn and how to pick the right method for your data. What Calibration Means A well-calibrated classifier lets you read predict_proba as a confidence level. In the words of the scikit-learn user guide , among the samples that get a score close to 0.8, about 80% should actually belong to the positive class. Accuracy and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) cannot tell you whether that holds. Both look at labels or rankings, not at whether 0.8 means 80%. A model can score well on both and still be wildly over- or under-confident. Some models are more prone to this than others. The guide notes that logistic regression tends to be well calibrated by itself. Gaussian naive Bayes pushes probabilities toward 0 and 1, random forests tend to avoid the extremes, and maximum-margin methods like support vector machines (SVMs) produce a sigmoid-shaped distortion. You will see two of these behaviors yourself below. Setup and Data Install the libraries and check your version: pip install -U scikit-learn matplotlib numpy python -c "import sklearn; print(sklearn.__version__)" You need scikit-learn 1.6 or later. That is the release that introduced FrozenEstimator , which replaced the old cv="prefit" option, per the 1.6 changelog . Many older tutorials still use cv="prefit" , so keep that in mind if you borrow their code. The data is the Covertype dataset : 581,012 patches of forest with 54 features each, collected for predicting the dominant tree species . It is multiclass, so you will turn it into a binary problem: Spruce/Fir (class 1) against everything else. Create calibrate.py and start with this: import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV, CalibrationDisplay from sklearn.datasets import fetch_covtype from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier from sklearn.frozen import FrozenEstimator from sklearn.metrics import brier_score_loss, log_loss, roc_auc_score from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB RANDOM_STATE = 42 # ---- Step 1: data ------------------------------------------------------- X, y = fetch_covtype(return_X_y=True) y = (y == 1).astype(int) # 1 = Spruce/Fir, everything else = 0 # Work with a 100,000-row sample so everything runs quickly rng = np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_STATE) subset = rng.choice(len(X), size=100_000, replace=False) X, y = X[subset], y[subset] print("Rows:", X.shape[0], "| Share of positives:", round(y.mean(), 3)) # Split 50% train, 20% calibration, 30% test X_train, X_rest, y_train, y_rest = train_test_split( X, y, train_size=0.5, stratify=y, random_state=RANDOM_STATE ) X_cal, X_test, y_cal, y_test = train_test_split( X_rest, y_rest, train_size=0.4, stratify=y_rest, random_state=RANDOM_STATE ) print("Train / calibration / test:", len(X_train), len(X_cal), len(X_test)) fetch_covtype downloads the data on the first call and caches it in a scikit_learn_data folder in your home directory. The target holds the values 1 to 7, so y == 1 turns it into a 0/1 label. Sampling 100,000 rows keeps the random forest fast without changing the lesson. The part that matters most is the three-way split. The user guide explains that a calibrator should be fit on data independent of what trained the classifier, because a model is more confident on its own training data. Fit the calibrator on the training data, and it learns probabilities that are too close to 0 and 1. So you get a training set, a calibration set, and a test set that nothing touches until the final check. stratify keeps the class share the same in every split. Showing the Problem Now train two models that are known to misbehave in opposite ways. Add this to the same file: # ---- Step 2: train two models ------------------------------------------- models = { "Naive Bayes": GaussianNB(), "Random forest": RandomForestClassifier( n_estimators=200, n_jobs=-1, random_state=RANDOM_STATE ), } for model in models.values(): model.fit(X_train, y_train) # Predicted probability of the positive class on the untouched test set raw = {name: m.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] for name, m in models.items()} Both models fit on the training set only. predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] keeps the probability of the positive class, which is all you need for a binary problem. Next come three small helpers you will reuse for every comparison: # ---- helpers ------------------------------------------------------------ def ninety_test(name, p, y_true, low=0.85, high=0.95): """How often are samples scored in [low, high) actually positive?""" mask = (p >= low) & (p < high) if mask.sum() == 0: print(f"{name}: no test samples scored in [{low}, {high})") return print( f"{name}: {mask.sum()} samples scored in [{low}, {high}) " f"-> {y_true[mask].mean():.1%} are actually positive" ) def print_scores(y_true, probas): print(f"{'Model':<32}{'Brier':>8}{'Log loss':>10}{'ROC-AUC':>9}") for name, p in probas.items(): print( f"{name:<32}{brier_score_loss(y_true, p):>8.4f}" f"{log_loss(y_true, p):>10.4f}{roc_auc_score(y_true, p):>9.4f}" ) def reliability_plot(y_true, probas, title): fig, (ax_curve, ax_hist) = plt.subplots( 2, 1, figsize=(7, 9), gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [3, 1]}, sharex=True ) for i, (name, p) in enumerate(probas.items()): CalibrationDisplay.from_predictions( y_true, p, n_bins=10, name=name, ax=ax_curve, ref_line=(i == 0) ) ax_hist.hist(p, bins=10, range=(0, 1), histtype="step", label=name) ax_curve.set_title(title) ax_curve.set_xlabel("") ax_hist.set_xlabel("Mean predicted probability") ax_hist.set_ylabel("Count") ax_hist.legend(loc="upper center") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ninety_test is the "does 0.9 mean 90%?" check in plain code. It takes every test sample scored between 0.85 and 0.95 and reports how many were truly positive. print_scores reports three numbers. The Brier score is the mean squared gap between probability and outcome, and lower is better. Log loss punishes confident mistakes harder. ROC-AUC measures ranking and will help you show that calibration leaves it intact. reliability_plot draws a calibration curve, also called a reliability diagram . The samples are grouped into 10 bins by predicted probability. The x-axis is the average prediction in each bin and the y-axis is the share of real positives in it. A perfect model sits on the diagonal. The histogram underneath shows how many predictions land in each bin, so you know which curve points rest on plenty of data and which on very little. ref_line=(i == 0) draws the diagonal only once. Now run the diagnosis: # ---- Step 3: show the problem ------------------------------------------- for name, p in raw.items(): ninety_test(name, p, y_test) print() print_scores(y_test, raw) reliability_plot(y_test, raw, "Reliability diagram: uncalibrated models") Run python calibrate.py .

title: 7 Best AI Coding Plans for $10 or Less in 2026
abstract: 7 Best AI Coding Plans for $10 or Less in 2026 Compare affordable AI coding agents, AI-powered IDEs, open-source tools, and multi-model subscriptions from OpenCode, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Cline, Zed, and Xiaomi MiMo. By Abid Ali Awan , KDnuggets Assistant Editor on November 17, 2026 in Programming AI coding agents have become much better at writing, debugging, and testing code. You can now use them to build complete applications, work with large codebases, and automate repetitive development tasks. But there is one big problem: the price . For some people, \$20 is just the cost of lunch. But for millions of developers across South Asia, Southeast Asia, and other parts of the world, \$20 a month is a lot of money. And when subscriptions cost anywhere from \$20 to \$100 per month, with usage limits on top of that, it becomes even harder to justify. This is also why we are seeing more AI companies, including Chinese and Western providers, introduce cheaper plans and regional pricing to make their tools more accessible. And it is not just about where you live. Many developers, students, indie hackers, and vibe coders are paying for these tools out of their own pockets. They don't have a company covering the bill, so every subscription needs to provide real value and save enough time to justify the cost. The good news is that you no longer need to spend \$20 or more to get a useful AI coding assistant. Some affordable plans give you access to multiple AI models, while others provide dedicated coding agents and intelligent code editors. In this article, we will look at seven of the best AI coding plans that cost \$10 or less per month , what you get for the money, and which ones are actually worth paying for. 1. OpenCode Go OpenCode Go is easily one of the best-value AI coding subscriptions, and it is not surprising that developers on Reddit and in open-source communities love it. For just \$10 per month, you get access to models from Kimi, MiniMax, DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM, and other providers, all optimized for agentic coding. What makes it special is the generous usage allowance. For example, you can get up to \$100 worth of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash usage for just \$10 per month . Each model has its own limits, including five-hour, weekly, and monthly allowances. You can use it with OpenCode or other compatible coding agents. I would highly recommend it if you enjoy terminal-based coding and want to experiment with different models without spending too much. 2. Command Code GOAT Command Code GOAT is another great option if you want generous AI coding usage without spending too much. The subscription includes \$70 in model-specific credits, with special deals increasing the effective usage to around \$100 on selected models. For the price, you get access to models from DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, MiniMax, MiMo, GLM, and other providers. It also offers API access, usage analytics, and compatibility with popular coding agents. What I like most is that you can experiment with different AI models through one subscription instead of paying for each provider separately. However, the credits are not one shared balance. Each model has its own allowance, and rolling usage limits apply. So make sure you check the limits for the models you plan to use. 3. GitHub Copilot Pro GitHub Copilot Pro is one of the oldest and most consistent AI coding subscriptions. The price has stayed at \$10 per month for years, while GitHub has continued adding new features, models, and more included usage. For \$10, you get unlimited code completions, next-edit suggestions, model selection, and \$15 in monthly AI credits. What I like most is its mature ecosystem. It works directly with VS Code , Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs, Neovim, and other editors. You also get Copilot CLI, cloud coding agents, code review, and third-party agent integrations. The only downside is that advanced AI features consume your monthly credits, so heavy users may run into limits. If you are already comfortable with VS Code and want AI assistance without changing your workflow, I would highly recommend GitHub Copilot Pro. It is reliable, well-integrated, and offers a complete coding experience for the price. 4. ClinePass ClinePass is a new contender in affordable AI coding subscriptions, and I think it could be a game changer. Cline has also made major improvements to its agent harness, delivering impressive results on Terminal-Bench 2.0 , especially with open-weight models. For just \$9.99 per month, you get access to powerful models from DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, MiniMax, MiMo, and Qwen. The best part is that it offers 2–5 times more usage than standard API rate limits , making it great for longer coding sessions. What makes it even better is Cline's mature, open-source ecosystem. You get codebase understanding, planning, file editing, terminal execution, browser testing, and debugging. It works through IDE extensions, a CLI, and an SDK, and you can even use ClinePass with other compatible coding agents. There are still five-hour, weekly, and monthly usage limits, but for \$10, you are getting a lot of value. 5. Cursor Plus Cursor Plus is a new \$8-per-month subscription introduced after SpaceX acquired Cursor and brought it closer to xAI. With this acquisition, I think we can expect some exciting changes to the editor, especially with better Grok models and more affordable AI coding. For just \$8, you get access to Cursor's AI coding agent, intelligent code editing, and models including Grok and Composer. You also get access to Grok Chat, Voice, and image generation, with a shared usage pool that refreshes weekly. What I like most is that you can experience one of the most popular AI-first code editors without paying \$20 or more per month. You get a complete IDE that understands your project, modifies files, runs commands, and helps debug applications. The main limitation is that you cannot use third-party models like Claude or Gemini with this plan. You need a higher-tier subscription for that, and those models are billed separately. 6. Zed Pro Zed Pro is one of my favorite options if you care about speed. Zed is a super-fast, open-source code editor built using Rust, and a lot of developers love it for its performance, clean interface, and lightweight design. What makes it even better is that its AI ecosystem is becoming more mature. You now get built-in AI agents, intelligent code editing, parallel agent sessions, and support for external coding agents like Claude Code , Codex , and OpenCode. For \$10 per month, Zed Pro includes unlimited edit predictions, access to hosted AI models from providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, and \$5 in monthly token credits. The only downside is the relatively small AI allowance. Once you use the \$5 credit, additional hosted-model usage is billed separately. You can also connect your own API keys. 7. Xiaomi MiMo Lite Xiaomi MiMo Lite is probably the best deal on this list. I have personally used it multiple times, and I am genuinely impressed by how much value you get for just \$6 per month. You get 4.1 billion monthly credits with no five-hour or weekly usage limits . In my experience, that is more than enough to build five large projects from scratch. The models are fast, efficient, and really good at understanding existing codebases and making changes without breaking everything. You can use the subscription with popular coding agents like OpenCode, Claude Code, Codex, and Cline. This means you can keep using your favorite coding tools without changing your workflow. The only real drawback is the limited model selection. You get just two coding models, MiMo-V2.6-Pro and MiMo-V2.6-Flash , instead of models from multiple providers. Your monthly credits are also fixed, so usage is not completely unlimited. Comparing the Best Budget AI Coding Plans Here is how all seven plans compare in terms of pricing, model providers, usage allowances, and coding tools.

title: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
abstract: 01 Introduction Claude has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. Claude’s result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available here and here . Introduction Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space. One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality . The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail. The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer. The first problem Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page showed that this switch is abrupt: it’s a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100°C. But Hawking and Page’s calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle. In 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didn’t know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists set out the calculation that would settle the question , but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It showed that the phase transition is abrupt. The same sudden switch appears at both extremes, suggesting that black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory. The second problem concerns a simplified theoretical universe with two dimensions of space instead of three. This universe is straightforward enough to study in detail, but still has black holes and other mysteries similar to those of our own universe. Even in this simpler universe, physicists don’t know how to create a full theory of quantum gravity, so they approach it from the other direction: rather than building a single, correct theory, they try to rule out wrong ones by showing that they are internally inconsistent. This method is called bootstrapping . Since 2009, physicists have used a version of this method to set a ceiling on how heavy the lightest black hole in such a universe could be. Any theory that breaks the ceiling is ruled out, and each lowering of the ceiling narrows the search. Results from numerical calculations hinted at where the best possible ceiling lay, but they couldn’t prove it, and the best proven ceiling was well short of what the numerical results suggested. Claude Fable 5.2 noticed a pattern in the numerical results that physicists had missed and borrowed a method from elsewhere in math and physics to calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered. It doesn’t identify the correct theory, but it may point physicists in the right direction. Neither result describes our own universe directly, and neither has practical applications, but both contribute to a long-running theoretical effort to understand how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together. In the rest of this post, we explain in more detail what each problem was and what Claude did to solve them. A note about Claude’s methods In August, an Anthropic researcher, Hongbin Chen, was testing Claude’s capabilities as a side project. He asked Claude to draw up a list of interesting open problems in theoretical physics, specifically focusing on black holes and the bootstrap method. Claude came back hours later with 22 candidates, and Hongbin set up separate agents to work on each one; they could read each other’s progress posts and collaborate when working on related problems. The agents ran in the background, with no special setup, for about six weeks. The agents solved the two problems in this post. One was the Hawking-Page phase transition, the question of when a hot gas turns into a black hole. Weeks after one of the agents reached a solution, a physicist, who had independently used Claude to tackle the same problem, shared his result, and a colleague realized that Hongbin’s agent had reached the same answer earlier. The two solutions used different methods, so they were a useful check on each other. The modular bootstrap result came from several agents. The one that was assigned the problem spotted the pattern in the numerical results when surveying the bootstrap literature, and another one—which was working on a mathematically related problem about how tightly spheres can be packed into a high-dimensional space—turned that pattern into a method. It found that this method reproduced a sphere-packing result recently proved by an OpenAI model . Claude then applied the same method to the bootstrap problem, which an earlier Claude agent had tried, and failed, to solve in 61 parallel attempts. Two other agents also independently arrived at the same answer. One half of the final proof, showing that the ceiling can’t be lowered, follows the strategy of the OpenAI proof. In September, the results were formally verified in Lean, a computerized proof checker. Claude then wrote the paper with minimal guidance, and a physicist checked every main result. The Hawking-Page transition To understand the first problem, we need to start with something much more familiar: a walk through New York City. Two equally good routes from Penn Station (A) to the High Line entrance (B). In theory, a quantum particle can take both simultaneously. Imagine that you’re heading from Penn Station to the High Line entrance on West 30th Street and 10th Avenue, and there are two equally good routes.

title: Using a "chaos loop" to harden the Claude Docs launch: 60 server errors across billions of requests
abstract: Three weeks before Claude Docs opened to the public, it was running as a proof of concept on a single node, used by a few thousand people inside Anthropic. We were racing toward an ambitious launch date, and our own estimate said we'd see millions of docs within the first few days. We launched on September 16. By September 22, people had created over 4.6 million docs. Across 2 billion requests we saw only 60 server errors, and we never had to roll back. The whole Docs service ran on about 50 memory-optimized pods. Two decisions got us there: A chaos loop at launch scale. We set up a test harness on our staging environment where Claude ran constantly for two weeks to try and break the service. It load tested every part of our infrastructure and fixed whatever fell over. Improving legibility to Claude. Claude could only close the loop effectively on fixes if our system produced accurate telemetry every iteration. We made a call early to avoid any runtime that uses memory or CPU in ways our code can't easily control (e.g. runtimes with garbage collection). When a telemetry signal looked concerning, Claude could easily trace it to a bug or a specific design decision. But honestly, this only worked because our frontier models have gotten much better recently (I used an internal research model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.2). In our experience, they can now stick with one goal through a run like this for weeks, which is what helped us hit launch scale in a tight timeline. THE CHAOS LOOP A few thousand internal users on one machine told us nothing about whether the service would survive launch, and we obviously didn't have launch traffic to test with. We wanted real evidence to decide how fast we could roll out. So on September 4, about two weeks before launch, I had Claude drive a staging cluster that mirrored production at over a million synthetic docs a day and break core components on purpose. And then... I just left it running (I've included the full cost at the end of this article). My setup was pretty simple. The loop was a session in Claude Code that I left running: pick a scenario, run the harness, read the telemetry, propose a fix, ship it to staging, repeat. That session acted as a coordinator and handed most of the work to sub-agents. In the busiest week, that usually meant about 11 sub-agents running at a time, and 30 at the peak. The coordinator also talked to our internal variant of Claude Tag (beta) via the Slack MCP to learn from other infrastructure teams at Anthropic who had scaled similar services. Their agents checked our scaling approach for pitfalls they’d already hit. The fun part was picking scenarios I thought were paranoid: 10M new docs created in a single day 22,000 live connections reconnecting at once One hot doc with hundreds of viewers, a server killed while it was still loading a doc, and the database stalling Each iteration looked the same. Our testing harness selected a feature like document creation and pushed creation to saturation. Claude then read telemetry using the Datadog MCP and came back with a short menu of options and a recommendation. If the recommendation was easy to undo, Claude wrote and deployed the change to staging and reran the test. We had telemetry on every operation the service ran. Every database query, for example, reported its name and how many rows it scanned versus how many it returned, so Claude could spot a bad query and rewrite it. FIG 1 One iteration of the loop, with two decisions made by a person Before the loop started, I told Claude which decisions needed my approval; basically anything hard to undo, like changing the database schema or key layout, or changing how a doc is stored and materialized. When Claude ran into one of those, it stopped and asked me, usually with a recommendation that I ended up approving. Schema changes were the classic case where I wanted to be consulted: there are usually a few reasonable answers, and changing directions is often painful. And during the whole testing process, Claude had to conform to two invariants: Docs had to open almost instantly (even ones with a long history) Once the server acknowledged an edit, tests had to show the edit was still there MAKING THE SERVICE LEGIBLE TO CLAUDE My colleague Felix Rieseberg recently wrote a tutorial on being more ambitious with models . His main idea is to raise the "altitude" you prompt Claude at: ask for the outcome you want, not the individual task. So instead of asking Claude to fix individual crashes, you ask it to make your app crash-free. (Our own apps aren't all the way there yet, but this is how we're making real progress.) To work at that altitude, though, you have to set up your code so Claude can pull crash reports on its own and run a harness that reproduces each crash and checks the fix. For us, the outcome was a service that could handle launch. To get there, we did two things to make the service as legible to Claude as we could: A diagnostic loop. Claude read the telemetry on every iteration and added whatever it thought was missing. Legible technology choices. We picked a runtime and dependencies so any number Claude measured traced back to code we wrote. A diagnostic loop Every iteration, Claude read the telemetry and added whatever it thought was missing. Writing telemetry by hand is tedious, so in practice most telemetry would go in after something broke. Now Claude just writes it as it goes. Memory is the best example. Early in the harness run, one large doc was using about 3 GB on its pod (not a fun number to see). Claude’s first stab at fixing it was to shrink one of our caches so our server would evict docs sooner. The next harness run showed the memory was actually in a separate cache inside one of our dependencies, so Claude dropped the change. From there Claude kept narrowing it down with finer-grained memory profiling. Eventually it found that every keystroke was copying the doc into several different data structures, adding a few MB each time. Claude switched those structures to copy-on-write, so they now share one reference instead of each holding its own copy. After about three days of iterating, that doc topped out around 180 MB, and our estimate of what we’d need for launch dropped from more than 500 memory-optimized pods to about 50. FIG 2 The diagnostic loop Legible technology choices We were picky about the service’s runtime and dependencies. We wanted any number Claude measured to trace back to code we wrote. This is because our models hill climb best with a clean signal. We expected a garbage collector to add noise, because memory and latency shift on the collector’s schedule. Two choices helped the most. We wrote the service in Rust . With no garbage collector, all of a doc’s memory sits in structures we defined, so when it grew, Claude could point to the one responsible, change it, and see whether memory came down on the next iteration. We have great Go tooling at Anthropic too, and we didn’t bake off the two languages, so this is our experience with Rust. What I did appreciate, coming from past work in Go, was how little I had to think about memory sticking around after my code was done with it. We also kept dependencies to a minimum . Every library brings data structures we didn’t write and can’t easily account for. For the few we really needed, we vendored the code so we could read and measure it ourselves. Rust is hard for people to write, and a few years ago that would have weighed heavily on the choice. Claude writes it and most other languages fine, so that matters a lot less now. FIG 3 Legible technology choices: memory our code can explain, and memory it can't LAUNCH WEEK The service held at launch scale. The first million docs showed up in about 30 hours, and we were past 4.6 million by September 22. We rolled prod 629 times in September and never once rolled back. Launch week felt weirdly familiar.

title: Linked billing on the Claude Platform
abstract: Today we're introducing linked billing on the Claude Platform in beta. Third-party platforms, such as coding agents and workflow automation tools, can let their end customers pay for Claude API usage without sharing an API key. End customers keep their existing Anthropic billing and set their own spend limits, and platforms get a simpler, more secure way to offer Claude. A more secure alternative to sharing API keys Paying for Claude API usage on a third-party platform usually means sharing an API key, which works like a password: anyone who has the key can make requests billed to the customer, so the platform has to keep it safe. With linked billing, customers link their Claude Platform organization instead, and usage is billed directly to it. No API key changes hands, so platforms have no customer keys to store, encrypt or rotate, and customers’ API keys never leave their organization. Platforms can see usage for each linked customer. Customers approve each linked platform, set a spend limit, and can unlink at any time. Linked billing on the Claude Platform Platforms can offer Claude to customers without building the billing Linked billing gives platforms a new way to offer Claude to their customers. Platforms send requests, and Anthropic bills the end customers directly. With linked billing, platforms can: Launch faster. Anthropic hosts the approval flow and the billing, so there’s no metering or invoicing to build. Understand usage by customer. Get each linked customer’s request count, token usage and models used in Console, or programmatically with the Usage and Cost Analytics API (beta). Choose who pays. Decide on each request whether the platform or the end customer pays, so platforms can pass Claude API costs to customers or cover some features themselves by product or instance. Customers get more visibility and control Customers can easily link to platforms using Anthropic’s hosted flow. They can then draw down from their existing Anthropic commitment, or pay as they go. With linked billing, customers can also: Link once for the whole organization. A Console user with an Owner, Admin, or Billing role approves the link, so it works the same for individual developers and large teams. Set limits for each platform. Customers can set a monthly spend limit for each platform, or a default that applies to each one. See where API spend goes. Console shows spend for each linked platform. Unlink at any time. Customers can unlink directly from Console. Requests run in the platform’s organization, so settings in the customer’s organization, such as IP allowlists, encryption keys, and data retention, don’t apply. Platforms that support linked billing today include Asana, ClickHouse, Factory, Gumloop, Harness, Higgsfield AI, Kilo Code, Linear, Major, Mintlify, Omni, OpenArt, Niteshift, Railway, Ramp, Runlayer, Tessera, Tines, and Warp. Getting started Linked billing is available today in beta on the Claude Platform. Third-party platforms can add support by creating an app in Console and following the steps in the docs . Claude Platform customers can link their organization from any supported platform, and find platforms that offer linked billing on Claude Marketplace . “Our customers include some of the largest companies in the world. Linked billing lets them use their own Claude organization in Tessera, with no new keys to manage” Anirudh Sriram, CTO, Tessera “Claude is expanding what’s possible with AI, and Tines helps teams across the business build, deploy, and operationalize that work securely, with the visibility and control IT and Security need. Linked billing gives customers a simpler way to bring Claude and Tines together through their existing Claude Platform organization, without sharing API keys, making it easier to control spend and expand AI adoption across the business.” Charlie Ardagh, Vice President, Strategic Partnerships, Tines “Engineering teams should have the flexibility to build their software factories with the models and infrastructure they choose. Linked billing makes that easier and more secure, making it seamless for customers to link their own Claude Platform organizations to Warp without having to manage API keys or complex billing arrangements. We’re excited to bring this experience to Warp.” Zach Lloyd, Founder and CEO, Warp “Manually copying API keys is inherently insecure. With linked billing, admins can now use their committed Claude spend directly with the Linear cloud coding agent in a click.” Tom Moor, Member of Technical Staff, Linear “At Ramp, we want to save customers time and money wherever they work. Linked Billing makes it easier for our customers to use their existing Claude Platform account through Ramp Router, without the hassle of sharing an API key.” Amanda Carroccio, Director of AI Partnerships, Ramp “Linked billing with Claude Platform lets developers using Railway Agent focus on getting their applications built and deployed, instead of managing API keys manually. Linking their Claude Platform organization with Railway gives developers a more secure way of accessing their models and spend limits.” Cody De Arkland, GM, Agent Experience, Railway “Our customers want to bring AI into more of their work without adding overhead for IT and finance. Linked billing lets them use their existing Claude commitment to power Agentic Work Management in Asana, including AI Studio and AI Teammates, with less setup and spending limits they control as adoption grows.” Arnab Bose, Chief Product Officer, Asana “Linked billing makes Claude billing in ClickHouse Cloud turnkey: link your Claude Platform organization, no keys to manage, and Claude API usage is billed to your organization on the terms you already have.” Ryadh Dahimene, Director of Product Management, AI/ML, ClickHouse “Linked billing simplifies the onboarding process for our enterprise customers. Instead of creating an Anthropic API key and sharing it with us, an admin links their Claude Platform organization once. We don’t need to hold their key, furthering the security of the integration.” Leo Tchourakov, Member of Technical Staff, Factory “Gumloop takes security very seriously, and with linked billing our customers no longer hand their API key to a third party. They link their Claude Platform organization to Gumloop once, and their Claude API usage is billed directly to that organization.” Rahul Behal, Chief Technology Officer, Gumloop “Software factories are the next chapter of engineering, and many of our customers are building them with Claude. Using linked billing, they can link their Claude Platform organization to Cosmos by Harness, and Claude API usage in Cosmos is billed to that organization. We’re excited to be supporting linked billing for the Claude Platform.” Sanjay Nagaraj, SVP of Engineering, Harness “Our customers look to Claude for agentic capabilities in the tools they use to create. Linked billing lets them link their Claude Platform organization to Higgsfield, with Claude API usage billed directly to their organization. Operational simplicity lets their creative teams focus on what they do best.” Alex Mashrabov, CEO, Higgsfield AI “Linked billing means our customers link their Claude Platform organization and everything just works. We get to spend our time building instead of managing credentials.” Kyle Finken, Engineer Manager, Mintlify “Niteshift orchestrates cloud coding agents with full-stack dev environments. As agent usage grows in volume and scope, our customers are increasingly focused on both cost control and security. Linked billing allows them to set a monthly spend limit and keep their billing relationship with Anthropic, without sharing long-lived API keys.” Sajid Mehmood, CEO & Co-Founder, Niteshift “Claude is a core model in OpenArt’s agentic layer.

title: Build Training-Ready Physical AI Datasets with Two Prompts in NVIDIA Cosmos
abstract: World model accuracy starts with high-quality, diverse training datasets. Yet capturing rare defects, nighttime incidents, and other challenging scenarios is costly and time-consuming. Turning raw data into training-ready datasets adds complexity, particularly when using disconnected tools and manual processes for curation, labeling, generation, and evaluation. NVIDIA technology is helping developers more easily build high-quality, diverse training datasets at scale for physical AI . NVIDIA Cosmos is an open platform of frontier models , datasets, frameworks, and skills for world model development. As part of this platform, NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory (CDF) is a collection of five cloud-native blueprints and six composable skills to accelerate data curation, processing, and synthetic data generation (SDG) . Frontier AI agents can be used to orchestrate these blueprints, enabling prompt-to-data without human steering. This post walks you through how to curate and augment datasets or create anomalous events for physical AI model training with just two prompts in Cosmos. It features five different use cases. Video 1. Learn how to use a coding agent to turn a single warehouse image into labeled synthetic fall-event videos—with just a few prompts Set up and configure Cosmos blueprints and skills: Prompt 1 Cosmos Data Factory contains five reference blueprints for common tasks. All five blueprints run using the CDF Orchestration core skill , which coordinates workflow steps, deploys the required services, and manages execution on your cluster. To set it up, enter the following prompt into your coding agent: Example prompt: “Clone the CDF Orchestration repository, then run orchestration preflight and setup.” Preflight checks your environment without making changes and flags anything missing. Once those checks pass, setup prepares your environment to run the blueprints. Run the blueprint for your training data use case: Prompt 2 This section features five training data use cases for running the blueprint, including example prompts: Generate driving scenarios for autonomous vehicle (AV) training Augment image attributes for search and re-identification Augment videos across weather, lighting, and environments Generate rare event videos for model training Generate defect images for visual inspection If you already have footage or images and need to curate and add more variety, the first use case in this section covers generating driving scenarios, varying clothing attributes in person images, and transforming videos across weather, lighting, and environmental conditions. The augmentation use cases expand the variety in your existing data, but some training gaps call for creating entirely new events or defects. Your model might need to recognize a leaking product or a defective circuit board, but your dataset may contain few examples or none. Waiting to capture enough rare cases can take years, and staging them can be dangerous or expensive. The last two use cases cover generating rare event videos and defect images from images or 3D assets to fill these gaps. Use case 1: Generate driving scenarios for AV training The Autonomous Vehicle Dataset Generation blueprint helps you search large databases of driving scenarios and generate novel datasets for downstream model training and validation tasks. NVIDIA Cosmos Curator extracts metadata for your video dataset inputs, and NVIDIA Cosmos Dataset Search finds relevant videos through those embeddings. The retrieved videos are passed to NVIDIA Cosmos3-Super-Image2Video style transfer, and Cosmos Evaluator checks the generated videos for physical plausibility. Example prompt: “Search for driving scenes similar to our input video.mp4, transform them into rainy, snowy, and foggy while preserving layout and motion, and check physical plausibility.​” Figure 1. An AI agent orchestrates AV dataset generation, augmenting driving scenes with varied weather and lighting and checking physical plausibility Use case 2: Augment image attributes for search and re-identification The Image Attribute Augmentation reference blueprint generates variations of person-crops with controlled attribute changes such as clothing type, accessories, and color. An LLM turns your selected attributes into structured modification prompts, used to generate the augmented variations of the source image. Cosmos Evaluator confirms that the requested clothing attributes appear. The blueprint then auto-labels the results with clothing attributes and search queries for person search and re-identification. Example prompt: “Augment the person crops in <input-bucket>, three clothing variants per person, and write the output to <output-bucket>.” Figure 2. An AI agent generates outfit variations in images of people, verifies garment consistency, and annotates clothing attributes Use case 3: Augment videos across weather, lighting, and environments The Video Data Augmentation reference blueprint transforms your existing footage across weather, lighting, and environmental conditions while preserving scene structure. A vision lang uage model ( VLM) describes your source video and combines that with your requested conditions into a structured prompt, which Cosmos3-Nano uses to generate the augmented variant. Cosmos Evaluator checks each generated clip for motion artifacts that aren’t in your source, confirms that the conditions you asked for actually appear, and scores whether the motion is physically plausible. Next, the blueprint auto-labels both your source and generated videos with detection, tracking, and captions. It then provides you with a training-ready dataset. Example prompt: “Run video data augmentation on the videos in <input-bucket>, create 3 augmentations for yellow lighting, dim lighting and red table. Write the output to <output-bucket>.” Figure 3. An AI agent orchestrates visual variations of a robot-manipulation scene, changing lighting and tabletop appearance while checking physical plausibility Use case 4: Generate rare event videos for model training The Event Video Generation reference blueprint uses a source image to create videos of rare events, such as fires, falls, or shoplifting. A VLM combines its description of your scene with your requested event into a structured prompt. Cosmos3-Super-Image2Video generates the clip while preserving the source viewpoint and layout. Cosmos Evaluator checks whether the event appears and whether motion looks physically plausible, retrying failed clips. Passing clips are auto-labeled with detections, tracks, captions, and semantic annotations for downstream training. Example prompt: “Run the Event Video Generation blueprint on the image in <input-bucket> to generate 3 clips: normal traffic, stalled vehicle, and collision at the intersection. Write the output to <output-bucket>.” Figure 4. An AI agent orchestrates retail event generation from a grocery store scene, producing floor-level spills, falling boxes, and shelf smoke, followed by quality review and annotation Use case 5: Generate defect images for visual inspection The Defect Image Generation reference blueprint creates defective examples from clean inspection images or 3D USD assets of parts such as circuit boards, glass panels, or metal surfaces. For 3D assets, NVIDIA Isaac Sim renders inspection images and masks, and Qwen-Image-Edit creates realistic clean reference images, called golden images. Cosmos 3 Super uses these images, defect masks, and your requested defect types to generate defects while preserving the surrounding part. It ships fine-tuned for printed circuit boards (PCBs), glass, and metal, with further fine-tuning skills available for other use cases. You get golden images, synthetic defect images, and manifests tracing each result to its source and generation settings. Example prompt: “Run the Defect Image Generation blueprint and generate shift structural defects for images in <input-bucket> with full board coverage.

title: Tackling GPU Bottlenecks in Plane-Wave DFT with K-Point Batching and Mixed Precision
abstract:
Training a next-generation machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) requires ground truth: tens to hundreds of millions of density functional theory (DFT) calculations of energies, forces, and stresses across diverse structures and chemistries. Plane-wave DFT, with VASP as its dominant implementation, is the gold standard for generating that data. It is accurate, well-validated across materials classes, and ubiquitous at the national labs and research institutions running these calculations at scale. As MLIP training datasets have grown, so has the pressure to generate DFT data faster and cheaper. But the small unit cells and dense k-point grids common in MLIP data generation can leave significant GPU performance unused. VASP’s OpenACC implementation has delivered meaningful speedups, especially for large-system calculations. However, for smaller systems, sequential k-point processing limits GPU utilization. At the same time, AI workloads are reshaping GPU hardware development toward lower-precision data types, creating a growing gap between what modern NVIDIA GPUs can deliver and what FP64-only HPC codes are optimized for. This post introduces two new NVIDIA capabilities that address these bottlenecks. The first, Daviator, resolves the small-system GPU performance problem through k-point and spin-batched GPU kernels. In particular, a batched Davidson solver delivers significant performance gains. The second, a new mixed precision execution layer, enables further performance gains, especially on inference-class GPUs with a high FP32:FP64 throughput ratio. For a projected reference dataset workload, the results show up to 22x faster time-to-solution and up to 75% lower cost compared to CPU execution, depending on hardware and configuration. The GPU bottleneck in plane-wave DFT In periodic systems, electronic wavefunctions are parameterized by crystal momentum, a discrete set of k-points that samples the Brillouin zone. For periodic structures with small unit cells, hundreds to thousands of irreducible k-points are required to achieve well-converged results. Each k-point solve is largely independent; for instance, no inter-k-point communication is required during the Davidson eigensolver step. Despite this independence, VASP’s OpenACC GPU port processes k-points sequentially. For large systems, the work per k-point can fully saturate a GPU, but for small systems with dense k-point grids, the hundreds of small GPU dispatches per step causes kernel launch overhead to dominate compute time. The result: a single-atom iron system with 752 k-points ran 8x slower on the more expensive GPU hardware than on CPU. Thus, researchers working at this scale were left with a manual routing decision based on the size of the job. Additionally, plane-wave DFT traditionally runs in FP64, a conservative default that guarantees accuracy throughout the solver pipeline. But GPU hardware is no longer symmetric in this regard. On data center GPUs, FP64 throughput has held flat across NVIDIA Hopper, Blackwell, and Rubin GPUs, while FP32 throughput has continued to increase. Inference-class and workstation GPUs like the RTX PRO 6000 push this further, with a 64:1 FP32:FP64 ratio (Figure 1). As AI workloads drive hardware development toward lower-precision data types, the fraction of peak GPU throughput available to FP64-only codes is stagnating. Figure 1. A comparison of FP64 and FP32 throughput across different NVIDIA GPUs Daviator: Batching k-points for GPU saturation Daviator is a library of GPU kernels developed by NVIDIA that replaces sequential per-k-point processing in plane-wave DFT inner loops with batched GPU operations. At the core of the transformation lies a batched Davidson eigensolver that replaces sequential loops that cause latency with batched FFTs, GEMMs, and custom kernels. This drops the number of GPU kernel launches drastically, enabling SM occupancy to go from a fraction of capacity to near saturation. Data stays resident in GPU memory throughout. VASP retains full ownership of the SCF loop, mixing, symmetry, and I/O; Daviator integrates at well-defined call boundaries over data already on device. Running a calculation Daviator will be available through the NVIDIA ALCHEMI VASP microservice by setting LDAVIATOR=True in the INCAR. Existing VASP inputs work without modification. export CUDA_CACHE_DISABLE=0 # make sure caching is on Finally, run as usual: mpirun -np 1 vasp_std For now, VASP with Daviator is limited to single-node execution. Multi-node support, coverage of systems with non-collinear spins (vasp_ncl) and explicit gamma-only runs (vasp_gam) is expected to be released at a later stage. Results The benchmarks below compare Daviator against VASP 6.6.0 CPU and OpenACC baselines on NVIDIA H100s/H200s and B200s. Figure 2. Comparison of stock VASP OpenACC v6.6.0, VASP OpenACC (OpenMP/MPS) which optimizes between two parameters (number of MPI processes and OpenMP threads), and Daviator-enabled VASP execution times Daviator overcomes the OpenACC port’s limitations; a single iron atom achieves over 2x speed-ups relative to the CPU baseline (Figure 2). The gains increase for higher-accuracy functionals: the 22x Davidson speedup on LiFePO 4 r 2 SCAN enables higher accuracy meta-GGA runs at production scale. For mid-size systems like a 64-atom Bi-doped GaAs structure, VASP with Daviator cut execution time by more than 85%. Even at 348 atoms with a single k-point, Daviator delivers a significant improvement over the OpenACC and CPU baselines. VASP with Daviator improves the previous state-of-the-art for all system sizes, eliminating the need to route jobs between CPU and GPU based on system size. Going further with mixed precision Daviator eliminates the k-point bottleneck, but currently relies on FP64 arithmetic and storage. GPU hardware is shifting toward lower-precision data types, and HPC codes that adapt to mixed precision stand to recapture substantial performance from hardware they already own. Further increasing the throughput, especially on GPUs with a high FP32:FP64 ratio, requires leveraging the FP32 units, but developing a mixed-precision Davidson solver is non-trivial. Not every kernel in the Davidson pipeline is equally precision-sensitive, but simply running each in FP32 and comparing against FP64 only yields a pass/fail result. Additionally, the failures can be insidious. Hard failures are obvious: a solver rejects an ill-conditioned input. Soft failures are not: energy drift, incorrect convergence, diverging MD trajectories that appear valid on casual inspection. Genuine mixed precision requires knowing exactly where the precision boundaries lie. By using a generic floating-point type with configurable mantissa and exponent bits, we can identify the minimum required bit counts for each that still produce correct results.

title: Co-Designing Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Inference
abstract: Agentic workloads, long documents, and large codebases are pushing context lengths from tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds of thousands. At those lengths, attention becomes the most expensive part of a transformer layer. Dense attention scores every query against every key, so its cost per query grows with the context length N, and at 128K tokens it can take most of the prefill time in a layer. The model-level solution is sparse attention, a transformer technique in which each query attends to only a small subset of the context, chosen per query, instead of all of it. This cuts both the compute and the memory traffic of attention on long context. This post is a practical primer for model developers designing sparse attention that runs well on NVIDIA GPUs. It focuses on model-level sparse attention, where sparsity is trained into the model, rather than drop-in methods applied after training such as BLASST , MInference , or Quest . A production FP8 kernel is used to sweep the indexer’s design knobs (query heads, key heads, head dimension, compression ratio, and speculative-decoding depth), measure how Top-k cost scales, and compare token-level with block-level core attention. Each section explains what the hardware rewards and why, and ends with a guideline you can apply to your own design.
