This post follows the same co-design approach as the earlier posts on dense attention and hardware-friendly LLM design . What is sparse attention and why does it matter? Sparse attention is an AI optimization technique that limits which prior tokens each query attends to. Instead of attending to the entire context, each query attends to only the \(k\) most relevant keys, typically a few thousand. Core attention then stops scaling with context. But those \(k\) keys have to be found, and the component that finds them, the indexer, still scores all \(N\) keys. The cost does not disappear; it moves into the indexer. In Figure 1, the indexer and Top-k take 47% of the DeepSeek V3.2 prefill layer. Figure 1. Per-layer prefill time at ISL = 128K tokens. DeepSeek-R1 (dense MLA) versus DeepSeek V3.2 (DSA) Sparse attention has three stages (Figure 2). An indexer scores every key, Top-k keeps the \(k\) highest scores, and core attention runs softmax attention over those \(k\) keys and values. The last two stages scale with \(k\), the indexer with \(N\). Figure 2. The three stages of sparse attention The indexer design space An indexer is a small attention-like block. Query heads score the current query against a cache of indexer keys, and post-processing operations (such as a ReLU and weighted sum) turn the scores into one logit per key. Table 1 shows how recent models fill that in. Table 2 provides a key to the notation used in this post. Model / method \(Q\) heads \(K\) heads Hsz Post-processing CR Selection granularity Notes Dense attention None None None All keys Baseline. No indexer, every query attends to every key DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) 64 1 128 ReLU + weighted sum 1 Token Separate FP8 index cache GLM 5.2 32 1 128 ReLU + weighted sum 1 Token Index shared across layers GLM 5.3 Flash 32 1 128 ReLU + weighted sum 4 Block of 4 + tail LongCat LSA-Flash 32 1 128 ReLU + weighted sum 1 Token Hierarchical, index shared CSA 64 1 128 ReLU + weighted sum 4 Compressed token Qwen QSA 4 1 128 ReLU + sum 4 Block of 4 + tail MiniMax MSA 4 (1 per group) 1 128 MaxPool over scores 1 Block of 128 Scores every token, pools scores per block, no cross-head reduction NSA 64 4 192 Softmax 16 Block of 16 MoBA 32 8 128 MeanPool on \(K\) 4096 Block of 4096 Pools keys before scoring, no cross-head reduction Table 1. Indexer design choices in recent sparse attention methods Symbol Meaning \(N\) Context length: ISL in prefill, KVSL in decode PB, DB Prefill and decode batch size QH, KH Indexer query heads and indexer key heads \(G\) Group size = QH / KH: query heads scoring against one shared K head Hsz Indexer head dimension ISL, KVSL Input sequence length (prefill), KV cache length at the current decode step CR Compression ratio of the indexer key cache (one indexer key per CR tokens) \(D\) Draft tokens per decode step (speculative decoding), query rows per step = \(D\) + 1 B, B_out Bytes per input element (1 for FP8), bytes per output logit (4 for FP32) Table 2. Notation symbols and meanings Most designs use KH = 1, 32 to 64 query heads reduced to one score with a ReLU and weighted sum, Hsz = 128, and token or small-block selection. The measurements in the next five sections, one per design knob, show which of these are efficient on NVIDIA GPUs and which should change. How does the indexer compute? The indexer is one batched matmul with a fused epilogue (Table 3). Prefill scores all ISL query tokens at once, so the matmul is large and compute-bound. Decode scores only \(D\) + 1 query tokens per KH per step and streams the whole key cache from HBM for a few rows of logits. Operation Phase Prefill shape Decode shape Runs on Scoring BMM (Q · Kᵀ) Main loop [PB·KH, ISL·G, ISL/CR, Hsz] [DB·KH, (D+1)·G, KVSL/CR, Hsz] Tensor Cores Post-processing (ReLU) Epilogue [PB·KH·ISL·G, ISL/CR] [DB·KH·(D+1)·G, KVSL/CR] CUDA cores Cross-head reduction (weighted sum over G) Epilogue [PB·KH·ISL, ISL/CR] [DB·KH·(D+1), KVSL/CR] CUDA cores Logit store Epilogue [PB·KH·ISL, (ISL/CR)] [DB·KH·(D+1), KVSL/CR] HBM write Table 3. The indexer as a matmul with a fused epilogue (designs with a cross-head reduction). The causal mask halves every prefill shape Counting FLOPs, \(Q\) and \(K\) reads, and logit writes gives each phase’s arithmetic intensity. In prefill the \(Q\) and \(K\) terms shrink as 1 / ISL, so at long context only the logit write survives. Figure 3. Equations for indexer arithmetic intensity in prefill and decode Three observations follow from Equations 1 and 2 shown in Figure 3: Sequence length (ISL, KVSL) and CR appear in neither equation: they scale total work but not the ratio of FLOPs to bytes. Both intensities are proportional to \(G\) = QH / KH. Reducing the \(G\) heads of a group to one logit gives \(G\) times more FLOPs per logit written. Designs without this reduction (MSA, MoBA) lose that factor. Decode intensity grows almost linearly with \(D\) + 1 and is nearly independent of Hsz, as long as all \(D\) + 1 query tokens fit in one pass over the key cache. Unless noted, measurements use an FP8 indexer kernel with 64K indexer keys (CR = 4), Hsz = 128, KH = 1, PB = 1, and DB = 128. Query heads, group size, and speculative draft length Intensity is proportional to group size, but prefill and decode respond differently. Prefill is compute-bound, so more query heads mean proportionally more time. Decode is memory-bound: reading the key cache is the main bottleneck. More query heads add FLOPs but no new bytes, so runtime stays the same. Figure 4 confirms both. Figure 4. Normalized runtime versus group size \(G\) Decode runtime moves only 2% while \(G\) grows 16x, because the single key cache read sets the runtime. Prefill runtime grows more slowly than \(G\) at small \(G\): doubling \(G\) from 8 to 16 costs 1.66x, not 2x. This is because the FP32 logit write happens once per logit regardless of G, and at small G it dominates. Above about \(G\) = 16, the matmul dominates and runtime grows with \(G\). Equation 2 has a second lever on decode intensity: \(D\) + 1, the query tokens scored per step. Without speculative decoding , it is 1. With speculative decoding, the model drafts \(D\) tokens and verifies them with the new token in one step. This means that the indexer scores \(D\) + 1 query tokens against the same key cache. Like extra query heads, the extra query tokens add FLOPs but no new bytes, so the draft tokens are nearly free while they fit in one pass. Figure 5 shows where this process stops. Figure 5. Decode indexer runtime versus query tokens per step, for \(G\) = 32 and \(G\) = 8 One Tensor Core tile holds up to 256 query rows.

title: Integrating QPUs into Supercomputing Centers Using Slurm HRES Plugins
abstract: Quantum processors are being integrated into supercomputing centers worldwide. National programs in North America, Europe, and Asia are driving the installation of quantum processing units (QPUs) alongside high-performance computing (HPC) systems. Every supercomputer will eventually be a hybrid quantum-classical device, drawing on quantum processors to expand what’s possible in scientific research. The scientists that will become the first power users of quantum-GPU supercomputing already run their simulations and workflows on HPC systems. Chemistry, weather modeling, engineering simulation, and other traditionally HPC-centric fields stand to benefit from quantum acceleration for certain workloads. For these scientists, the QPU is simply another accelerator, alongside the CPUs and GPUs that supercomputing centers already provide. Making quantum computers readily available, easily programmable, and familiar to access, reserve, and execute at scale is imperative for scientific researchers to be able to adopt quantum processors into workflows. Until now, a key missing piece has been a workload manager. Slurm 26.11 changes that with Hierarchical Resources (HRES) plugins, which allow a site to schedule a QPU as a native, cluster-level resource through a short, portable Lua plugin. This post covers why QPUs have not fit the previous scheduling models Slurm used for CPUs and GPUs. It then explains the solution: how HRES models a QPU, and what HRES plugins add in Slurm 26.11, including the API callbacks and capabilities that middleware teams build on. It also addresses how community-driven interfaces such as QRMI and QDMI have already built open source plugins on these APIs, as well as initial adoption by the quantum ecosystem and supercomputing centers. Building quantum-GPU supercomputing Integrating a QPU at a supercomputing center requires more than just its physical installation. The QPU must be networked with the existing computing infrastructure, and users must be able to request it at job submission the same way CPUs and GPUs are requested. Its usage must be tracked, monitored, and accounted for, and it must abide by site-specific policies. In other words, the scheduler, or workload manager, must manage the QPU like it would any other computing resource. Until now, schedulers have had no native way to model a QPU, so most integrations are repeatedly custom-built for each new supercomputing site or QPU builder. The cost of that fragmentation falls on everyone involved: Users face a different interface at every site. Administrators must maintain custom code that complicates upgrades. QPU vendors rebuild their integration for each customer, with no portability. Global systems integrators (GSIs) cannot deliver a repeatable deployment. On the QPU side, open source efforts such as QRMI and QDMI are unifying how such devices are described to, and controlled by, HPC software. What has been missing is a unified interface in the scheduler used by supercomputing centers for integrating QPUs into HPC deployments. Why existing Slurm resource models don’t accommodate QPUs A QPU is typically a cluster-wide accelerator, not part of a node. Slurm generic resources (GRES), the mechanism used for GPUs, belong to individual compute nodes. Modeling a QPU as a GRES binds it to one node, so only jobs on that node can use it. If that node fails, for example, the QPU stays unreachable until an administrator reconfigures the cluster. Many integrations instead combine licenses, which represent cluster-wide resources, for scheduling, and use SPANK plugins for the user interface and node setup. This approach works, but it has several problems: Idle nodes: Without a license, SPANK only acts after Slurm has allocated nodes, so a job can hold compute nodes idle while it waits for the QPU. Two-flag requests: Nothing stops a job from passing device options without holding the license. Multiple QPUs: Hosting several QPUs on one cluster is difficult, because their SPANK plugins compete for the same command-line options. Upgrade risk: In practice, many SPANK plugins tie third-party code to Slurm internal APIs, so every Slurm upgrade risks breaking the integration. No device awareness: Slurm cannot tell on its own when a QPU is recalibrating or offline, so it keeps starting jobs that cannot use the device until it is back online. How HRES plugins in Slurm 26.11 enable integration Slurm 26.11 introduces an HRES plugin interface to address these gaps, so that the HPC and quantum communities can integrate with Slurm without changing Slurm itself. Its first implementation, hres/lua , runs a short Lua script. The plugin reports device health to the scheduler, accepts device options as part of the resource request, and runs setup and teardown code at each stage of the job. A site describes the QPU as a cluster-level HRES in resources.yaml and points it at the plugin. The two files divide the work. resources.yaml holds site-specific details and policies, such as endpoints and which nodes can reach the device, under the system administrator’s control. The plugin holds the device logic, so the community or a QPU vendor can write it once and ship it to every site that deploys Slurm 26.11. Modeling a QPU as a hierarchical resource HRES was added to Slurm 25.05 as a beta feature and is the evolution of licenses. Like a license, an HRES is a count of a resource that does not belong to any single node. Unlike a license, that count is associated with a specific set of nodes: the ones allowed to use it (Figure 1). Slurm 26.11 also starts to allow more dynamic modeling of the relationship between nodes and HRES. Figure 1. GRES schedules devices inside a compute node, licenses count a cluster-wide resource, and HRES also associates that resource with the nodes allowed to use it An HRES is defined in resources.yaml , in the same directory as slurm.conf . Each resource has one or more layers, and each layer has a name, a list of nodes, and a count. For a QPU, the simplest definition is a single layer covering the nodes that can reach the device, with a count of one. The plugin block attaches the Lua script and its site-specific settings: - resource: qpu mode: MODE_1 plugin: type: hres/lua config: - name: path value: /etc/slurm/hres_qpu.lua - name: endpoint # site settings, never secrets value: https://qpu-gateway.example.org maintenance_cycle: 30 # seconds between health checks layers: - layer_name: qpu1 nodes: ["node[0001-0123]"] count: 1 With this definition, a request is satisfied when a layer that overlaps the job’s allocated nodes has enough of the resource available. A job that requests the QPU runs only on nodes in that layer. Jobs request the resource with --resources=qpu:1 . The middleware is the boundary between HPC and QPU In the model shown in Figure 2, neither Slurm nor the Lua plugin talks to the QPU directly. A third-party access middleware sits between the HPC system and the QPU and provides a unified interface to different quantum hardware APIs. The middleware is therefore the boundary between the HPC system and the QPU. Figure 2. Slurm schedules the QPU as a single unit through an HRES Lua plugin, third-party middleware handles device access, and what happens inside the QPU stays hidden from Slurm Slurm treats the QPU as a single schedulable unit. It decides whether the unit is available, which job holds it, for how long, and from which nodes. Importantly, Slurm does not orchestrate anything inside the unit: calibration, error correction, and device control stay within the QPU and its own software runtime. The approach therefore applies both to today’s noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices and to future error-corrected systems. The plugin translates between the two sides. It asks the middleware for status and reservations, and reports the results to Slurm in Slurm’s terms: whether a layer is disabled, whether a job can start, and a payload for the job’s nodes.

title: Introducing workload recovery and expanded infrastructure checks on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
abstract: Large training jobs can fail even when every node looks healthy. A GPU with a subtle fault can pass its stress tests and still return wrong values. When a job stalls on an NCCL timeout, it keeps its GPUs, and Slurm still shows it as running. If a device plugin crashes on one node, the job fails with an error that never mentions the plugin. Teams usually find these problems only after the loss diverges or the job fails, and by then the compute is spent. Each of these failures lowers goodput, the share of your cluster’s time that goes to useful training. Today, we’re introducing workload recovery and infrastructure checks on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod that catch these failures sooner and raise the goodput of your training workloads. SageMaker HyperPod already handles nodes that report hardware faults. The health monitoring agent (HMA) watches each node for GPU errors, deep health checks test nodes during provisioning, and automatic node recovery reboots or replaces faulty hardware. These features look at one node’s hardware at a time. They can’t tell whether the GPUs train correctly, whether a job is still making progress, or whether the Kubernetes components a job depends on are working. In this post, we walk through the three new capabilities that catch these failures. For each one, we show how to set it up and what it reports when it finds a problem: The existing HyperPod resiliency features check a single node at a time. The health monitoring agent (HMA) watches each node for GPU errors such as Xid and NVLink faults, Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) errors, and kernel errors. The InstanceStress deep health check runs DCGM level 4 diagnostics and tests each instance’s GPUs, GPU memory, NVLink, and EFA devices. The InstanceConnectivity check runs NCCL tests across GPU instances, or NCCOM tests on AWS Trainium. Together, these confirm that each node’s hardware works. They don’t show whether the GPUs compute correctly, whether a job is still making progress, or whether the cluster’s Kubernetes components are healthy. Three kinds of failure get past them: Each capability covers a different point in a training run. MultiNodeTrainingValidation runs when instances are provisioned, or on demand, and confirms that their GPUs train correctly. Hung job detection runs alongside each Slurm job and catches a job that has stopped making progress. The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent watches the cluster continuously and, when a job fails, reports the pods and nodes that were involved. The following table summarizes the three. Hung job detection is new for Slurm clusters. On EKS clusters, HyperPod already detects hung jobs that run through the HyperPod training operator , and Ray Train jobs get hang detection by default . We describe both options in the hung job detection section. Each capability targets a different source of lost goodput. Scheduling goodput is the share of time that all the resources a job needs are available. Runtime goodput is the share of that time in which the job makes forward progress. Program goodput is the share of the hardware’s peak performance that the job gets. The following table shows the effect of each capability. Consider a pre-training job running on 32 ml.p5.48xlarge instances (256 NVIDIA H100 GPUs). If the job hangs at 1:00 AM and no one notices until 9:00 AM, it wastes 256 instance-hours or 2,048 GPU-hours. At the SageMaker HyperPod on-demand price of approximately $66 per instance-hour in US East (N. Virginia), the hang costs about $16,900. With a 15-minute hung job detection rule, HyperPod cancels the stalled job and Slurm requeues it. The hang costs about $530 instead, saving approximately $16,400. The MultiNodeTrainingValidation deep health check trains a fixed, known-good workload, first on each instance and then across instances. It catches GPUs that pass InstanceStress and InstanceConnectivity but produce NaN or infinite loss once they train together. If an instance fails, HyperPod labels it as failed and, with automatic node recovery turned on, reboots or replaces it. When the check runs during provisioning, this happens before your jobs can use the instance. MultiNodeTrainingValidation adds two tests to the deep health check run: Either test fails an instance if the training loss becomes NaN or infinite, or if training doesn’t finish within the time limit. The workload is fixed, so a failure points to the hardware rather than to a model or code change. The following table shows how it fits with the other deep health checks. HyperPod runs deep health checks when it creates or updates instances. To include MultiNodeTrainingValidation , add it to OnStartDeepHealthChecks in the instance group configuration that you pass to create-cluster or update-cluster . We turned on all three checks: To confirm the setting, run the following command: The output lists the three checks: You can also check instances that are already in the cluster, for example before a long pre-training run. Use the StartClusterHealthCheck API: To check specific instances instead of the whole group, add "InstanceIds": [...] to the configuration. HyperPod writes one line per test to the DeepHealthCheckResults/<id> log stream in your cluster’s CloudWatch log group, /aws/sagemaker/Clusters/<cluster-name>/<cluster-id> . Here’s the stream from our run on two ml.p5.48xlarge instances. TINY_MEGATRON and MEGATRON are the two MultiNodeTrainingValidation tests: When the run finishes, each instance carries the result as a node label: For the training details, read /var/log/aws/clusters/sagemaker-deep-health-check.log on the instance, for example through an AWS Systems Manager session. On the instance that ran rank 0, the log ends with a summary of the Megatron test: The other instance’s log has a line for every iteration, with the loss and a running count of NaN iterations: In our run, the loss fell from 11.57 to 3.62 over 300 iterations, with no NaN or skipped iterations, at about 507 milliseconds per iteration on 16 H100 GPUs. On our two-node cluster, the full deep health check took 1 hour 28 minutes after the instances finished their lifecycle scripts. DCGM level 4 diagnostics took most of that. The two MultiNodeTrainingValidation tests added about 8 minutes. Instances can’t take workloads until the checks finish, so plan for this additional time when you add capacity. Keep in mind that MultiNodeTrainingValidation tests the hardware with a fixed reference workload. A pass means the instances trained that workload correctly. It doesn’t guarantee that your own job will converge. We recommend running it on new capacity, on replacement instances, and before long pre-training runs. HMA watches the hardware on each node, but many failures that stop a training job happen in Kubernetes. A device plugin can crash-loop until its node stops offering GPUs to the scheduler, or a taint can evict a job’s pods. The job error rarely names the pod or node involved, so engineers piece together what happened from kubectl output, per-rank logs, and timestamps. The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent watches these resources from one place in the cluster. When something breaks, it tells you what changed and which nodes, pods, and jobs are affected. It reports through Kubernetes events and structured CloudWatch logs. The agent only reports. It doesn’t reboot nodes or restart jobs, because the cause might be in the workload. HMA and HyperPod node recovery still handle hardware faults, and the HyperPod training operator still handles job restarts. The agent runs as a single pod per cluster in the aws-hyperpod namespace and prefers CPU nodes, so it doesn’t use GPU capacity. It watches the following: The agent reports what it finds in two places: The following table lists the events you’re most likely to see. For the full list of events, see the documentation .

title: Introducing the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard
abstract: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart gives you hundreds of open-weight foundation models you can deploy quickly. That choice is powerful, but it also creates a real question: Which model should you start with? Comparing models usually means reading model cards one at a time and hunting for benchmark scores that different sources published under different conditions. Then you still must guess how each model will perform, and what it will cost, for your use case. Today we are launching the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard , a new way to compare JumpStart models side by side on quality, speed, and cost, directly in Amazon SageMaker Studio. In this post, we explain what the leaderboard shows, define the key terms in plain language, and walk through how to go from a shortlist to a deployed model. The leaderboard is a new view of the JumpStart base models page in SageMaker Studio, right next to the Categories and All models views. It uses the same search bar and filters you already know, and it opens on a leaderboard of large language models (LLMs). You see rankings immediately without answering setup questions first. For each model, it shows two kinds of information: Because both kinds of numbers come from the same place and the same method, you can make a like-for-like comparison instead of stitching together data from different websites. At launch, the leaderboard covers 70+ models from providers including Meta, Google, Qwen, IBM, and Arcee, with more added over time. The following screenshot shows the leaderboard in SageMaker Studio, with benchmark scores, performance metrics, and estimated cost for each model. Figure 1: Leaderboard overview in SageMaker Studio This section defines the terms the leaderboard uses: the quality benchmarks, the use case profiles and optimization goals that shape the performance numbers, and the performance metrics themselves. A benchmark is a standardized test: a fixed set of questions with known answers. Running every model through the same test gives you a score you can compare. At launch, the leaderboard reports three reasoning benchmarks for LLMs: Higher is better for all three. The leaderboard shows each benchmark separately rather than blending them into one number. That keeps the results transparent: You can weigh the benchmarks that matter for your application and check each score against the public definition of the benchmark. Speed and cost depend on your workload and on how the model is deployed. Two menus above the leaderboard control which performance and cost numbers you see: Each optimization goal picks a different configuration: A note on cost: Estimated cost reflects SageMaker instance cost only, based on the on-demand hourly rate for the configuration’s default instance type. It does not include data transfer, storage, inference component costs, or discounts such as Reserved Instances or AWS Savings Plans. Your actual bill will vary. Use the AWS Pricing Calculator for billing estimates. Published benchmark scores often come from different teams using different prompts, settings, and hardware, which makes them hard to compare. We took a different approach: For full details, including prompts, generation settings, and how configurations are measured, see JumpStart leaderboard methodology . The following steps show how to go from browsing to a deployed model. You need access to SageMaker Studio and permission to deploy JumpStart models. In SageMaker Studio, open the Models page, then select the Leaderboard view. The leaderboard keeps the same search bar and filters as the other views, and it has its own URL. You can bookmark it or share a direct link with your team. The following screenshot shows the Models page with the Leaderboard view selected. Figure 2: JumpStart base models page with the Leaderboard view selected Use the same search and filters you already use elsewhere in JumpStart to keep only the models that fit your requirements. Common filters include license, provider, and input and output modality. Start with hard requirements, for example a license that allows commercial use, before you look at scores. The following screenshot shows the leaderboard filtered by input modality, output modality, and license. Figure 3: Leaderboard with filters applied Above the leaderboard, select the profile closest to your workload from the View benchmarks for your use case menu (default: Max Context). Then choose a goal from the Optimized for menu (default: Balanced). For a chatbot your customers interact with, Latency optimized is a sensible start. For overnight document processing, Throughput optimized or Cost optimized may fit better. The performance and cost columns update, and quality scores stay the same. The following screenshots show the View benchmarks for your use case and Optimized for menus above the leaderboard. Figure 4: View benchmarks for your use case menu Each column has a blue heatmap, so the top-performing models stand out at a glance: the deeper the blue, the stronger the result in that column. Sort any benchmark column to rank models by the metric you care about most. Use the column settings (gear icon) to hide metrics you don’t need, and scroll horizontally to see more. The model name columns stay frozen as you scroll, and a fade at the edge shows when more columns are available. The following screenshot shows the heatmap and the column settings menu. Figure 6: Heatmap and column settings Choose a model to open it. From there, you have options to deploy the model or, for models that support serverless customization, to customize it. If you deploy, choose the same use case and optimization goal you compared on the leaderboard. Each metric applies to the configuration it was measured on, and a different configuration can change quality, latency, throughput, and cost. The following screenshot shows a model page with the Deploy and Customize options. Figure 7: Model page with the Deploy and Customize options Suppose you are building an internal help-desk assistant. Employees ask questions and expect fast, accurate answers that follow a set response format. You need a commercially licensed model and want to keep costs predictable. After filtering by license and choosing a chat-like use case profile with Latency optimized, your shortlist might look like this: Reading the table, Model A has the highest knowledge score but also the highest cost and the slowest first response. Model B scores almost as well, holds up on multi-step reasoning, and runs on a smaller, cheaper instance. For a help desk, where reasoning through a question and responding quickly matter more than the last few points of general knowledge, Model B is the better starting point. A bigger model is not always the better choice, and the leaderboard makes that trade-off visible in seconds. From there, you would deploy Model B, test it with real questions from your help desk, and keep Model C in mind as a lower-cost option if quality holds up. We’re continuing to expand the leaderboard. Areas we’re exploring include: The SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard brings quality, speed, and cost together in one place, measured consistently on SageMaker. Instead of comparing numbers from different sources, you can filter to the models that fit your requirements, compare them on the configuration you plan to run, and deploy with a few clicks. To get started, open the Models page in SageMaker Studio and select the Leaderboard view. To learn more, see the following resources: Open the leaderboard, shortlist two or three models for your workload, and deploy them to test with your own prompts before you choose one for production.

title: How Airbnb uses cost per task to operate coding agents on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Amazon Bedrock provides access to foundation models from multiple providers through a common API, with AWS managing the model infrastructure. It integrates with AWS access controls and monitoring, and processes prompts, code, and model responses within AWS. As coding agents move into production, changes in models and usage can affect latency, capacity, and cost. Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics in Amazon CloudWatch help teams investigate latency increases, throttling, and changes in token consumption. Evaluations, or evals, complement these operational metrics by assessing the quality of an agent’s work on a fixed set of representative tasks. In this post, we show how Airbnb evaluates models for coding agents and monitors their use on Amazon Bedrock. We explain how cost per task guides model selection and how production data helps us revisit those choices as usage changes. We also describe the runtime signals used to investigate latency, throttling, and spend. At Airbnb, thousands of engineers and engineering-adjacent people use AirChat, our internal tool for running coding agents, every week. The agents send their model requests through our large language model (LLM) gateway, which runs on Amazon Bedrock. Bedrock processes Airbnb’s code, prompts, and model responses within AWS. Eight new models came out in about five weeks. By mid-October, about two thirds of the requests our engineers sent through coding agents went to those new models. Each release can change output tokens, cost, latency and capacity at once, and the benchmark charts published with a launch don’t show how a model handles our engineers’ work. So we run two systems side by side. Before a rollout, we run evals on our own tasks to measure each model’s score and cost per task. Cost per task is the list-price cost of all the tokens an agent uses to finish one task. After a rollout, observability shows us what changed in production. When production usage doesn’t match the eval results, we find out why. You can diagnose most production problems with a few signals in the AWS/Bedrock namespace in CloudWatch: On top of these metrics, we add cost per task. Our evals measure a score and a cost per task for every model and every reasoning effort we allow. Reasoning effort is a setting that controls how much a model reasons before it responds. We use the results to choose each default, which is the model and effort that our coding tools use unless an engineer picks another, and each effort ceiling, which is the highest effort we allow for a model. Engineers run AirChat on their AirDev workspaces, which are personal development machines in the cloud. They can also hand a task to AirChat Remote, which runs cloud agents in separate cloud workspaces while the engineer does something else. Both paths go through our LLM gateway to Amazon Bedrock. Figure 1 shows how AirChat and AirChat Remote reach Amazon Bedrock through our gateway. It also shows how evals and production monitoring guide model defaults and effort ceilings. Figure 1: Coding agents and cloud agents call Amazon Bedrock through our LLM gateway. Our usage records and CloudWatch metrics show real use, and we use eval results to set defaults and effort ceilings The gateway records the model, client, team, and user for each request. We use these records only in aggregate, for cost and capacity planning. CloudWatch supplies token counts, latency, errors, and throttles. We compare those production signals with our eval scores and cost per task to decide when defaults or effort ceilings need to change. Tagged IAM roles for your callers, with cost allocation tags activated. Activate them before you start collecting, because activation doesn’t backfill earlier costs. You also need three things of your own: Before rollout, define what the agents can access and which actions need human review. Run code in isolated workspaces and test generated changes before merging. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can help filter harmful content and sensitive information in prompts and responses. For responses based on supplied reference material, contextual grounding checks can flag unsupported claims. Test these controls on your own tasks and include their latency and cost in your measurements. Start by measuring what a complete task costs. Then use those results to choose model defaults, check production behavior, manage capacity, and attribute spend. A coding agent takes many requests to finish one task, and on each request the model re-reads the context so far. So we price the whole task. Bedrock reports four kinds of tokens for each request: uncached input, cache reads, cache writes and output. In an eval run we price all four for every request and add up the requests in the task. Every cost in this post uses the public list prices dated for that run. We record the average cost next to the score for every model, reasoning effort and agent client we test, and the average includes low-scoring attempts. Reasoning effort changes both score and cost. On one model we tested, moving from low to high effort raised the score by 0.8 points. Cost per task was 2.5 times as high. We use these results to set effort ceilings, which the gateway enforces. On the afternoon a new model came out, a single request to our agents started an eval campaign, which runs the new model through all our task suites. A suite is a fixed set of tasks of one type, and we have seven. Agents spread hundreds of tasks across the suites and several cloud workspaces, and each result appeared as soon as a grader scored it. First results arrived within hours. By the next morning, every suite had a score and a cost per task, and we had what we needed for a deployment decision for the entire org. That speed depends on tasks that are already written down. Each task is a folder that holds everything one run needs. Here is a trimmed task from our machine learning work: The grader recomputes the right answer from frozen data on every run, and the agent earns a reward of 1 only if every check passes. To test one model at every effort, list each effort as its own agent in a job config: Both examples use the formats of Harbor , an open-source framework for running agent evals in sandboxes. It’s one option if you’re starting out. Running the evals can be optimized. Writing the rubric, the scoring guide that a grader follows, is the hardest part. Our long tasks run over several rounds, with a simulated reviewer pushing back between rounds. A model grader scores each run on eight weighted dimensions. Each dimension gets a score from 0 to 3. Because of ceilings like this one, an agent that needed rescuing can’t score well on polish alone. When latency rises, chart three signals before you open a support case: TimeToFirstToken for the wait before generation starts, OutputTokenCount for response length, and OTPS for generation speed. Bedrock has no native OTPS metric. You derive it with metric math, as the Amazon Bedrock User Guide describes: In the example from our session, latency rose 40 percent while time to first token and OTPS stayed flat. Someone had changed the system prompt to ask for more thorough answers, and output tokens per request rose 50 percent. The model generated at the same speed and wrote longer responses. Treat prompt changes and model upgrades as deploys, and mark them on your dashboard. Each week we put the CloudWatch runtime metrics next to the usage records from our gateway for each model. For cost and capacity planning, we also look at usage in aggregate: cost per request and the average number of requests per user each week. A new model can move both. After every rollout, we compare them with what we expected from the eval’s cost per task. One model, which we call model A, looked good in our evals. On our coding tasks, it scored more than three points above our previous best model. Cost per task was about the same, and the same grader scored every model.

title: Design responsible AI controls for Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL
abstract: A customer support chatbot that queries historical tickets and knowledge base articles stored in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition can deliver fast, context-aware answers. However, it also introduces challenges around privacy, accuracy, safety, and governance, especially when the underlying data contains sensitive customer information. In this post, we map the eight AWS Responsible AI (RAI) dimensions to Aurora PostgreSQL capabilities. We then walk through a design pattern for the Explainability dimension, using a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) based customer support chatbot as the reference use case. This post implements one dimension, Explainability, in depth. Treat it as Part 1 of a series rather than a full build-out of all eight. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition makes it more straightforward to operationalize responsible AI through its native Aurora Machine Learning (Aurora ML) capabilities. With Aurora ML, you can invoke Amazon SageMaker endpoints and Amazon Bedrock foundation models directly from SQL, without data movement, custom extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipelines, or complex integrations. This post uses Aurora ML to generate vector embeddings from SQL, keeping the embedding pipeline inside the database layer. AWS defines eight core Responsible AI dimensions, published through the AWS Well-Architected Responsible AI Lens , Amazon Bedrock Guardrails , and the Responsible Use of AI Guide . These dimensions (Fairness, Explainability, Privacy and Security, Safety, Controllability, Veracity and Robustness, Governance, and Transparency) provide a structured framework for evaluating and implementing trustworthy AI systems. Customer support systems often struggle to provide accurate, context-aware responses while maintaining privacy and compliance. Consider a customer support chatbot built on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL that uses RAG with pgvector embeddings, Amazon Bedrock model inference, and AWS Responsible AI guardrails to deliver grounded, explainable responses. A customer can ask questions such as “Why was my last bill high?” or “Where is my last order?” and receive accurate answers with citations, while sensitive data remains obscured through personally identifiable information (PII) redaction and access controls. The following table maps the eight AWS Responsible AI dimensions to practical implementation strategies for a customer support chatbot built on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition. It highlights how database features, AWS AI services, and governance controls work together to deliver a trustworthy, secure, and explainable RAG-based chatbot. Note: These are example approaches and may vary by use case. This reference architecture shows how Responsible AI controls map to each component of a RAG-based chatbot on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition. An ingestion pipeline redacts PII from support tickets, FAQs, and product documents, then converts them into vector embeddings. When a user submits a query, AWS Lambda runs a semantic search over Aurora PostgreSQL, applies Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for privacy and grounding, sends the guarded context to an Amazon Bedrock foundation model (FM), and logs every interaction for explainability and governance. Lambda grounds responses in enterprise data, redacts PII and applies Row-Level Security (RLS) for privacy, records citations and interaction logs for explainability, and writes audit records for governance. When to build this versus use a managed service: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides built-in RAG with citations and is the simpler choice when default retrieval and citation behavior meets your needs. Build the custom logging design in this post when you need provenance stored in your own schema. That provenance includes retrieved versus cited sources, similarity scores, and guardrail traces that you can query with SQL and retain under your own policies. The following diagram illustrates the end-to-end architecture of this solution, showing the data ingestion flow (left), the query and response flow (center), and the responsible AI controls applied at each stage (center and right). Figure 1: Architecture of RAG-based customer support chatbot with Responsible AI controls on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL An ingestion pipeline loads historical support tickets, FAQs, and product documentation into Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL after redacting PII, using the pgvector and aws_ml extensions for vector operations and Aurora ML integration. The Aurora ML aws_bedrock.invoke_model_get_embeddings function transforms the text into Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 vectors (1,024 dimensions), and pgvector stores them. Aurora PostgreSQL functions as both a relational store for structured customer data and a vector database for semantic search. When a user asks a question, the chatbot follows these steps (see Figure 1): Supporting operations run separately from each request: Before you begin, make sure you have the following in place: Note: The prerequisites listed here focus on the database layer. Your application layer (for example, AWS Lambda, Amazon API Gateway, and a chat UI) is separate and depends on your deployment architecture. This section presents the database-layer design patterns that make every AI-generated response traceable, from the user query, through retrieval and guardrail evaluation, to the final answer and its citations. Create the core tables for customer data, chat sessions, interaction logging, and feedback: Start by creating the schema and the tables you need. Each table serves a specific Responsible AI dimension: The customers table stores profiles for tenant-aware access control: The chat_interactions table is the core of the Explainability implementation. It logs every query-response cycle with full RAG provenance, including retrieved chunk IDs, similarity scores, cited versus retrieved sources, guardrail traces, and the model used: Because chat_interactions stores raw request_text and response_text , protect it the same way as the source data: redact PII before the INSERT (reusing the ingestion-time guardrail), or encrypt those columns with pgcrypto , and apply Row-Level Security to the log tables so tenants cannot read each other’s interactions. Logging unprotected customer content would undercut the Privacy and Security control this design is meant to demonstrate. The chat_feedback table captures user ratings and comments on chatbot responses, which supports the Controllability dimension. The ON DELETE CASCADE clause makes sure the 90-day retention purge does not fail with foreign key violations: Create the retrieval layer with vector embeddings, tenant isolation, and Aurora ML integration: Create an HNSW index for fast approximate nearest neighbor search: Enforce tenant isolation with Row-Level Security so that vector search results are scoped to the current tenant before data leaves the database: Generate vector embeddings directly from SQL using Aurora ML, keeping the embedding pipeline inside the database layer: Always redact PII before inserting data into the knowledge base. Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails (the ApplyGuardrail API) or Amazon Comprehend (the detect_pii_entities API) to identify and mask PII in your ingestion pipeline, as shown in the following example: When a query reaches your application layer, retrieve the top matching knowledge chunks using the pgvector cosine similarity operator. The following SQL query shows this pattern: Note: The 0.7 cosine-similarity cutoff drops weakly related chunks so the model is not grounded on noise. Tune it against your own data. The category filter and this threshold both post-filter HNSW results and may return fewer than 5 rows. Raise hnsw.ef_search or use iterative index scans ( pgvector 0.8.0+) to compensate. The following pseudocode shows the key patterns for contextual grounding, guardrail-intervention handling, citation parsing, and interaction logging.

title: Private certificate authority support in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity
abstract: Many teams that build applications self-host their identity provider (IdP), such as Keycloak or PingFederate, inside a private network. These IdPs usually present a TLS server certificate from a private certificate authority (CA). With private CA support in AgentCore Identity , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, your agents can now connect to these IdPs while trusting the private CA that your organization already uses. AgentCore Identity now supports private CA certificates for private identity providers. You store the PEM-encoded CA certificate in AWS Secrets Manager or Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and reference it from your credential provider . The CA certificate contains only the public certificate, not its private key. AgentCore Identity uses it to validate the server certificate presented by your IdP’s discovery, JSON Web Key Set (JWKS), and token endpoints. The CA certificate must be a root or intermediate CA certificate. In this post, we show you how to issue an IdP certificate with AWS Private Certificate Authority. We then configure an AgentCore Identity credential provider to trust it and rotate the CA while minimizing downtime. We also show how to protect the CA certificate so that only your IdP team can change it. Although AgentCore Identity supports any private CA, including enterprise, third-party, and self-signed root CAs, the walkthrough in this post uses AWS Private CA and Keycloak as the IdP. Consider an agent that needs to call an internal wiki API protected by your Keycloak IdP. The agent runs on AgentCore Runtime , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which hosts your agent code. To get an OAuth 2.0 access token from Keycloak, the agent uses an AgentCore Identity credential provider, which holds the IdP connection details and client credentials. The following diagram shows this setup. Keycloak runs in your virtual private cloud (VPC) behind an internal Application Load Balancer. The load balancer presents an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) private certificate signed by AWS Private CA. The CA certificate that AgentCore Identity trusts is stored in Secrets Manager or Amazon S3. AgentCore Identity reaches the IdP privately through Amazon VPC Lattice , which connects to your VPC through a resource gateway , an entry point for VPC Lattice traffic into your VPC. VPC Lattice is required for private CA support. If you choose the managed option, AgentCore Identity creates and manages the VPC Lattice resources for you. Figure 1: Connecting AgentCore Identity to a self-hosted IdP that uses a private CA Agents that use machine-to-machine, on-behalf-of, and user-delegated flows can also use the private CA without changing their code. To follow this walkthrough, you need: Keep the following in mind when you plan your deployment: The walkthrough has four steps. If your IdP already presents a certificate from your enterprise CA, skip to Step 2. Start by creating a root CA in AWS Private CA. For instructions, see Create a private CA and Install the CA certificate . Choose general-purpose mode, because short-lived certificate mode issues certificates that are valid for 7 days or less. When you create the CA, authorize ACM to renew certificates, so that ACM can renew the IdP’s server certificate before it expires. Next, request the server certificate. AgentCore Identity checks that the certificate matches the IdP hostname, so include each hostname that appears in your IdP’s discovery document as a subject alternative name (SAN). In most Keycloak deployments, the discovery, JWKS, and token endpoints share one hostname. For example, if your discovery URL is https://keycloak.example.local/realms/agents/.well-known/openid-configuration , add keycloak.example.local as a SAN. To request a private certificate for the IdP (console) AgentCore Identity needs to trust the CA certificate to validate the IdP’s server certificate. Because it trusts the CA rather than the server certificate itself, you don’t need to update the credential provider each time the server certificate renews. Export the CA certificate from AWS Private CA in PEM format: Before you upload the file, check it against the requirements . The file must be PEM-encoded and meet size requirements, containing only CA certificates that are within their validity period. The following commands show the CA flag, expiry date, and file size. The last command confirms that the IdP’s certificate chains to this CA. Run it from a host that can reach the IdP. It returns Verify return code: 0 (ok) when the chain is valid. The output looks similar to the following: Store the file in Secrets Manager or Amazon S3. A Secrets Manager secret must be a string secret in the same account as the credential provider. An S3 object can be in another account, which suits organizations that run the IdP in a central account. Give write access to the secret or object only to the team that operates your IdP. For an example policy, see Protect the CA certificate later in this post. You can create the credential provider in the AgentCore console or with the AWS CLI. The private CA settings appear on the console only after you connect the OAuth client to a VPC, because private CA support applies only to private IdPs. To create a credential provider that trusts your private CA (console) The Root certificate authority field accepts either a root or an intermediate CA certificate. Figure 2: Adding a root certificate from AWS Secrets Manager To create the same credential provider with the AWS CLI, add certificateConfigurations to the custom OAuth 2.0 provider configuration: To use Amazon S3 instead, replace the certificateConfigurations entry with {"s3": {"uri": "s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/trust-anchors/keycloak-root-ca.pem", "bucketOwnerAccountId": "444455556666"}} . If you leave out bucketOwnerAccountId, AgentCore Identity expects the bucket to be in your own account. To keep the client secret out of your shell history, you can reference a client secret that you store in Secrets Manager . AgentCore Identity validates the certificate and sets up private connectivity in the background, so a new credential provider starts in the CREATING status. Check the status after a few minutes: On the console, the credential provider’s details page shows the configured certificate under Root certificates . When the status is READY, your agents can request tokens from the IdP. If the status is CREATE_FAILED , the failureReason field explains why. For example, Leaf certificates are not allowed, must provide CA certificates only means that you uploaded the server certificate instead of the CA certificate. If you see Unable to access S3 object or Secrets Manager can't find the specified secret , check that the URI or Amazon Resource Name (ARN) is correct. Also confirm that your identity can read the object or secret. If the provider is READY but token requests fail, confirm that the IdP’s server certificate was issued by the configured CA and has a SAN that matches the IdP hostname. After you verify that the credential provider trusts the private CA, monitor the CA certificate’s expiration and rotate it before it expires to prevent token request failures. AgentCore Identity publishes the EarliestCertificateDaysToExpiry metric to Amazon CloudWatch in the AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore namespace when your agents request tokens through a credential provider that uses a private CA. The metric reports the days remaining until the earliest certificate in your PEM file expires. It has ProviderName , ProviderArn , and TokenVault dimensions. When you create an alarm, specify all three. We recommend a CloudWatch alarm that notifies you well before the value reaches zero, because token requests to the IdP stop working when the CA certificate expires. NOTE : AgentCore Identity reads the certificate only when you create or update the credential provider.

title: How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI
abstract: Thanks to Amit Gupta, Senior Director- AI/ML and Mark Wang, Software Engineering PMTS from Salesforce for your contributions in the vision and partnership of cross-Region inference routing on SageMaker AI. Salesforce’s Agentforce Foundation team serves a wide variety of models for products across Salesforce, including Agentforce and the Salesforce Trust Layer, in 30+ global Regions. These include both models trained in house and open source models. Hosting models separately in each Region splits capacity and makes traffic spikes harder to absorb, which turns a capacity shortfall into an availability problem. This post shows how Salesforce set up the cross-Region inference routing in SageMaker AI and how it lets the team add capacity securely while keeping its data residency commitments. It also walks through how Salesforce sees where each request was served and why. The cross-Region inference routing gives an application one invocation path across SageMaker AI endpoints in several Regions and accounts, and sends each request to an endpoint that can serve it. Those endpoints are Salesforce’s own, already deployed. The post starts with the capacity problem Salesforce faced, explains how the router works and how Salesforce integrated it into its Internal Gateway, walks through an example setup, and then describes what the team observed. Salesforce’s Agentforce Foundation team serves customers from the Region their requests come from, across 30+ global Regions and hundreds of AWS accounts, and they provision capacity based on each customer’s traffic. Every customer has its own peak window, and those windows often overlap. Provisioning for the overlapping peak would be the safe choice, but it costs too much. Customers also onboard new business units at short notice, so they must grow the fleet quickly. Adding capacity quickly, Region by Region, leaves Salesforce with capacity fragmentation: some Regions have idle instances while others run out. Before the cross-Region inference routing in SageMaker AI, Salesforce used its Internal Gateway to send traffic that the local endpoints couldn’t handle to other Regions. The team built and operated this path, supported by basic health checks, retries, and Region-switching logic. That approach had two gaps. First, the gateway had no capacity signals from either the local or the remote endpoint, so it couldn’t tell when to shift traffic or whether the destination had room. Second, cross-Region traffic had to leave the virtual private cloud (VPC) through a NAT gateway and an internet gateway and travel over public AWS networking. In design reviews, the team also raised the risk of cascading failures: moving traffic during an incident can overload the next Region, so Salesforce needed a cap on cross-Region traffic. Building this logic separately in every application doesn’t scale across Salesforce. The team needed a managed, capacity-aware routing path. The inference router is a Regional SageMaker AI resource in your account. Your application invokes the router instead of an endpoint, passing a routing target name with the same request body and content type it sends to InvokeEndpoint today. A routing target is a name you choose for one logical model, such as a toxicity classifier, and it lists the endpoints and inference components that may serve that model by their full Amazon Resource Names (ARNs). A router holds one routing target per model, and a problem with one model’s endpoints does not move traffic for the others. A routing target can mix single-model endpoints and inference components. Because each destination is named by its ARN, it can be in another Region or another AWS account. The account that owns an endpoint grants access through a resource-based endpoint policy that allows one named router to invoke it, which is how Salesforce runs it. The router prefers its own Region, and while the local destination serves successfully, requests stay there. The router judges each destination by the outcomes of recent requests. Platform faults, 5xx errors from the model container, throttles, and timeouts lower a destination’s health. As they persist, the router moves a growing share of new requests to healthy destinations, typically starting within about a minute. It can take several minutes for a destination with little traffic. Signals such as scaling progress and failed instance launches affect how quickly the router responds once errors appear, but they do not move traffic by themselves. After recovery, traffic returns over several minutes, more slowly than it left, so it does not swing back and forth. When a destination fails a request without running the model, for example by throttling it, the router retries that request once on another destination. Client errors such as invalid input do not move traffic, because they would fail the same way in any Region. Model latency does not move traffic either, because a slow response often reflects a long prompt or output and does not by itself mean the endpoint is unhealthy. The router also does not deploy models, copy artifacts, or add instances. It uses the capacity you have deployed, and each endpoint’s own autoscaling keeps adding instances as its traffic grows. In Salesforce’s Internal Gateway, the router call sits exactly where the direct InvokeEndpoint call used to be: in the per-request egress path, after the data residency check and before response handling. That check is the one routing decision the gateway keeps. A request tagged with a residency requirement is pinned to its in-Region routing target, whose only destination is the local endpoint, so it can never fail over across a boundary. Everything else goes to the router with the same body, content type, and accept type the gateway already sent. Capacity awareness, health assessment, and failover now live in the routing layer instead of in Salesforce’s code. Figure 1: End-to-end architecture for cross-Region inference routing at Salesforce. In each Region, the Internal Gateway sends client requests through a VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink). Requests with the data residency flag set to true go directly to the in-Region Endpoint A and never leave their Region. All other requests go to the local inference router, which sends traffic to its local Endpoint A by default and fails over to Endpoint A in another Region when the local endpoint shows signs of capacity constraints Salesforce treats the two routing fields on every response as first-class telemetry. The gateway logs InvokedRoutedResourceArn and RoutingReason on the same structured line as the existing request ID and trace ID, and emits them as application performance monitoring (APM) tags. Because the ARN carries the Region and account, a single log line shows whether a request ran locally or crossed a boundary, and why: local-preferred, failover, capacity-available, or only-healthy. The team joins these fields against the router’s Amazon CloudWatch metrics when investigating a traffic shift. The gateway’s timeout accounts for cross-Region round-trip latency, so a request that fails over has time to complete in the remote Region. Because the router already retries once on another destination, the gateway adds no retries of its own, which keeps attempts from multiplying during an incident. The following walkthrough shows the configuration Salesforce tested, using example IDs and names. Salesforce first created a router in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2) with a local destination and confirmed that requests were routed to it. The team then registered an endpoint in the US East (Ohio) Region (us-east-2) owned by a different account, removed the local destination, and confirmed that requests reached the remote endpoint across the account and Region boundary. In the examples, the router account is 111122223333, and the account that owns the us-east-2 endpoint is 444455556666.

title: How Social Department built culture-aware video discovery
abstract: This post is co-written by Mariah Miller and Sirajus Salekin from AWS and Nicholas Chase from Social Department. Entertainment marketing teams manage tens of thousands of video assets across studios, networks, and streaming applications. Most campaigns begin with the same video discovery problem: finding the one moment in the footage that will resonate with an audience. When a brief lands, the clock starts, and what they need is almost never something a database can describe. Semantic search, on its own, has a ceiling: It answers the question you can articulate. Ask it for a character holding a coffee mug and it will find every coffee mug in a thousand episodes. The queries that actually drive entertainment campaigns look nothing like that. They are questions of judgment: which moment in a show will travel, which line is quotable, and which single frame will work as a meme. Those questions can’t be typed into a search box. Answering them requires two things the search index doesn’t have: an editorial definition of what “quotable” or “memeable” means for a given library, and a continuously refreshed view of what is moving outside the library. Historically, answering them meant a person with deep knowledge of the show watching footage for a week, and that person doesn’t scale across a catalog. In this post, we describe how Social Department, the AI operating system for entertainment marketing, set out to encode those editorial questions as executable retrieval pipelines. The result is QuickSearch, a set of single-action queries that return the clips a marketer is looking for without requiring them to describe it: Shareable Scenes, Quotable Quotes, Memeable Moments, and Trend Align. The models in this solution run on Amazon Bedrock, so customer data stays within the AWS data boundary. It isn’t shared with model providers and isn’t used to train the underlying models. Social Department’s approach to responsible AI is that AI proposes and people decide. In production, code checks generated output against the source material (for example, a quote is discarded if it isn’t in the episode transcript). Amazon Bedrock Guardrails helps screen customer search text for prompt attacks, and a person on the customer’s team approves every post before it publishes. Social Department owns the pipeline architecture, the retrieval system, and the editorial criteria behind each action. TrackIt, an AWS Premier Tier Services Partner, implemented and delivered against that design. TwelveLabs’ Marengo 3.0 and Pegasus 1.2 models on Amazon Bedrock provide the scene-level video reasoning the pipeline builds on. AWS supplies the infrastructure, the model access including Anthropic’s Claude models, and Amazon OpenSearch Service , using its serverless option, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, for retrieval. A note on scope: This post describes the AWS portions of the system: the ingest and indexing pipeline, the retrieval path, and the services that run them. The components Social Department owns, including its media and data backbone, content analysis and discovery engine, editorial criteria, and evaluation program, are described only to the depth needed to follow the architecture. The named services that follow are the ones this post is about, not an inventory of Social Department’s full system. Social Department is the AI operating system for entertainment marketing, serving major studios, networks, streamers, and FAST applications. It automates campaign strategy, asset creation, publishing, and performance optimization across a client’s full content library. Most of those functions depend on locating the right moment inside the footage first, and semantic clip discovery has been core to the product from the beginning. Entertainment marketing operates under two constraints that a general-purpose search layer can’t satisfy. A marketer can describe an object, a location, or a line of dialogue, but not what will travel. That judgment, this moment lands and that one doesn’t, is the actual skill in the job. It was never automatable because it depends on knowing how an audience behaves rather than what a video contains. A search layer that only understands content requires a human to supply the intent, and supplying that intent well requires having already watched the show. No amount of video understanding tells you what audiences are talking about this morning. That information is created outside the library and changes hourly, while a library changes only when new content is added. A system that answers these queries has to acquire trend signal continuously and reconcile it against the library at request time. That distinction drove the core architectural decision: content understanding and trend acquisition run as independent pipelines on their own schedules and are joined only when a user selects a QuickSearch action. With QuickSearch, teams can interact with a video library in a different way, one where the system proposes rather than waits. It provides four actions, each with its own retrieval strategy, editorial criteria, and ranking model. The walkthrough that follows describes how each is implemented. The list here introduces what they do. Alongside these, Social Department keeps natural-language search for everything the actions don’t cover, and image-based search, where a reference image returns visually similar content across the library. The following diagram shows how the three parts of the architecture connect. The content understanding pipeline makes the library searchable, and the trend acquisition lanes pull in external trend signal. The QuickSearch job layer joins the two at request time. Figure 1: High-level architecture The system has three parts that run on independent schedules. Two acquire and structure information. The third resolves a user’s single selection into a multi-stage retrieval operation across both. This pipeline makes the library legible. It works asynchronously on ingest. An AWS Step Functions state machine orchestrates roughly two dozen Python AWS Lambda functions end to end. The following steps trace one video from upload to indexed clips. The pipeline is event-driven end to end. Every Lambda task retries with exponential backoff. The scene-description stage adds a dedicated throttling retry with full jitter. Non-critical enrichment steps degrade gracefully rather than failing the run, and a hard failure routes to an error handler that records the reason and reports the asset as failed. Same-Region staging for Marengo. Marengo is available in a specific set of AWS Regions. Asynchronous invocation in Amazon Bedrock reads input from and writes output to an Amazon S3 bucket in the same Region as the endpoint. The pipeline is built around those parameters. It stages each video into a dedicated bucket in US East (N. Virginia) before invoking Marengo, then reads the embedding output back from the same bucket. The rest of the infrastructure stays in its home Region while each embedding job runs alongside the model. For model availability by Region, see Model support by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . This pipeline operates continuously and independently of any library, and it is what makes Trend Align possible. Quotable Quotes draws on a second, narrower input: an external dialogue popularity signal, used strictly to weight lines that have already circulated. It’s optional by design, so if the signal is unavailable a line gets no boost rather than failing the job. This layer is where a single selection becomes a retrieval strategy. It executes each action asynchronously and returns a ranked set of clips. Three choices made culturally informed retrieval tractable. A library changes when new content is added. Trends change daily, and early-stage trends faster than that. Coupling the two would mean either reprocessing content against fresh signal, which is computationally untenable, or serving stale trend judgment.

title: Connect Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway to private APIs in a hub-and-spoke network with centralized inspection
abstract: In many enterprises, a central network team owns every virtual private cloud (VPC) and subnet, and every flow between VPCs must pass a central firewall in both directions. Agents that call internal REST APIs and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, must meet the same two requirements. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This post shows a pattern that meets both requirements. The network team keeps ownership of every subnet, and traffic between the Gateway and your private APIs and MCP servers crosses the central firewall in both directions. It covers where to place the Amazon VPC Lattice resource gateway that the Gateway uses to reach private targets. It also covers who owns each piece, six configuration decisions, and the checks that confirm the pattern works. We built and tested the pattern in the US East (N. Virginia) AWS Region ( us-east-1 ), in a lab with three member accounts and a management account in AWS Organizations. The AWS CloudFormation templates, test scripts, test evidence, and reference material (address plan, full validation checks, troubleshooting, quotas) are in the companion repository . Use the pattern as a guideline and adjust it to your own account architecture. Use this pattern when all of the following are true: Otherwise, one of the options in Table 1 fits better. Table 1: When another option fits better. We also considered managed mode in subnets that AgentCore owns, a resource gateway in each tool VPC or in the central endpoints VPC, and internet-facing load balancers with AWS WAF per tool. The alternatives write-up explains why each falls short under these constraints. AgentCore Gateway reaches private targets through a VPC Lattice resource gateway, and the two private endpoint modes place it differently. Managed mode creates it in the Gateway account, which fits environments where that account can own the subnets it runs in. Self-managed mode, as documented, places it in subnets with direct access to the backend, which fits environments that do not require inspection between the Gateway and the tool. This environment needs both conditions at once, so the pattern uses self-managed mode with one change. The network account owns the resource gateway and places it in subnets routed through AWS Transit Gateway, so every request and reply passes the inspection VPC. Give the resource gateway its own VPC and subnets in the network account. Don’t share them, and keep backends out of them. Route them through the transit gateway so every request and reply between VPCs crosses the firewall. Share one resource configuration per backend with the AgentCore account through AWS RAM. Figure 1 shows the accounts, VPCs, and traffic path. Figure 1: The network account owns every VPC and the resource gateway. The other accounts own only what they place in shared subnets. Solid lines cross the firewall in both directions. Step numbers match the following traffic path How does Gateway traffic enter the network account’s VPC without a transit gateway attachment in the AgentCore account? When you create a target, AgentCore associates the shared resource configuration with its own VPC Lattice service network. VPC Lattice then delivers connections from that service network to the resource gateway’s network interfaces in your VPC. AWS operates that hop, and from there your routes and firewall take over. What this pattern doesn’t do. Check these limits against your requirements before you adopt it: A new operation or tool on an existing target needs no new target: update the OpenAPI spec with UpdateGatewayTarget , or call SynchronizeGatewayTargets for an MCP server. The repository’s build order lists the steps in each account and the values the teams pass to each other. The snippets are excerpts from the lab templates and use the lab’s address plan . RGW_NET is the resource gateway subnets (10.0.1.0/24–10.0.3.0/24), TOOL_NET is the tool VPC (10.12.0.0/16), and ALB_NET is the ALB subnets in it. Create a dedicated VPC in the network account for the resource gateway, with subnets you don’t share and no central endpoints or backends. Route those subnets to the transit gateway. Keep one resource gateway per trust zone. Used only with AgentCore, the resource gateway consumes one IP address per subnet , so small subnets are enough. Two settings can’t be changed after creation, Ipv4AddressesPerEni and ResourceConfigDnsResolution , so choose them up front. Use Availability Zone IDs that VPC Lattice and your AgentCore features support. The lab layout lists them for us-east-1 . Point the resource configuration at the internal ALB DNS name and share it with the AgentCore account. Don’t start the name with rcfg- , which VPC Lattice reserves. VPC Lattice delivers the connection to the resource configuration’s domain. AgentCore sends the target URL’s host name (for example tools.example.internal ) as the SNI and checks the ALB certificate against it. The certificate’s subject alternative name must match that host name. The host name doesn’t need to resolve in DNS. For private API Gateway REST APIs, point one resource configuration at the network account’s execute-api interface endpoint. Each API’s target uses its own URL, and each API’s resource policy must allow that endpoint through aws:SourceVpce . In our tests, a second API in another account worked through the same resource configuration with no network change. Your firewall needs two stateful allows: from the resource gateway subnets to the tool VPC on port 443, and from the ALB subnets to the identity provider’s host name on port 443. Session-based firewalls pass replies of an allowed flow. In the lab we used AWS Network Firewall with strict rule order and the default actions Drop established and Alert established . With these defaults, the firewall drops client-to-server packets that no rule passes, and lets replies through unless a rule drops them. The rule-order notes explain the semantics. The first rule allows only the resource gateway subnets to reach the tool VPC on port 443. The second allows the ALB to fetch its identity provider’s signing keys (JSON Web Key Set, or JWKS), only from the ALB subnets and only to the identity provider’s host name. The tool VPC needs a default route to the transit gateway for this fetch to reach central egress. If your identity provider isn’t Amazon Cognito, replace the host name. Without this rule, in our tests, the ALB returned HTTP 500 and the agent received MCP invocation failed . To prove replies cross the firewall, we added a drop rule for the reply direction preceding the pass rule: Tool calls then hung until timeout, and the firewall logged to_client drops for sid 100098. Removing the rule restored the calls. Run the same test on your own firewall. The tool account keeps its own identity provider (Amazon Cognito in the lab) and creates an app client for the Gateway. Validate that client’s token on every path to the backend. Internal ALB – Make the listener’s default action a fixed response, and put a jwt-validation action on every rule that forwards. Pin client_id to the Gateway’s app client so that other clients in the same user pool are rejected. In our tests, a target with no token, one with another identity provider’s token, and one with a different app client’s token were all rejected with HTTP 401 before the backend ran. The agent saw only An internal error occurred , so use the ALB access logs to diagnose token problems. Private REST API – An API key doesn’t authenticate the caller, so add an authorizer to every method, such as a Cognito user pool authorizer with a required scope (as in the lab). Also attach an endpoint policy to the execute-api endpoint that limits it to APIs owned by approved accounts. It controls which APIs the endpoint reaches, not who calls it.

title: How Stretto built an AI voice agent with Amazon Nova 2 Sonic
abstract: This post is co-written with Danya Gordin from Stretto and Marcelo Wzorek from CI&T. Before Stretto built an AI voice agent, consumers considering bankruptcy on its Bankruptcy.com site filled out a web form with a few fields: debt amount, attorney status, and contact information. These form-generated leads carried thin margins. The gap between a web form lead and a fully qualified lead is significant. Bankruptcy attorneys place more value on a lead that includes detailed financial data: debts, assets, vehicles, real estate, employment history, and prior filings. The web form could have been extended to capture that detail, but the longer it got, the more visitors abandoned it partway through. A phone interview would have drawn the information out naturally, because people are more willing to share financially sensitive details in conversation, but staffing and training a human intake team to run those interviews was cost-prohibitive. Stretto saw an opportunity: replace the web form with an AI voice agent that conducts the intake interview by phone.
