The agent would guide callers through the full bankruptcy questionnaire conversationally and extract structured data in real time. It would then sort leads against attorney-defined rules to support attorney decision-making. The challenge was finding a voice AI solution that could handle sensitive financial conversations naturally, with low latency, clean interruption handling, and emotional awareness, at a cost that made the unit economics work. In this post, we walk through how Stretto worked with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center and CI&T (an AWS Partner) to build Tara, an AI voice agent powered by Amazon Nova 2 Sonic , a speech-to-speech model in Amazon Bedrock. Tara conducts multi-phase bankruptcy intake interviews and sorts leads against attorney-defined rules. We cover the architecture, the phased build from validation through production deployment, and how the team tested voice quality for sensitive conversations. Tara is an AI voice agent that conducts bankruptcy intake interviews over the phone. When a caller dials the Bankruptcy.com number, Tara picks up, introduces herself, and guides the caller through a structured conversation. She collects personal information, financial details, asset inventories, and employment history while adapting her tone to the caller’s emotional state. At the end of the call, Stretto’s system applies attorney-defined rules to sort the lead as qualified, disqualified, or needs-more-information for attorney review. The solution is built on Amazon Nova 2 Sonic, a speech-to-speech foundation model (FM)available through Amazon Bedrock. It processes speech input and generates speech output natively in a single model rather than chaining separate speech-to-text, language model, and text-to-speech components. This architecture is designed to reduce latency and produce more natural-sounding conversations, both critical for the sensitive nature of bankruptcy intake calls. Building on Amazon Bedrock gave the team both Amazon Nova 2 Sonic and Anthropic’s Claude through one managed service, with no model infrastructure to run. It also brought AWS security and governance controls to a workload that handles sensitive financial data. Access to both models is governed by AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Traffic to Amazon Bedrock stays on the AWS network through virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoints (AWS PrivateLink). Amazon Bedrock doesn’t use prompts or model outputs to train models (for details, see Data protection in Amazon Bedrock ). Because the models run in the same AWS environment as the voice bridge, the database, and Amazon CloudWatch monitoring, the team could secure and operate the whole solution with one set of tools. Amazon Nova 2 Sonic and Amazon Bedrock are not available in all AWS Regions. For current Region availability, see Amazon Bedrock supported Regions . The team chose Amazon Nova 2 Sonic over the previous voice solution for three reasons: The following figure shows the end-to-end architecture. Figure 1: Tara architecture showing the end-to-end call flow from telephony to data persistence A caller reaches Tara through Twilio, which opens a WebSocket connection into AWS. Traffic passes through AWS WAF and an Application Load Balancer to the voice bridge on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate, which streams audio with Amazon Nova 2 Sonic (accessed through Amazon Bedrock). After the call, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) with a dead-letter queue hands the transcript to an asynchronous processor. The processor uses Anthropic’s Claude 3 Haiku on Amazon Bedrock to extract structured fields, which persist in Amazon Aurora Serverless v2. Qualified leads route to attorneys by jurisdiction. Supporting services include NAT gateways, VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink), Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), AWS Secrets Manager, and Amazon CloudWatch. Stretto used Twilio for telephony because Tara’s intake is fully automated, with no human agents taking calls, and because Stretto wanted a direct integration with Amazon Nova 2 Sonic that kept its existing AWS backend in place. Twilio Media Streams delivers the caller’s raw audio over a WebSocket, which is the input the voice bridge needs, and CI&T had already integrated it with Amazon Nova 2 Sonic. For contact center workloads that route calls among human agents, Amazon Connect also supports Amazon Nova 2 Sonic. The architecture uses the following AWS services: The team took a phased approach: validate voice quality first, build the production integration, then expand the questionnaire scope after proving the system worked with real callers. Bankruptcy conversations are emotionally charged. Callers are often stressed, hesitant, or embarrassed. The voice agent needs to sound empathetic and natural, not robotic or transactional. Before writing any integration code, the team spent a dedicated week testing the voice quality of Amazon Nova 2 Sonic against several caller scenarios. This validation step produced a comparison report documenting the performance of Amazon Nova 2 Sonic against the previous solution across each dimension. The report became the go/no-go gate for proceeding to integration. With voice quality validated, the team built the end-to-end integration over three weeks. The call flow works as follows: The full attorney-designed intake can run 15–20 minutes, which is longer than the maximum duration of a single Amazon Nova 2 Sonic streaming session (for the current value, see Getting started with speech-to-speech ). The team treated that session duration as a design parameter and implemented the session continuation pattern , an approach that carries conversation context across session boundaries. The voice bridge tracks how long each bidirectional stream with Amazon Nova 2 Sonic has been open. Shortly before the limit, it opens a new stream with the same system prompt and tool configuration and sends the conversation so far as text history. When Tara finishes her current response, the bridge switches the caller’s audio to the new stream and closes the old one, so the conversation continues smoothly for the caller. The initial deployment covered the existing 13-field intake form, collecting the same data points the web form captured but through natural conversation. This gave the team a production baseline to measure against before expanding scope. With the production pilot running, the team expanded the questionnaire to the full attorney-designed intake over four weeks. This was a significant increase in scope: The Amazon Aurora schema expanded to a full relational data model supporting one-to-many relationships. A single caller record might include four vehicles, two properties, and dozens of individual debt line items. The final phase focused on collecting production data and tuning the system based on real caller behavior.

title: From reporting to reasoning: Getting enterprise data ready for AI agents
abstract: AWS Quick User Group DC inaugural meetup recap Many organizations are asking how to move beyond static reporting dashboards and begin using generative and agentic AI. But before an AI agent can answer questions or help teams act, it requires a trusted data foundation. Figure 1: AWS Quick User Group DC inaugural meetup, October 2026 On Wednesday, October 7, 2026, data leaders, developers, and practitioners gathered at the AWS Skills Center in Arlington, Virginia, for the AWS Quick User Group DC meetup. The session brought together founders, software engineers, and enterprise leaders, among them a team from Financial Independence Group (FIG). Attendees explored practical strategies for modernizing legacy architectures, preparing structured data for agentic workflows, and automating routine tasks with no-code tools. User groups like this provide a forum for peer-to-peer learning and collaborative problem-solving. The event offered attendees an inside look at how organizations are putting AWS Quick to work to drive productivity gains. For many in the room, this meetup was a first look at what agentic AI looks like in practice with AWS Quick. Figure 2: Arun Ganesan presenting what’s new with AWS Quick The meetup kicked off by exploring the latest product capabilities across AWS Quick, focusing on its evolution into a unified AI assistant for work. Rather than functioning solely as a traditional business intelligence visualization tool, AWS Quick unifies analytics, natural-language interaction, and multi-step task orchestration. The core of the day highlighted a real-world customer journey showing how one enterprise is rethinking its data architecture so AI agents can work from governed, trusted data. Vanessa Gonzalez, Vice President of AI at Financial Independence Group (FIG), shared how FIG keeps pushing past what’s possible today. They’re adopting new tools and platforms as technology changes, and building toward AI-powered analytics and agentic systems on top of their data with AWS Quick. Figure 3: Vanessa Gonzalez, Vice President of AI at FIG, presenting Technology is changing fast, and FIG wants to be at the front of that change. Building on its existing analytics, FIG moved to AWS Quick, a platform that brings AI into its dashboards, reporting, and analytics. AWS Quick is FIG’s “single front door” for enterprise analytics. It brings together structured data such as customer relationship management (CRM) systems, databases, and finance data. It also pulls in unstructured content such as internal knowledge bases, policy documents, and collateral, through a governed data layer. That gives FIG a base for AI-powered insights and agentic workflows built on its own data. Figure 4: FIG’s vision for its future with AWS Quick Attendees worked through two hands-on exercises: Figure 5: The DC user group building apps together One of the key takeaways is how quickly teams can go from an idea to a working solution with AWS Quick. New ideas now take hours or even minutes to build, not weeks or months. The event concluded with an open group discussion where attendees shared practical observations on bridging the gap between legacy infrastructure and generative AI. As organizations move toward agentic architectures, the consensus from the DC user group was clear: successful AI adoption isn’t only about selecting a foundation model. It starts with intentional data design, unified access, and empowering teams to build practical automations. Building fast isn’t only about tools. It also means learning from each other, which is why events like this matter. Ready to try it yourself? Start with the AWS Quick product page and the AWS Quick user guide , then connect a data source you already use and ask your first question. From there, try building an app or an AWS Quick Flows automation for a task your team repeats every week.

title: Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference
abstract: Serving large language models (LLMs) efficiently requires sufficient GPU memory and careful coordination of prompt processing and token generation. GLM-5.3’s FP8 weights, for example, exceed the 640 GB of GPU memory on a single ml.p5.48xlarge instance, before accounting for KV cache and runtime overhead. Long prompts can also slow token generation when both share the same GPUs. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference now supports NVIDIA Dynamo , combining Dynamo’s distributed inference capabilities with the infrastructure management of HyperPod to address these challenges. Dynamo is an open source distributed inference framework that supports multi-node deployment, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV-aware routing with engines such as vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM. HyperPod supports these deployments with high-performance Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking, coordinated GPU scheduling, and node health monitoring and recovery. In this post, we illustrate multi-node and disaggregated serving through a deployment example, share benchmark results, and outline best practices for optimizing inference on HyperPod. The HyperPod Inference add-on installs the Dynamo custom resource definitions and these serving and scheduling components: AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) provide the Dynamo runtime, while the add-on manages integrated component versions. To adopt a supported Dynamo release, update the add-on. The following diagram shows the deployment paths, serving components, and infrastructure management for disaggregated inference on SageMaker HyperPod. The Dynamo frontend routes requests to prefill workers, which process prompts, and decode workers, which generate tokens. These separate pools allow independent scaling and tuning. Both pools load the full model weights, and KV cache transfers between them over EFA. Dynamo also supports aggregated serving, where prefill and decode run in the same worker. In either topology, workers can run on one instance or span multiple instances using tensor and pipeline parallelism. Dynamo’s KV-aware router considers reusable prefix KV cache and active worker load in both topologies. Prefix reuse can reduce prompt recomputation and improve time to first token, while load awareness helps avoid overloading workers. For more details on the Dynamo architecture, see the Dynamo Knowledge Base overview . HyperPod provides node, GPU, and EFA health monitoring and manages node replacement, while the orchestration components recreate affected workers. Deployments configured through InferenceEndpointConfig with dynamoSpec support invocation through SageMaker endpoints. Figure 1: Deployment paths, serving components, and infrastructure management for NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Whether you are new to HyperPod, new to Dynamo, or both, the add-on offers two deployment paths to fit your workflow: Bring-your-own DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD) lets existing Dynamo users continue using upstream documentation, recipes, and manifests, with the Dynamo operator managing the deployment. To bring an existing DGD to HyperPod, use a supported container image and configure storage, networking, and pod placement for your cluster. InferenceEndpointConfig with dynamoSpec lets existing HyperPod Inference users deploy a new Dynamo endpoint using the same configuration format and OpenAI-compatible interface they already know. For the inference engine, you can choose vLLM, SGLang, or TensorRT-LLM, with vLLM used by default. The operator also supplies defaults for KV-aware routing and replica counts. Both paths support single-instance and multi-node deployments. In either case, HyperPod manages node health and replacement. The table summarizes the responsibilities for each path. The following excerpts use the InferenceEndpointConfig (IEC) deployment path with vLLM on ml.p5.48xlarge instances. Dynamo-specific settings belong under spec.dynamoSpec . Model source and endpoint settings are included in the complete manifest. This configuration runs one model-worker replica across two instances (16 GPUs), with two frontend replicas for request handling. Setting dynamoSpec.frontend.routingMode to kv-aware turns on KV-aware routing. Here, spec.replicas controls the number of model-worker replicas, while frontend.replicas controls the number of frontend replicas. Replace aggregation under spec.dynamoSpec with the following disaggregation block, keeping the preceding frontend configuration. Replica counts are set separately for prefill and decode. This example runs one prefill replica and two decode replicas, each spanning two instances, for a total of six instances. Apply the complete manifest with kubectl apply . The HyperPod Inference Operator makes the configured model weights available to the workers and generates the DGD. Grove and KAI Scheduler coordinate placement so that the pods required for each multi-node worker are scheduled together. After the SageMaker endpoint is ready and configured for chat completions, clients can send an OpenAI-compatible request payload through the SageMaker Runtime API: We benchmarked Dynamo on SageMaker HyperPod across two models to compare serving configurations. We used AIPerf to compare aggregated and disaggregated serving for Qwen3-235B-A22B-FP8 using Dynamo with TensorRT-LLM on two p5en.48xlarge instances (16 H200 GPUs). Requests contained 4,000 input tokens and 200 output tokens. We retained measured points that met two targets: P90 time to first token below one second, and median generation speed of at least 50 tokens per second per user. Among these points, disaggregated serving achieved 2.05× the highest aggregated throughput: 207 versus 101 output tokens per second per GPU, at concurrency 80 and 32, respectively. Figure 2: Aggregated compared to disaggregated serving throughput for Qwen3-235B-A22B-FP8 Dynamo supports multi-node serving in both aggregated and disaggregated modes for models that exceed a single instance’s GPU memory. To evaluate a worker spanning nodes, we used AIPerf to benchmark multi-node aggregated serving for Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 with Dynamo and vLLM, using TP4 × PP2 and eight active H200 GPUs. This model fits on one instance, so in practice you would not split it. It serves here as a controlled baseline. We compared eight GPUs on one p5en.48xlarge against four GPUs on each of two instances, using the same model, parallelism, and workload configuration. With an agentic workload featuring high prefix reuse at concurrency 32, the two-node configuration delivered 126.4 output tokens per second per GPU, retaining 99.1 percent of single-node throughput. This shows that Dynamo on SageMaker HyperPod can serve a model that needs more than one instance across nodes. The node boundary itself does not become a significant throughput penalty. Figure 3: Single-node compared to two-node throughput for multi-node aggregated serving of Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 NVIDIA Dynamo provides recipes and tools to help you select a serving configuration, benchmark performance, and tune your deployment on SageMaker HyperPod. NVIDIA Dynamo on SageMaker HyperPod Inference simplifies deploying and operating large models with multi-node serving, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV-aware routing. The managed add-on installs the serving components, and configuration defaults simplify endpoint setup. HyperPod manages model weights, auto-scales clusters based on GPU and inference metrics, monitors node health, and replaces failed nodes. Together, these capabilities reduce undifferentiated infrastructure work so teams can focus on their models and applications. Get started with the setup instructions and complete deployment examples in the linked repository. The authors would like to thank Eliuth Triana, Felipe Garcia, Sanjana Checker, Junyuan Yang, Jiahong Liu, Anish Maddipoti, Jacob Kern and Abdullahi Olaoye from NVIDIA for their contributions to this post.

title: Reducing token costs and latency in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore JSON workloads
abstract: As enterprises build production agents with dozens of tools and large structured inputs, token consumption and latency become the primary blockers to a good user experience. When these agents process large JSON data, every additional tool invocation injects the full payload into the large language model (LLM) context window, causing token usage and response latency to spike. Over multi-turn conversations, this pressure compounds, driving up costs and degrading response quality. Effectively managing context-window pressure in agentic systems is key to reliability and responsiveness at scale. In this post, we share three composable strategies we used to build a production agent for Flightscape that handles 20 MB+ JSON payloads. You can apply them to reduce token costs, lower latency, and maintain full reasoning capability across extended sessions. Together, these optimizations reduced token consumption by up to 71% and cut average latency by up to 80% across our benchmark runs on a representative 23 MB payload. Flightscape is an airline operations platform that helps airlines plan and manage their crews, flights, and operations. As part of Flightscape’s crew management capabilities, we built a Training Schedule Optimization agent that verifies crew training schedule assignments against business rules. With 40+ tools and JSON inputs in megabytes, this agent could answer complex queries across crew assignments, scheduling, and resource allocation. Although the agent delivered the required functionality, average request latencies exceeded 15 seconds across most calls. Every tool call injected its full payload into the model context, inflating token counts and costs. On larger datasets, the context window filled up before the agent could finish reasoning. The following diagram (Figure 1) details the agentic architecture and data flow: Figure 1: Agent architecture and data flow In Figure 1, the Optimizer receives a Request JSON and produces a Response JSON, which is then validated by a Business Rules Validator to generate a Validation Report JSON. All three JSON documents are ingested by an AI Agent that provides a conversational interface for users to query optimization results, understand validation errors, and explore scheduling assignments. The agent is built with LangGraph , an open source framework by LangChain, and runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can be applied to validate and filter the agent’s conversational responses, helping facilitate responsible AI practices in production deployments. We defined a custom agent state that holds the data needed by our tools: optimization request JSON, optimization response JSON, and validation report JSON. We also added basic statistics and cache data to state for rich queries. The agent uses an Amazon Bedrock model for reasoning and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to persist chat interactions across turns, and each turn follows this flow (Figure 2): This is what the state structure looks like. The state references TOPT (Training Optimizer) request and response objects, which represent the crew scheduling inputs and optimization results: Note: This state originally held heavy payloads inline. Later sections explain how we moved large artifacts out of conversational context to reduce token usage. We implemented three strategies to reduce the token costs, latency, and memory overhead caused by passing large JSON payloads through the model context. The following diagram (Figure 3) shows how the three strategies fit into a single agent turn. Strategy 1 runs at the start and end of each turn, and Strategies 2 and 3 run each time a tool returns a result. Figure 3: Overview of the three optimization strategies in one agent turn At the start of a turn, the hydrate_state() function restores lightweight session state from AgentCore memory. When a tool returns an oversized list or dictionary, the agent stores the full result in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and passes the model a compact summary with a handle. The model can then retrieve more detail with get_result_page_tool() . At the end of the turn, the dehydrate_state() function writes heavy payloads to the S3ArtifactStore and saves only references to AgentCore memory. The following sections describe each strategy in detail. To implement these strategies, make sure the following are in place: The companion code is available in this GitHub repository . Our first optimization was to change how we persist session state. Initially, large payloads were being stored too close to the conversational state. We therefore moved heavy artifacts (request JSON, response JSON, validation data, and other large derived payloads) to Amazon S3. AgentCore memory then persists only stable references to these objects, keeping the session state lightweight. To support this, we introduced a dedicated persisted-state schema that keeps only lightweight fields and artifact references. The live graph state still includes parsed domain objects for tool execution, but persistence now writes a dehydrated form. At runtime, tools hydrate heavy payloads on demand using those references, instead of loading everything on every turn. This PersistedState schema is what gets written to AgentCore Memory: The updated GraphState mirrors these references alongside the live domain objects: The dehydrate_state function strips heavy payloads from the live state and returns the lightweight persisted form along with the artifacts to upload: Rehydration reverses this process. When a session resumes, we rebuild the live graph state: deserialize LangChain messages, re-parse raw payloads into domain objects, and restore every reference key so later turns can locate their artifacts: Both dehydration and rehydration rely on the artifact store returning a consistent reference for each payload. Instead of minting a random key, we derive the reference from the payload itself. This approach, known as content addressing, serializes the JSON with sorted keys and compact separators, and uses the SHA-256 digest of those bytes as the reference. The _content_hash helper produces a deterministic SHA-256 reference from a JSON-serializable payload: Content addressing makes writes idempotent. Identical payloads map to the same key, so a turn that re-serializes an unchanged request JSON reuses the object already in the bucket instead of uploading it again. The S3-backed store exposes a put_json and get_json interface. It also keeps a small in-process cache, so payloads already read or written during the current invocation do not require a second S3 round trip. The S3ArtifactStore class wraps the put_json / get_json interface with an in-process cache and content-addressed keys: Offloading heavy artifacts to S3 and persisting only lightweight references reduced per-turn latency and the volume of data stored in AgentCore memory. With heavy payloads no longer persisted inline, tool-call responses became the dominant consumer of context tokens, prompting us to introduce result paging. Even after moving heavy payload persistence to Amazon S3, we still had a major token bottleneck at tool-response time. Many tool results were too large, which created two problems. First, we were sending full lists to the model even when it only needed a small subset, making each turn slower and more expensive. Second, those full list payloads were injected into context, which quickly consumed the context window over multi-turn conversations. In some cases, a single tool response exceeded 80,000 tokens, and the cost compounded as users continued interacting with the agent. We wanted to preserve full data access without sending everything by default. To solve this, we introduced on-demand result paging for large tool outputs.

title: Cut generative AI costs: Code for rules, models for judgment
abstract: The biggest cost lever in a generative AI system is whether you call a model at all. We often see teams route every task through a large language model (LLM), including input validation, formatting, and routing. Each call is cheap in isolation, but at production scale these small costs become one of the largest line items in the architecture. Wherever a deterministic rule can do the job, skipping the model saves money, cuts latency, and removes a source of non-determinism. In this post, you learn how to decide whether each step in a workflow needs a model at all. You can then map each option to AWS: deterministic code, a constrained decision call, or a right-sized model on Amazon Bedrock . The pattern usually starts in a prototype. A model call works for one step, so it becomes the default for the next. Those steps include validating input, reformatting a request body, and picking a route. At prototype volume, nobody notices the cost. At production volume, unneeded model calls cost you in three ways: Each new model launch then restarts the debate about which model to use. The earlier question, whether the step needs a model at all, goes unasked. Cost guidance, including the AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens , often starts at model selection. This post starts one step earlier: Does the step need a model at all? Figure 1 shows the whole decision as a flowchart with three labeled lanes: Runs as code, Questions, and Runs on a model. Take each workflow step through three questions in order, and stop at the first option that meets the step’s requirements: If the answer to all three is no, the step is open-ended and runs on a right-sized model. Figure 1: Deciding whether a workflow step needs a model, and which one Consider a customer support assistant. The following table shows how five of its steps go through the chart. You can use a model when a task is open-ended, ambiguous, or generative: summarizing a document, drafting a reply, extracting meaning from prose. Use deterministic code when the task has a checkable rule: an email format, a schema, an exact keyword, a numeric range. The following table shows what you trade away when you send a rule-shaped task to a model. A model can also hallucinate and return different answers to the same input. A temperature of 0 makes varied answers less likely, but it doesn’t guarantee identical output. Amazon Bedrock model evaluation and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails help you measure and contain these risks. A rule has neither problem, which is one reason regulated workloads favor rules. A useful test: If you can write the acceptance test as a rule, you can usually write the step as a rule. For more information, refer to Orchestration models: From rule-based to AI-native in AWS Prescriptive Guidance. Most routing and classification steps sit between a rule and open-ended generation. A rule can’t decide every case, but these steps don’t need generated text either. They need one answer from a fixed list of options that you define in advance, like the support queues in the preceding example. Use a component that limits its output to the allowed answers and gives you a signal for when to escalate. Confident answers proceed, and uncertain ones escalate. The AWS Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens describes this tiered, confidence-based escalation . On AWS, you can build it four ways: The following JSON schema limits a structured-output answer to four queues plus ‘unsure’. Amazon Bedrock requires every object in the schema to set additionalProperties to false . Whichever option you choose, check its escalation signal against your own labeled data, and set any threshold there. Keep your authorization decisions, such as a refund limit, in a rule. Many cost patterns focus on routing between models. The fast path goes one level earlier: Run the deterministic check first, and send only what the rule can’t settle to a model. Intent routing is one example. Many messages carry an unambiguous signal, such as “refund” or “reset my password”, which a keyword match resolves in single-digit milliseconds or less. If rules resolve 95 percent of requests, only 1 in 20 requests reaches a model, before any savings from model selection. (Illustrative arithmetic, not a benchmark.) On AWS, you compose this from existing building blocks: The following Choice state is a keyword fast path. It uses JSONata to send refund and password-reset messages straight to code, and it sends everything else to the constrained decision call. You can also let a model write the rule once instead of running it every time. Have it draft a regular expression or a JSON schema, review it, and commit it. At runtime the rule runs at rule speed and cost. Review a model-written regular expression, and test it against known good and bad inputs. Avoid nested quantifiers such as (a+)+ , which can make matching very slow on some inputs (regular expression denial of service, or ReDoS). When you do generate, Amazon Bedrock structured outputs constrain a response to a JSON schema that you define. The response then matches the schema, so your code can parse it without custom parsing logic (check content for correctness). Keep range checks, such as numeric bounds and length limits, in code. For supported models and schema features, refer to Get validated JSON results from models . If your rules live in configuration, allow only known primitives, such as regular expressions, schema checks, keyword lists, and range checks. Never run arbitrary code from a configuration file. Choose the cheapest and fastest model that meets your quality floor. That is often not the newest or largest model. The Generative AI Lens covers this in its best practice on right-sizing model selection . Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock covers it in depth. Define the requirements before you compare models: Amazon Bedrock offers many model families and sizes behind one API, so you can right-size each task without changing your integration. Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing routes each request to a suitable model within a supported model family. Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation transfers knowledge from a larger model to a smaller, cheaper one for your use case. Model providers evaluate a new frontier model on broad benchmarks, but your workload is one task with one quality floor. A larger model can add cost and latency without improving that task. Before you switch, evaluate each launch against your requirements, such as quality on your golden evaluation set and your latency target. The Generative AI Lens recommends testing candidate models against your ground truth data and having a way to update the model quickly. Go further and treat the decision as a tested configuration: Spend model capacity where judgment is needed, and nowhere else. You can get there in four steps: In this post, you learned how to decide whether a workflow step needs a model at all. Rules belong in deterministic code, and fixed choices belong in a constrained decision call. Open-ended work goes to a right-sized Amazon Bedrock model. Aim to meet each requirement at the lowest cost and latency that your quality floor allows. Ask whether a step needs a model before you ask which one. For more information, refer to these posts on the AWS Artificial Intelligence Blog: To try a constrained decision call, open the Amazon Bedrock console , or deploy Strands Decider from its GitHub repository . Start with one high-volume workflow and measure how much of it never needed a model.

title: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing
abstract: Today, Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing (KV-aware routing), a new routing strategy for real-time endpoints. It uses the cache state that the model container reports. It sends each request to an instance that already holds a long cached match for its prompt and isn’t too busy. It’s for teams that serve large language models (LLMs) with multi-turn conversations, long shared prompts, or heavy load. You turn it on in two places: add one environment variable to your model so the container reports its cache contents, and set RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the endpoint configuration. Your clients call the endpoint with the same APIs as before. Here’s the problem it solves: LLM applications such as chat assistants, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), and agents with long system prompts send many requests that start with the same text. A model keeps the work it did on a prompt in GPU memory, the KV cache, and skips that work when the same start reaches the same instance again. In part 1 of this series , we introduced prefix-aware routing for Amazon SageMaker AI, which sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. Prefix-aware routing infers where a prefix is cached from the request alone, so it can’t tell when an instance has evicted that cache. Prefix-aware routing picks an instance from the request alone. It hashes the start of the request, up to the PrefixLength you configure (bytes of the InvokeEndpoint payload, or characters of the message text for the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API), and sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. It never sees what an instance actually has cached. This works well when every request starts with the same shared text, and less well in two cases: The cache on an instance changes over time. An instance evicts older KV cache entries when its GPU memory fills up, but the router keeps sending matching requests there as if the cache were still warm. A conversation starts out short. In a multi-turn chat, each turn adds to the history. While the request is still shorter than PrefixLength , every new turn changes the text the router hashes, so the next turn can land on a different instance than the one that cached the earlier turns. The turns of a conversation stay on one instance only after the request grows past PrefixLength . In this post, we explain how KV-aware routing works, when to use it, and how to enable, invoke, and verify it on single model endpoints and inference component endpoints. KV-aware routing has three parts: the model container reports what it has cached, SageMaker AI keeps a managed cache index of that state for the endpoint, and the endpoint uses the index to choose an instance for each request. When you turn events on with SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG , the container publishes a KV cache event each time it stores or evicts cache entries, and SageMaker AI uses these events to keep the index current. The index holds only pointers: one-way, truncated hashes of cached content, each mapped to the instance or inference component copy that holds it. It never stores prompts, token IDs, request payloads, or KV tensors. When a request arrives, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks up the tokens in the index. The index returns the instances or inference component copies that hold part of the prompt in their cache, and how much of it each one holds. For example, if instance A holds the cached start of a conversation, the next turn of that conversation goes to A. Because the index matches on tokens rather than a fixed number of bytes, a multi-turn history can match in full as it grows. A request that shares only part of its prompt still goes to the instance with the longest match. The endpoint then picks among these candidates by weighing how much of the prompt each one has cached against how busy it is. A candidate that is too busy is skipped, so if the instance with the longest match is busy, the request goes to the next-best one that is available. If no candidate has a useful match or all of them are busy, the request falls back to load-aware routing, as described in Routing overhead and fallbacks. You don’t configure a concurrency threshold for this, as you do with prefix-aware routing. The index also follows the fleet. When you scale in, entries for removed instances are dropped. When you scale out or an update replaces instances, the new instances start with empty caches, so latency can be higher for a short time. Figure 1: KV-aware routing on a SageMaker AI endpoint. The router looks up the managed cache index and forwards the request to the instance that holds the longest cached match. Each instance reports KV cache events back to the index In Figure 1, the endpoint has three instances, A, B, and C. Each instance runs the same model in its own model container (the AWS vLLM Deep Learning Container listed in Requirements and limits) and has its own KV cache in GPU memory, so each instance holds different cached content: A holds turns 1 to 3 of conversation 1, B holds conversations 2 and 3, and C holds document 7. When turn 4 of conversation 1 arrives (step 1), the router tokenizes it and looks it up in the managed cache index (step 2). The index shows that A holds the first 6,000 of the request’s 6,200 tokens, so the router sends the request to A (step 3), and A only has to compute the remaining tokens. If A is busy, the router sends the request to the least busy instance instead (step 4). KV-aware routing needs a choice of destinations, so it is active only with at least two instances, or at least two copies of an inference component. With a single instance, every request goes to that instance and the setting has no effect. With this launch, SageMaker AI offers four routing strategies for real-time endpoints. You set the strategy per production variant in the RoutingConfig of your endpoint configuration. Both strategies send requests to where their prefix is likely to be cached. They differ in how they know where that is, and in what they need from your container. We measured KV-aware routing against random routing in two ways: a large-scale benchmark on production-sized instances, and a smaller, reproducible comparison you can follow in Verify that KV-aware routing is working. In our benchmarks with Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on seven ml.p5.48xlarge instances, we ran 30-minute tests with 20 or 100 simulated users holding multi-turn chats and document Q&A sessions, with prompts of up to about 64,000 tokens. Compared with random routing, and with long prompts under load, KV-aware routing reduced p50 time to first token (TTFT) by up to 97 percent and increased throughput by up to 234 percent. It raised the KV cache hit rate from 3–48 percent to 80–93 percent. Long prompts gained even at lower load. The gain was smallest with short prompts, where there is less prefill to save. Results depend on your workload. To measure them for your own traffic, use the checks in Verify that KV-aware routing is working. Before it routes a request, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks it up in the managed cache index. The lookup takes a few milliseconds for short prompts and longer for long ones, mostly for tokenization, but it stays small next to the time a cache hit saves. For text-only requests that use standard options, the tokens it computes are passed to the model, so the prompt isn’t tokenized twice. If the lookup is slow, finds no useful match, or all matching instances are busy, the endpoint routes the request with load-aware routing, the same behavior as the LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS strategy. The request is still served, without the cache benefit. The same happens when the endpoint can’t tokenize a request, except in the two error cases described in Invoking the endpoint.

title: Govern and discover records with common metadata in AWS Agent Registry
abstract: As organizations build more agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and skills, they need a consistent way to describe, govern, and find them. AWS Agent Registry provides a catalog for registering, approving, and discovering these resources and custom records. Each record carries a name, a description, a protocol descriptor, and an approval status. However, every organization has attributes and facts that it wants to track, and some are unique to that organization, such as its business units, resource owners, risk classifications, and development environments. Organizations want one common definition for each of these attributes, and they want every agent, MCP server, and skill in the registry to carry these facts. Until now, organizations had no way to define these facts in AWS Agent Registry and store them on each record. Custom metadata schemas are now available in AWS Agent Registry. A custom metadata schema is a set of organization-defined key-value pairs that records in an AWS Agent Registry carry. An administrator defines the schema and applies it to the registry, and all records within the registry must then adhere to the schema. When publishers create or submit records, they supply values for the fields specified in the applicable schema, and AWS Agent Registry validates those values against the schema set by the admin. Approvers can rely on the validated values when reviewing a record, and consumers and agents can use them to discover and filter records. Administrators, publishers, security and governance teams, approvers, consumers, and agents all work from a shared set of facts to govern, discover, and understand the resources in their agentic fleet. In this post, we follow the AnyCompany organization publishing an MCP server with custom schema definition, enriching that record, and making it available for discovery by humans or agents. We use an MCP server as the example, but the same steps apply to other record types. With custom metadata, an organization can use standardized vocabulary for describing its resources. The registry administrator defines the custom metadata schema : field names, types, allowed values, and whether each field is required or optional. The registry enforces the schema on every record, so a field such as environment has the same name and the same allowed values whichever team publishes the record. The schema has common attributes that apply to every record type, and you can add dedicated fields that only apply to specific record types. Each field is Text, Enum, URL, or Boolean. When a record is created or updated, the registry validates the custom metadata against the schema set up by the admin. If a record is created without any custom metadata, AWS Agent Registry saves it as NON_COMPLIANT . A team can save work in progress this way, but it can’t submit the record for approval until it has the required fields and values. If a record includes custom metadata with an unknown field, a missing required field, or an invalid value, AWS Agent Registry rejects it with a ValidationException . GetRegistryRecord returns the record’s custom metadata values and its compliance status. ( COMPLIANT means that the values match the administrator’s schema. It is not an approval. The approvers make that decision.) Discovery APIs also allow filtering records based on custom attributes. Because teams can describe the AWS Agent Registry records with the same fields and values, the registry can support and scale governance and compliance. Fields such as environment ( prod , staging , or dev ), businessUnit , ownerTeam , supportContact , and costCenter record where a resource runs, who is responsible for it, and who pays for it. A configuration management database (CMDB) ID links the record to your existing inventory, and a support-tier field sets expectations for anyone who depends on the resource. Data classification, compliance scope such as Payment Card Industry (PCI) or Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), risk tier, scan status, and a scan report URL turn an approval into a check of structured evidence. Your existing scanners, CMDB sync jobs, and classification tools write these values through the API before a record is submitted. You can build your record approval process or automation using these values, as this post shows. Custom metadata values are indexed for search. A consumer or agent can combine a natural-language query with specific metadata filters, such as environment=prod AND businessUnit=payments AND securityScanStatus=PASSED . Only approved records are returned, so a record that matches the filters but hasn’t been approved stays out of the results. Figure 1 shows how each role, from administrator to consumer, moves a record through schema definition, registration, enrichment, approval, and discovery. Figure 1: Swimlane diagram showing how a record moves through AWS Agent Registry, by role AnyCompany operates anycompany-governed-registry , an AWS Agent Registry without auto-approval. Its payments team publishes an MCP record, payments-ledger-mcp , a read-only server for ledger lookups. Existing security and inventory systems enrich this MCP record before an approval function decides whether consumers can discover it. The five numbered steps in Figure 2 match the walkthrough: define, register, enrich and submit, review, then discover. Figure 2: Custom metadata gathers publisher context and values from your existing tools, so approval and search can use the same facts To follow the walkthrough, you need: An AWS account in a supported AWS Region . AWS credentials available to Boto3 and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for AWS Agent Registry. Python 3.11 or later and boto3 1.43.113 or later. The sample implementation is in the GitHub repo. The snippets are shortened: cp and dp are the agent-registry-control and agent-registry boto3 clients. The sample repository has the complete code. AnyCompany’s admin creates a registry with a custom metadata schema that every record must follow. Every record must have its environment , businessUnit , and securityScanStatus fields. Records can also carry optional fields that the publisher or automation fills in later: ownerTeam , cmdbId , dataClassification , and securityScanReportUrl . MCP servers also record their networkEgress , which is optional. Figure 3 shows this schema and the values payments-ledger-mcp will carry once enrichment completes in Step 3. The empty autoApprovalRules list means that the registry approves nothing on its own. Every submitted record stays in Pending approval until someone or something approves it. You decide whether that is done by automated checks you build (Step 4 uses an AWS Lambda function), a human approver, or both. Figure 3: Diagram showing the registry’s common attributes, the fields added for MCP records, and the validated customMetadata map for payments-ledger-mcp Administrators can also review the schema in the AWS Agent Registry console. Figure 4 shows the common attributes and the MCP-specific field as they appear on the registry’s details page. Figure 4: The custom metadata schema in the AWS Agent Registry console The payments team’s pipeline registers payments-ledger-mcp with its custom metadata. Its first attempt uses production instead of one of the administrator’s allowed values. The registry rejects the record. After the pipeline sends prod , the record is created as a compliant draft. This is how the schema keeps every team using the same values. Next, AnyCompany’s automation adds what its own systems know: the result from its security scanner, the asset ID from its CMDB, and the approved data classification. It then submits the record for approval. An update replaces the whole metadata map , so the automation reads the current values, adds its own, and writes them back together. In the sample, the scanner and CMDB calls are stubs that you replace with your own tools.

title: Secure OAuth patterns for Snowflake Cortex AI through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: Enterprises today need a clear way to extend their authentication and authorization controls into the agentic layer, often requiring either broad service account permissions or custom-built auth integrations that add operational overhead. When an AI agent running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model) needs to call the Snowflake-managed MCP server (which exposes Snowflake Cortex Agents as one of its tool types) through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the first question enterprises must answer is: how does the agent authenticate? In this post, we walk through three Open Authorization (OAuth) configurations we tested on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Snowflake OAuth (per-user, no external Identity Provider, or IdP), three-legged OAuth with a third-party Identity Provider (corporate single sign-on, or SSO), and two-legged OAuth with a third-party Identity Provider (shared service user). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity also supports an on-behalf-of (OBO) grant (TOKEN_EXCHANGE) that delivers per-user identity for unattended workloads without a consent prompt. We focus on the three configurations we tested end-to-end, flagging where OBO fits as we go. By the end, you will be able to identify which pattern suits your enterprise scenario. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, connects AI agents to external tool providers through MCP server targets. It targets the Snowflake-managed MCP server, which surfaces Cortex Search and Cortex Analyst as MCP tools that an MCP-aware client can discover and invoke. Rather than acting as a wrapper, the Gateway aggregates the capabilities of its configured targets into a single unified catalog, which it presents to the agent as one tools/list response. The core focus of this post is the outbound authentication for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway: how it obtains and presents OAuth tokens to the Snowflake-managed MCP server. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity acts as the credential broker: the Gateway obtains a workload token by calling GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT (because the Gateway uses JSON Web Token (JWT) inbound authentication), then calls GetResourceOauth2Token against the configured provider. AgentCore Identity owns the token vault, the token refresh, and the user-to-token binding, and it fetches, caches, and refreshes tokens automatically. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity supports three OAuth configurations spanning two grant types (authorization_code and client_credentials): Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity also offers an API-key credential provider (which supports Snowflake Programmatic Access Tokens). We focus on OAuth here for per-user attribution and automatic token refresh. Each configuration uses a credential provider in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity (CustomOauth2, OktaOauth2, or MicrosoftOauth2) and a corresponding security integration on the Snowflake side. Note: We tested these patterns with the Snowflake-managed MCP server using Okta and Microsoft Entra ID. Patterns 2 and 3 (external IdP) follow standard OAuth flows, so they can extend to other OAuth-protected MCP servers, but validate the token claims, scopes, and audience settings for your SaaS provider. Only Pattern 1 is Snowflake-specific, because it relies on Snowflake’s built-in OAuth authorization server. The Snowflake-specific elements are the OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER issuer-lock parameter, the session:role: / session:scope: grammar, BLOCKED_ROLES_LIST, LOGIN_NAME / EMAIL_ADDRESS mapping, and QUERY_HISTORY attribution. If your SaaS exposes its own internal OAuth server, you configure outbound OAuth the same way as Snowflake OAuth. The following diagram shows the solution we built and the components it uses: a user-facing AI application, a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Bedrock for reasoning, with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails redacting personally identifiable information (PII) from prompts and responses, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases , the fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability, over policy documents in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) , Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with the Snowflake-managed MCP server as its target, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity holding the token vault. The outbound OAuth path has the same shape in all three patterns: the Gateway resolves a token through AgentCore Identity, which obtains and renews it from an authorization server, and the Gateway then presents that token to the Snowflake-managed MCP server. What changes between the patterns is which authorization server issues the token and under which grant: Snowflake’s own built-in OAuth server, or a third-party IdP. Those differences are set out in the Pattern comparison table, and each pattern’s runtime flow has its own sequence diagram later in this post. Figure 1: Solution overview: the reference agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, combining Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Snowflake Cortex AI through the Snowflake-managed MCP server, and the authorization server that differs across the three OAuth patterns The following sections examine each pattern in detail: the authentication flow, configuration steps, and trade-offs to help you select the right approach for your use case. The Snowflake OAuth pattern uses a three-legged OAuth (3LO) flow to deliver per-user authentication without requiring an external identity provider. Each user authenticates to Snowflake with their own credentials, consents to a specific Snowflake role, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity caches that user’s access and refresh tokens. Every subsequent Snowflake call executes as that user, and QUERY_HISTORY records their real username. Note that per-role consent is not the default. The Snowflake-managed MCP server advertises session:role:all and falls back to DEFAULT_ROLE, so you set OAUTH_SCOPES_SUPPORTED (an account-, database-, or schema-level parameter set with ALTER) to narrow the role scope the server advertises, and restrict ALLOWED_ROLES_LIST on the integration to enforce which roles a user can consent to (PRE_AUTHORIZED_ROLES_LIST does the opposite: it lists roles that skip the consent step). What makes this pattern appealing is its simplicity: no external identity provider is required. Snowflake acts as both the authorization server and the resource server, exposing its own built-in OAuth endpoints (/oauth/authorize and /oauth/token-request). Setup follows a specific order, because the callback URL does not exist until the credential provider is created. The administrator first creates the CustomOauth2 credential provider in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity with placeholder client credentials and records the callbackUrl that AgentCore Identity returns. That callbackUrl is then registered as the redirect URI on a Snowflake security integration created with TYPE = OAUTH and OAUTH_CLIENT = CUSTOM. Finally, the administrator updates the credential provider with the real client ID and secret issued by Snowflake and configures the provider’s oauthDiscovery with explicit authorization server metadata: the issuer (the Snowflake account URL), the authorization endpoint (/oauth/authorize), and the token endpoint (/oauth/token-request). The following screenshot shows the configuration steps for credential provider vendors in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity with Snowflake OAuth (3LO) settings. Figure 2: Configuring the Snowflake OAuth (3LO) credential provider vendor in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity Next, the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway configuration points to the Snowflake-managed MCP server endpoint and references the custom Snowflake OAuth for outbound authentication.

title: Announcing AI data preparation capabilities in Amazon SageMaker: Build high-quality datasets for model development workflows
abstract: Teams that ship generative AI to production know that a model is only as good as its data. That is why preparing high-quality training and evaluation data comes first. Fine-tuning an open-weight model, running reinforcement learning, or building an evaluation suite all depend on data that is accurate, well-labeled, and representative of your task. For narrow, well-defined tasks, a smaller model customized on clean, task-specific data can often match or exceed the accuracy of a larger general-purpose model prompted into shape, at a lower cost per inference. In practice, though, preparing that data is often the slowest part of the project. Labeled examples are scarce or expensive, and privacy rules limit what you can use. Quality problems such as duplicates, label noise, and answer leakage go unnoticed until a training run disappoints, and every training technique expects data in its own format. As a result, data scientists spend weeks wrangling data instead of building models. Today, we’re expanding Amazon SageMaker AI with new AI data preparation capabilities for model development workflows. You can generate synthetic examples, assess and improve existing datasets, and bring expert feedback into the process through Python SDK APIs and the AWS AI-ML agent skill. You work in your notebook or IDE, with specifications and code that you can inspect and change. With AI Data Preparation capabilities, you don’t need to stitch together labeling tools, generation scripts, and validation jobs. Each capability is a standalone building block. You can use one of them on its own or chain them together according to the workflow you want. You work wherever you already work. Use the SageMaker Python SDK directly or provide your coding agent the AI-ML skill in the agent toolkit and let your agent invoke the APIs according to established data science best practices. Describe what you need, and the agent selects and runs the right capability in SageMaker Studio JupyterLab, Kiro, or your local IDE with your coding assistant of choice. For teams building specialized models, the hardest part is often finding enough task-specific data. Splunk, a Cisco company, faced exactly this when building evaluation models for its Agent Observability product. “For Splunk Agent Observability, our ability to train robust GenAI Eval models relies on access to high-quality, diverse datasets which are hard to curate for very specific tasks. Amazon SageMaker AI data preparation capabilities for synthetic data generation is meaningfully helping us scale these capabilities. We’ve been able to generate statistically representative synthetic datasets reliably and fast, while preserving the underlying patterns our models depend on. The seamless integration with the rest of our SageMaker workflow means our data scientists and customers spend less time wrangling data and more time building models that drive real enterprise value through Splunk.” — Yash Sheth, Director of Engineering, Splunk Agent Observability The value grows when you combine the capabilities. Some common patterns: Build a golden evaluation dataset: Auto-label your raw data from a small seed set. High-confidence rows are accepted automatically, and low-confidence rows go to human reviewers. Their corrections improve the next labeling pass, resulting in a trusted, human-validated dataset to benchmark your models against. Go from raw documents to a trained model in one workflow: Consider a team preparing data to evaluate agentic customer support assistants. Its product guide says that a factory reset erases saved settings. The team wants to test whether the assistant preserves that warning when answering reset questions. One pass through the preparation workflow looks like this: This example workflow illustrates how the capabilities fit together. With the AI-ML skill, you describe the task in natural language while your coding agent helps build specifications, prepare code, and coordinate the data preparation steps. You can open those artifacts to see how the workflow is configured and make changes directly. If you prefer to invoke the APIs yourself, use the Python SDK APIs to call individual capabilities from your own code. The SDK APIs take a specification as input, so we recommend creating it with the help of an agent. You can add quality assessment to an existing process, generate data for a new task, or combine several operations. You choose the preparation steps your project needs and how they fit into your model customization and evaluation processes. AI Data Preparation runs with an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution role that you control. Your source data, generated datasets, and labels stay in your own Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets, in the AWS Region you choose. The AI data preparation capabilities are generally available in the US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) Regions. There are two ways to get started: For more information, see the Amazon SageMaker AI documentation.

title: Getting AI out of the demo and into businesses globally
abstract: AWS Forward Deployed Engineering is now available in 15 countries including U.S., Mexico, Brazil, Canada, Australia, Singapore, India, South Korea, Japan, UK, Germany, Netherlands, France, Sweden, and Saudi Arabia for commercial and public sector customers; and powered by dozens of built in production-ready accelerators. Every enterprise I talk to has built something with AI that works. A prototype that reads a claim. An agent that resolves a card dispute. A model that answers a customer question in seconds. The prototype works. The demo impresses stakeholders. Then the organization tries to put it into production, and the real problems begin. Production data is messier than the test set. Auditors want to know why the agent made each decision. Volume grows from a pilot group to the whole company. The rules that matter most turn out to live in people’s heads. None of these are model problems. They’re business problems, and they decide whether AI ever pays off. The stretch from demo to production is the last mile, where most AI stalls. It’s also where our teams spend their time. We launched AWS Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) in June to close that gap. Since then, we’ve worked through these problems with commercial and public sector customers in financial services, healthcare, sports, media, retail, and more. Here’s what we’ve learned, and how it shaped what we built. Model providers, cloud providers, and consulting firms are all embedding engineers with customers. At AWS FDE, we measure success by what remains after our engineers leave: a foundation your team owns, workflows that keep learning, and governance you can trust. Across customers, the hardest problems show up in three layers: the foundation, the workflows, and governance. Each one is harder than it looks, and each one builds on the one before it. That holds whether you’re starting fresh or building on existing systems. On a greenfield build, you can move fast, but there’s no foundation to stand on yet. On a brownfield system, agents must work within decades of data, rules, and integrations. Before an agent can do useful work at scale, it needs a foundation: identity, security, context, governance, and operational controls. That foundation must be production-ready from day one and shared by every use case that follows. Context is often the biggest gap. Most customers have data spread across systems and no common ontology, the shared model of how the business works that agents need to reason over. Without a shared foundation, the second pilot costs nearly as much as the first. Integrations get rebuilt, and lessons fail to carry forward. Most organizations reach a point where they stop and build the foundation first, so each new use case starts from what the last one built instead of from scratch. We call this the AI reset. Samsung Life Insurance had four affiliates, each building its own AI point solutions from scratch. In 45 days, the FDE team built a governed agentic platform with a single control plane and compliance built in. New agents now deploy through registration and policy assignment instead of a rebuild. Next is the work itself: High-volume, rule-heavy processes such as claims processing, know your customer (KYC) reviews, card disputes, loan origination, invoice reconciliation, permitting, and customer service. This is where AI can deliver immediate and measurable outcomes. The payoff is fast, but the knowledge that drives these processes rarely lives in a system. It lives with the people who do the work. The hard part isn’t automation itself. It is uncovering the business rules behind each decision. When an invoice and a purchase order disagree, which record wins? When can an exception clear on its own, and when does it need a person? Experienced employees answer these questions from judgment, and that judgment is rarely written down. Sometimes the knowledge is buried in the systems themselves. Rio Tinto Iron Ore runs one of the world’s most complex mine-to-ship supply chains on a 30-year-old Oracle system. That system has more than 5,000 database tables and 140 applications. Mapping it had been a multi-month exercise. The FDE team built agents that mapped it in weeks, surfacing the dependencies that Rio Tinto’s teams could validate and build against. Mapping what exists is only the start. The biggest opportunities emerge when organizations stop asking how AI can make existing work more efficient and start asking how it can change how work gets done. Governance isn’t a phase of the project. It’s part of the architecture. As agents multiply, so do security risks, costs, and decisions you must explain. Every agent needs its own identity, permissions, and audit trail, separate from human identity. And because the models underneath are probabilistic, agents need monitoring that keeps their results predictable and auditable long after launch. The system also must keep working as everything around it changes. Models drift, business rules shift, data formats change, and regulations tighten. New security issues appear, and code falls out of date. As newer models arrive, the instructions and tooling around them will change too. You need evaluations and guardrails that keep agents predictable where they must be and creative where they can be. When governance comes at the end, it becomes the gate that stops production. When it’s built in from day one, it’s what lets your business move fast. Marsh, a leading global professional services firm, needed agents that would hold up under its own audit standards. The FDE team built those controls in from the start, and the first use case reached production about two months after work began. Efficiency gains in the targeted areas have been as much as 70 percent, with some process steps moving from hours to seconds. Marsh has since expanded the work and keeps extending the system itself. Our perspective comes from building and running these systems ourselves. AWS FDE pairs a small team of AWS engineers, scientists, and product managers with your engineers and a crew of specialized AI agents. Many of our FDEs come from the service teams that build Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Kiro, AWS Quick, and AWS Security Hub. They’ve built and run AI products at AWS scale, and they bring those engineering practices into your environment. Together, our teams take a high-value business problem to production in 45-day sprints, in your own AWS account. Customers shouldn’t need to choose between speed, scale, and control. FDE is built to deliver all three. Speed – You might come to us with a broad goal or an ambiguous problem. We refine it with your business stakeholders, then build in your environment from day one, on your data and through your identity and security controls. We build in short cycles alongside the people who do the work. Each cycle puts real cases in front of them, and the unwritten rules come out as they react. We capture those rules in a living context, so the system keeps learning after we step back. Nothing gets rebuilt between prototype and production. You see working demos throughout, evaluations track progress against the outcomes you care about, and you have a production system within a quarter or less. Scale – A point solution can move fast on one use case but leaves no foundation for the next five. Every FDE team works the same way, using the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), the method our own service teams use to take a broad problem to a working outcome. We deploy an opinionated AWS stack that reflects what we’ve learned building AI services, adapted to your environment: a living context of how your business works, a workbench where your engineers and agent crews build, a runtime on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and a control tower for governance, outcomes, cost, and agent performance.

title: Build WhatsApp AI agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: Across Latin America, India, and Southeast Asia, WhatsApp is one of the most widely used messaging applications. That makes it an obvious place to build an AI agent. For many end users, it is how they expect to interact with businesses. However, it is also a genuinely difficult surface to build for, even when your agent already runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . The agent is rarely the hard part. The integration is. Inbound messages arrive as deeply nested, type-dependent payloads that must be authenticated and normalized before your agent can read them. Media such as voice notes, images, and documents each require their own processing pipeline. Beyond message handling, you need conversation memory that survives sessions, durable schedules for reminders, and an authenticated path for external systems to trigger outbound messages. And anything you send more than 24 hours after the end user’s last message must use a pre-approved Meta message template. Wiring that up means configuring more than 10 AWS services and learning a set of WhatsApp system behaviors that most teams discover only by hitting them. None of it is visible to a customer, but all of it has to work. Most teams either build it from scratch or hand the integration to a third-party service. SMART (Social Messaging Agent Runtime Toolkit) is a third option: an open source Python SDK and Terraform stack that gives you the full channel layer. You provide an agent that runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, and SMART handles the rest. One command deploys the entire infrastructure to your AWS account. Teams are already running on SMART with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Webmotors, originally scoped as a two-month engagement, compressed delivery to six weeks and moved their internal team into controlled production ahead of a full launch. Whether you are starting from scratch or migrating an existing agent, you own the agent’s logic. You let SMART handle the channel. The following table compares what each concern costs to build yourself against what SMART provides. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. SMART builds on two of its main capabilities: Because AgentCore is framework-agnostic, so is SMART. Strands Agents gets memory wired automatically. LangGraph, Pydantic-AI, or another framework that gives you control over the conversation loop can integrate too. The SDK exposes the same memory and session hooks regardless of framework. You keep full control over the elements that differentiate your product: framework, model, prompt, and business logic. The contract between SMART and your agent is deliberately small. Your agent receives the inbound message and returns text, optionally with rich message attachments. Everything else, session wiring, memory binding, delivery scheduling, is handled for you. The following example is a complete agent.py for a SMART project. The scaffolding command ( socialagent init ) creates the project structure and configuration around it. This file is where your agent logic lives. The create_session_manager() function binds the agent to AgentCore memory scoped to that phone number, so history survives across sessions and deployments for the memory retention period (7 days by default). The socialagent_notify_context() wrapper is the other pattern worth keeping. Tools sometimes need to send something while the agent is still working, such as a button list or a progress update. Sending it immediately corrupts the conversation history, and the user’s next message fails. The wrapper collects those messages instead, and they go out in order once the turn finishes. Your tools send messages normally and do not deal with the timing. The following diagram shows how an inbound message travels from WhatsApp to your agent and back, and where the shared infrastructure sits. Figure 1: How an inbound WhatsApp message flows through the SMART channel layer to the agent and back The SMART core stack is organized into distinct layers: message processing, an agent layer, and a service layer. AWS End User Messaging Social receives inbound WhatsApp messages and routes them to the processing layer. An AWS Lambda function handles the channel logic, while Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides the runtime, memory, and observability for the agent itself. Supporting services such as Amazon DynamoDB (optional, for per-user state), AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon CloudWatch, and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) supply state management, credentials, monitoring, and storage across the stack. Inbound events arrive through Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS). On each event, the webhook Lambda function verifies the SNS message signature, normalizes the payload, and rate-limits each user (20 messages per minute by default, with the DynamoDB state table enabled). It then fires a read receipt and typing indicator, so the conversation feels alive before the model finishes. Voice notes go through Amazon Transcribe. Other media becomes a descriptor or goes to a hook you register if you want custom handling. When the agent throttles or fails, the user receives a readable message that you can customize, rather than silence. Agents built on SMART interact directly with end users, so production deployments should include appropriate safeguards. The Terraform stack creates and configures an Amazon Bedrock Guardrails resource by default. With a single guardrail variable in your environment configuration, you can use the stack’s default guardrail, bring your own, or opt out entirely. The controls that you apply are up to you. SMART makes sure the wiring is already in place. After the message is ready, the webhook function passes it to AgentCore runtime. AgentCore memory maintains conversation context across sessions, and AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, traces every step for debugging and audit. The webhook function sends the reply and messages your tools queued during the turn. A notification function handles sends outside a turn, such as proactive or scheduled messages. External systems trigger your event handlers by posting to an Amazon API Gateway endpoint protected by an API key and a Lambda authorizer. The event is published to Amazon SNS and the event Lambda runs your handler. Amazon EventBridge Scheduler handles time-based outreach, such as reminders and recurring check-ins. With message templates managed through AWS End User Messaging, you can send structured notifications outside the 24-hour WhatsApp session window. A single socialagent deploy provisions the following resources (it runs terraform apply under the hood). The agent container image and the Lambda layer build in AWS CodeBuild during the apply. Docker isn’t required locally. Before you deploy, confirm that you have the following. Note: This is sample code, for non-production usage. You should work with your security and legal teams to meet your organizational security, regulatory and compliance requirements before deployment. Start by cloning the repository and scaffolding a project. The --blueprint flag selects a project blueprint. Three blueprints ship, and minimal is the default if you don’t pass an argument: You get a project with your agent.py , socialagent.dev.yaml (the project’s deployment configuration), handler stubs for the webhook, notification, event, and scheduler paths, and a vendored copy of socialagent_runtime/ . The personal assistant and appointment-scheduler blueprints also bring tools, skills, and a templates.yaml for your message templates. minimal ships none of those, so you add them as required. Next, iterate locally, with no infrastructure at all. The socialagent dev command runs your real agent loop and real tools in a terminal read-eval-print loop (REPL), with AWS channel I/O stubbed. Memory becomes a local file-backed session, and state becomes a local JSON file shared across your dev sessions.

title: Reason over time-series data with OpenTSLM on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
abstract: Across industries, decision-making starts with understanding what is changing and why. Industrial organizations collect data that informs decisions across their operations.
