title: 李沐加盟的Aimotion，是一傢什麼AI公司？
abstract: 李沐加盟的Aimotion，是一傢什麼AI公司？ 思邈 2026-11-17 19:40:37 來源： 量子位 瞄準「產業級世界模型」 允中 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號QbitAI AI大神 李沐 ，悄悄多了一個新身份。 最新訊息，這位前AWS AI資深首席科學家、Apache MXNet創始人之一、卡內基梅隆計算機博士，已經正式出任矽谷AI公司 Aimotion 的 聯合創始人兼CTO ，親自帶隊搭建其下一代產業級AI技術體系。 這家公司來頭不小，Aimotion主要面向汽車等高價值、長決策週期行業，提供AI銷售與營銷解決方案，業務覆蓋美洲、歐洲、亞太等市場。近期，他們剛剛完成了 數千萬美元A輪融資 ，領投方是BAI Capital。 △圖源：Aimotion官網 需要說明的是，李沐並未因此離開他所創立的Boson AI。據瞭解，他將繼續擔任Boson AI聯合創始人兼CTO，促成兩家公司聯合攻關： 產業級世界模型與商業AI Agent技術。 具體而言，就是將Boson AI的底層模型能力與Aimotion的真實產業場景沉澱深度融合，打通基礎技術與產業應用閉環，共同打造面向商業環境的產業級世界模型。 什麼是產業級世界模型？ 區別於通用模擬類世界模型，這一技術將對商業規則、客戶決策邏輯、業務因果關係進行建模，實現場景推演、趨勢預判與長週期任務規劃。 藉此，AI Agent將從被動問答升級為可自主執行複雜銷售業務的智慧主體，推動AI由營銷輔助工具轉變為 創造實際收益的商業智慧系統 。 李沐表示，AI下一階段的發展核心在於 深度落地複雜商業場景，充分釋放下一代商業智慧體的價值 。 關於更多技術與產品細節，Aimotion表示將於後續擇機披露。 *本文系量子位獲授權刊載，觀點僅為原作者所有。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 Agent 世界模型 李沐 思邈 材料科學智慧體MatOS正式開源！大幅提高材料研發任務成功率 2026-11-17 龍芯、海光老兵集結，通研院孵化的AGI晶片公司浮出水面！半年連融數億元 2026-11-16 提速2.48倍且畫質不掉線，AI影片“降本增效”有了新解法 2026-11-16 高難盲測超越GPT-6-Astra與Opus-5！無界前沿開源Fx-Bio-1031，把RSI帶進生命科學 2026-11-13 相關閱讀

title: Introducing Gemini 4 Neon
abstract: Introducing Gemini 4 Neon Nov 18, 2026 | Bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Koray Kavukcuoglu SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article [[duration]] minutes This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X In this article Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the Vals Index , Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index . Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing. The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window. Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio , Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app . Delivers across enterprise, analytical, and scientific work Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index , it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench . Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI , ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. Finally, it debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on Arena's new Agent Arena Index across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions. On scientific and mathematical reasoning, spanning quantitative analysis, mathematics, and technical research problems, Neon is best in class on Terminal-Bench Science (70.5%), RiemannBench (84.0%), and HLE-Diamond (71.3%). Built for production-ready code Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity. It cuts down on redundant file reads, shares progress as it works, and handles context compaction reliably in long sessions. Across core developer and researcher workflows, Neon achieves frontier performance and is competitive with the leading models in its class, ranking #1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6), with a score of 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% (at its default high setting) on FrontierCode 2.0 . For production-ready code, Neon handles multi-file debugging and refactoring across repositories with targeted, surgical edits. On SWE-sweep, it already leads on the mini-SWE harness (12.8%) and more than triples to a state-of-the-art 39.0% in Google Antigravity showing what the Antigravity harness unlocks. Driving Blender MCP in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon used /swarm to build a photorealistic 3D lab bench visualizing the model names with elemental accuracy pairing Bunsen flames for Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen with high-voltage gas discharge tubes for Gemini 4 Argon and Neon. In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon wrote a first-person WebGL2 freeride ski simulator from scratch on real Mont Blanc and Chamonix elevation terrain — combining 10,200 lines of custom shaders, 120 Hz ski physics across six alpine lines, dynamic carved tracks, slab avalanches, and spatial Web Audio with zero pre-made assets. Using /swarm in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon pulled archival photos to recreate Alan Turing’s 1936 study at King’s College, Cambridge in interactive 3D — from King’s Chapel outside to Room X.8 inside, complete with a working Universal Turing Machine running on his desk. In Google Antigravity, a Gemini 4 Neon agent swarm turned a single image into a 100,000-cell Google Sheet with zero embedded images and zero Apps Script — using over 500,000 live spreadsheet formulas to run edge detection, map 3D depth, and relight the scene across six interactive modes. Brings efficiency and control to production-grade workflows We’re refining thinking levels with each new model release to give teams finer control and a smoother progression from one tier to the next. Neon’s four levels scale steadily, letting teams dial intelligence and token spend to what each workload needs. Neon delivers high performance at a lower cost per task across third-party benchmarks. At its default high thinking level, it pairs a high Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score with a 32% lower cost per task than Carbon. It also sits on the Pareto frontier on both the Vals index and Agent Arena at high, with roughly 50% to 80% lower cost per task than top competing frontier models. xhigh thinking adds deeper, multi-step reasoning for the hardest engineering, analytical, and scientific workloads. Neon shows its highest intelligence score here, while still costing 36%+ less per task than competing models at their highest setting. Built for fast, efficient, frontier-level cyber defense As agentic coding scales, generating secure code from the start is critical. Gemini 4 Neon for cyber produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench , achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%). Securing systems also means proactively finding flaws before attackers do. Penetration testing has served as a cornerstone of enterprise cybersecurity. On WebExploitBench v1.2 , Neon is state-of-the-art (51.26%) at half the cost of competing large models. To fortify existing code, Neon for cyber delivers frontier-level performance across the code hardening lifecycle — vulnerability finding, validating, and patching — all while being faster and more cost efficient than large frontier models. Finding code vulnerabilities: Neon achieves state-of-the-art performance on SEC-bench Pro (90.5%), while costing roughly half as much per challenge. Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate, defenders rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. On ExploitGym, it achieves frontier-level performance using half the tokens of Carbon. Patching vulnerabilities: Fixing the root cause of vulnerabilities is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Neon reaches 70.7% on Collinear’s CWE-bench v2 , driving a 3.4% uplift over Carbon. Gemini 4 Neon for cyber is rolling out to trusted defenders in the coming days as part of the Fairwind Program .

title: Genie 4 is now available
abstract: Genie 4 is now available Nov 18, 2026 | Explore a new Project Genie experience for Google AI Ultra subscribers, featuring Genie 4, the Project Genie agent, and a community gallery. Diego Rivas Group Product Manager, Google DeepMind Pavan Kumar Group Product Manager, Google Labs Read AI-generated summary We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, offering more responsive, social, and interactive world generation. You can now use natural language to edit environments in real time, add native audio, and share your creations in our new community gallery. Visit the Project Genie website to start building your own worlds or join the waitlist if you are a Google AI Pro member. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers for creating interactive worlds. You can now modify environments in real time using text prompts and native audio features. Our updated Genie 3 model supports longer sessions, panorama grounding, and linked world sequences today. The new Project Genie agent helps you build custom worlds through simple natural language conversations. You can publish your creations to our community gallery for others to explore and remix. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are updating Project Genie to help you create and explore interactive digital worlds. With our new Genie 4 model, you can change weather, add characters, and hear adaptive audio in real time just by typing prompts. You can also use our new creative agent to build complex environments through simple conversation. If you subscribe to Google AI Ultra, you can start building, sharing, and remixing these custom worlds in our community gallery today. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie , an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them. So today, we are rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, making these worlds far more responsive, creative, and social. This update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, new upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent which helps users build their vision, and a community gallery to discover, explore, and remix worlds. Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser. Experience Genie 4 in Project Genie With Genie 4 , our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a new prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue. Discover new Genie 3 capabilities While Genie 4 delivers our highest-fidelity visuals, physics, and native audio, Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie’s model picker when you want longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces. Today’s Genie 3 updates include: Extended sessions and world chaining: Explore for up to 3 minutes per generation (up from 60 seconds), or link multiple worlds together for longer journeys. 360-degree panorama image grounding: Seed new worlds from 360-degree panorama images. Real-time in-world events: Dynamically change the environment with natural-language prompts while you explore. Genie 3 uses real-time promptable events to connect different worlds into one continuous flight across forests, underwater ruins, and icy seas. See how 360-degree panorama grounding in Genie 3 keeps Petra’s canyon and facade consistent as you look around. Watch how Genie 3 combines longer runs, 360-degree panorama grounding, and real-time promptable events - transforming the world as you fly and even summoning a dragon to ride on command. Create new interactive experiences The new Project Genie agent takes creation beyond a single text or image prompt. Now crafting an interactive universe is as effortless as having a conversation. Simply describe your vision in natural language, and the agent orchestrates Google’s suite of multimodal models to craft initial visuals establishing your world’s signature look, paired with custom background scores tailored to the mood. You can also bring Gemini models into the session as you explore: it observes what is happening on screen, surfaces context-aware suggestion chips for where to go next, or triggers in-world events automatically as your journey unfolds. Turns a natural language prompt into an interactive spacewalk, then an alien spaceship appears on command Remix a hillside cafe into a glass pavilion in the desert. Publish custom worlds to the gallery for others to explore and remix. Explore the new gallery When you just want to jump straight into exploring, the new Project Genie gallery brings together a rich collection of curated worlds alongside creative work from the community. Transform personal photos into explorable spaces in “Living Memory,” wander through rich prehistoric habitats grounded in 360-degree panoramas in “Dino Field Guide,” or pit themed objects against one another on a desk with Gemini serving as your real-time referee in “Rock Paper Scissors.” Browse curated and community-built worlds and jump straight into exploring. “Villa Giallo,” created with Will aka BLVCKL!GHT, uses Genie 4 to turn a gothic manor into an interactive, room-by-room mystery. “The Life of Ants,” built with filmmaker Anand Gandhi, uses Genie 4’s photorealism to let you navigate a colony from an ant’s perspective. The gallery also showcases inspiring collaborations with pioneering creators who had early access to these tools. Teaming up with creative technologist Will aka BLVCKL!GHT, we created “Villa Giallo,” an atmospheric, room-by-room mystery inside a gothic manor. And with filmmaker Anand Gandhi, we built “The Life of Ants,” inviting you to navigate a complex colony from an ant’s perspective, drawing on Genie 4’s stunning photorealism. Beyond exploring curated worlds, you can also launch your vision with a simple prompt or remix existing gallery experiences alongside the Project Genie agent — tweaking the underlying world structure, soundtrack, or rules to make it uniquely your own. Once you’ve crafted something special, publish your creation to the community gallery for others to explore and remix. Learn how we are building responsibly We are committed to developing and rolling out interactive world models responsibly. All video and audio generated in Project Genie includes SynthID watermarking, and all model inputs and outputs go through safety screenings. Genie 3 and Genie 4 remain world models in the frontier research space. As the research continues to evolve, we are actively tackling key challenges such as camera latency, intricate physical interactions, real-time audio precision, and long-term scene permanence. For a deeper look into model limitations and our progress on these fronts, read our Genie 4 model research overview . Try Project Genie today Eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers can try the new Project Genie experience starting today, and Google AI Pro members can join the waitlist on the same page. Posted in:

title: Can AI help build a healthier future?
authors: Doug Burger, Ava Amini, Eric Horvitz, Dr. Eric Topol
abstract: Technical advancement is moving at such a rapid pace that it can be challenging to define the tomorrow we’re working toward. In The Shape of Things to Come , Microsoft Research leader Doug Burger and experts from across disciplines tease out the thorniest AI issues facing technologists, policymakers, business decisionmakers, and other stakeholders today. The goal: to amplify the shared understanding needed to build a future in which the AI transition is a net positive. Microsoft Principal Research Manager Ava Amini , Microsoft Chief Scientific Officer Eric Horvitz , and physician-scientist and Microsoft AI health advisor Eric Topol (opens in new tab) of Scripps Research join Burger to tackle a question with ramifications for every individual on the planet: What might the future of medicine look like with AI, and what needs to happen first? Drawing from experiences in machine learning, bioscience, and clinical care, the group explores AI-assisted medical diagnosis, the untapped potential of leveraging AI in medical imaging, whole-patient models, virtual cells, and the role of biological foundation models in scientific discovery. The group also examines why promising research can be slow to reach patients, how AI could guide experiments and drug discovery, and why better biological data and real-world validation remain essential. This episode delivers a research-grounded conversation of what AI can do today in the health space, the challenges and opportunities still ahead, and the shape of things to come. DOUG BURGER: This is The Shape of Things to Come, a Microsoft Research Podcast. I’m your host, Doug Burger. In this series, we’re going to venture to the bleeding edge of AI capabilities, dig down into the fundamentals, really try to understand them, and think about how these capabilities are going to change the world—for better and worse. Today, I’m bringing three experts in the fields of biomedicine working on the frontlines of AI, biology, and medicine to see where healthcare is going, where the deep understanding of biology is going, what medical advances are coming, and how will AI change the future of health. These questions are really important because they will determine the shape of things to come. In today’s podcast, I’ve invited three leading researchers in medicine, biology, and machine learning/AI. Eric Horvitz is Microsoft’s chief scientist [chief scientific officer] and is both a PhD and an MD. How you spent all those years in school, I have no idea. I’ve known Eric for decades and his work has shaped the entire field of machine learning. He’s a legend in the machine learning community and is a good friend. Eric Topol is our second guest. He’s the executive vice president of Scripps Research (opens in new tab) , the largest nonprofit biomedical research institute in the United States. He’s published over 1,300 peer-reviewed papers. Shocking, [LAUGHTER] shockingly productive. Authored four books (opens in new tab) . So just an amazingly impressive, prolific scientist and physician. Finally, Ava Amini is a principal research manager in Microsoft Research. She’s a rising star in our organization, an expert in the intersection of AI and precision medicine, and she’s a co-lead of Project Ex Vivo , a collaborative effort between Microsoft and the Broad Institute that is focusing on defining, engineering, and targeting cell states in cancer. So thank you all for joining today. I think we’ve got a really, really amazing set of people, myself excluded. And I’d like to start to my guests here. It’s clear there’s a huge disruption happening at the intersection of biology and medicine and AI right now. Just, you know, we’re seeing things, breakthroughs, happening at an accelerating pace. Models are helping us to discover structures and create abstractions that are really useful for moving forward the field of medicine. I’ve seen some recent talks where scientists with cancer used AI to design drugs for themselves. I mean, just unbelievable. And today, I’ve got some long-term questions for us to discuss, maybe a little bit provocative. But I’d like to start with what each of you see as what’s happening right now, like, on the, on the intersection of medicine and biology and AI. I think each of you has a unique vantage point. I’ll go around the horn, and I know, Eric, there’s a, you know, you have a cover article on Science magazine (opens in new tab) that’s really exciting, and so maybe you could talk a little bit about that, as well. So I’ll start with you, and then I’ll go to Eric Topol and then Ava. I think healthcare and the biosciences are fortunate disciplines as in that there’s been a digitalization of content—whether it be protein structure over, over decades, electronic health records, and so on—that makes these fields amenable to being at the ready for AI inferences and innovation. And therefore, I’ve been extremely optimistic about the long-term futures as well as what we’ll see early on at the frontiers of AI when it comes to the biosciences and healthcare. Just extraordinary to see what’s happened over just the last five to eight years in the biosciences with both discriminative and generative AI models. You know, the AlphaFold (opens in new tab) breakthrough was tip of the iceberg, and we see just a whole, in some ways, a crest and a crashing of the wave of possibilities now when it comes to experimental platforms, experimental design, data interpretation in the biosciences, hypothesis generation, I should say, as a, as an assistant and a companion to scientific reasoners and human scientists. In healthcare, we have an extraordinary opportunity to address long-term challenges in patient safety, in getting to timely diagnoses, in accessibility of healthcare. And after a couple of years of intensive work, I and just fabulous colleagues at Microsoft worked intensively on taking healthcare challenges when it comes to applications of AI and benchmarking—medical diagnostic challenges, for example—and moved it into what I would call the realm of medical cognition, where instead of looking at a whole case that’s given to an AI system and looking at the accuracies that are reported on its ability to diagnose, for example, a form of differential diagnosis, we instead put the AI system in the, in the shoes of a clinician. You get an initial set of symptoms, you get chief complaint, some history, a little window on what’s going on when a patient comes in in an ambulatory setting, and then it’s up to the clinician to ask the right questions and to then think about tests, balancing the information value with the cost of the tests. This is the sequential diagnosis challenge. And we applied AI to both the … formulating the hypothesis component of that as well as decision-making about the next best tests to order, questions to ask, and also when to call a diagnosis, even under uncertainty, as a concluding convergent diagnosis and getting on with things with therapy, for example. And showed just, I think, remarkable abilities of a number of frontier language models to do a fabulous job. And, you know, and again, did some comparisons with human generalist physicians, which have to be taken at face value and with limitations in what we did with … on the comparison, but still show the promise of the methods for assisting clinicians of the future. BURGER: Well, congratulations on the paper. It’s a really big deal. Eric [Topol], moving on to you. You know, you’re the one person on the podcast who’s not a Microsoft employee [LAUGHTER], and so you see a very different, I think, set of things than we might see from our vantage point, although I think each of the three of us sees different things in general. Could you just tell us what you’re seeing? Like, to somebody listening, you know, we have a broad listenership from all different segments, not just experts in AI or medicine.

title: Mathematical proof, powered by AI. And no hallucinations!
abstract: Every day brings new evidence of the awesome power of AI. There have been dramatic developments in mathematics: AI models are solving tough problems from Mathematical Olympiads and even some big open research problems. But AI agents are notorious for simply making stuff up, or “hallucinating”: don’t we have to check their solutions carefully? In fact, the computer can check the agent’s proofs for us, and better still, proof checking can be interleaved with proof generation, keeping it on the right track. To be checked, the proof must be written in some logical formalism: a precise language that expresses mathematical reasoning. Proof assistants are apps designed for writing and checking formal proofs. They include Lean, favored by many mathematicians; HOL Light, used at AWS to formally verify high-performance cryptographic code (including for post-quantum cryptography); and Isabelle, used at AWS to verify the Nitro Isolation Engine. They were originally built to help human users write proofs, but now the “user” will be an AI agent. Most proof assistants are suitable for this task. In this post, we’ll focus on Isabelle. To generate formal proofs, we need a way for the AI agent and the proof assistant to talk to each other. Fortunately, we have the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which is supported by all the leading AI agents. Conceptually, the MCP is a wire connecting an agent to a tool (here, a proof assistant), which may need to be modified to accept the connection. Some proof assistants, like HOL Light, provide a simple command-line interface, sometimes called a REPL (for read-eval-print loop): the user types commands, and HOL Light replies. Connecting an agent to a REPL is easy. But most proof assistants provide sophisticated user interfaces, such as the Lean extension for Microsoft VS Code. That’s great for human users, but an AI agent needs something simple and direct. So we are proud to announce the following tools, which are publicly available in the AutoCorrode verification suite: I/Q: This enables an AI agent to communicate with a live Isabelle session running on your computers. It allows you to temporarily hand over control of the proof assistant to the AI to fill in some formal material or to assess the context and provide advice. I/R: This enables an agent to develop proofs or other formal material while the user keeps working with the proof assistant. The agent still “talks” directly to the proof assistant to know if its proofs work, but it does not take control the way I/Q does. Isabelle Assistant: Powered by I/Q, this provides an Isabelle user with a chat window to an AI agent, which can observe and modify the user’s session, developing or fixing proofs. It’s less powerful than the full I/Q and I/R package but runs in a convenient window, right out of the box. To get an idea of how effective AI is at solving mathematical problems, let’s look at some well-known examples, done automatically with the help of Isabelle Assistant. The square root of two is irrational The ancient Greeks were already aware that the square root of two could not be written as a fraction. Suppose that √2 = a/b is a fraction in lowest terms. Then 2b2 = a2, implying that a is even. But then a = 2k for some k. Then 2b2 = 4k2, so b2 = 2k2 and now b is even. But in that case, a/b is not a fraction in lowest terms. From this contradiction, we conclude that no such fraction exists. Here is the same proof, formalized for Isabelle by Claude Opus 4.6: As with all proof assistants, the language is designed to be checkable by computer. But it is also designed to be human-readable. Here is a little guide: assume introduces an assumption have and show claim some formula to be true obtain claims that certain values exist by gives the justification of a claim We use show when proving facts that we are committed to proving and have when proving facts that we need along the way. The justifications invoke proof methods, which typically refer to existing theorems, but we needn’t go into detail about those. Now we can read the code and see the mathematics. We start by assuming that √2 belongs to the set of rational numbers, ℚ. Then we obtain integers a and b, etc.; note that the coprime statement expresses that its two operands have no common factor. The proof continues to the ultimate contradiction as outlined above. This AI-generated proof is surprisingly idiomatic, though more detailed than strictly necessary. Finding N consecutive composite numbers The claim is that for every integer N > 0, there exists a block of N consecutive integers that are composite, i.e., that are not prime numbers. So although the primes go on forever, they are spaced further and further apart. This example is not so well known, so when proposing it to Claude, we also gave it the following proof: Take N! (N factorial, i.e., the product of the integers from 1 to N). N! + 2 must be even, N! + 3 must be divisible by 3, and so forth to N! + N. I hope you can spot what is wrong with this “proof”. When I supplied it to Claude, it came up with three facts. The first states that if k > 1 is a divisor of n > 0, then n + k is not prime. The second states that if 2 ≤ k ≤ N + 1, then (N + 1)! + k is not prime. And that is essentially our conclusion. But the third fact is the theorem presented in the correct form. Claude noticed that our proof gave us only N - 1 consecutive integers and made the necessary correction. Let’s skip the lemmas and just look at the main theorem: The theorem statement (after shows) is in symbolic form, but it expresses that there exists m such that m + i is composite for all i.Definite integral of the sine function Now for something a bit harder: calculus. Let’s look at the integral of the function sin x over the interval [0, π]. (For those of you who prefer degrees, π corresponds to 180°.) The integral is the shaded area below, and it equals two. In mathematical notation, the integral is written like this: But with an AI agent, you don’t have to know how to code such a thing in your favorite proof assistant. All we asked for was “a nice simple example involving calculus”, and a plain English description of the integral would have worked, too. Claude generated this (even the comments): As you may remember from calculus class — for most people the happiest time of their lives — evaluating this integral requires finding the antiderivative (say ƒ) of the sine function and evaluating ƒ(π) - ƒ(0). This fact is called the fundamental theorem of calculus. “Antiderivative” means a function whose derivative is sin x, which turns out to be -cos x. The Isabelle proof above includes a proof that the derivative of -cos x is sin x. The calculation is a bit longer than necessary, but at least it is error free, thanks to our approach of interleaving generation and checking. Harder projects These examples were easy. Much harder problems can still be formalized automatically by a good agent. To manage the toughest problems, we need I/Q and I/R. Through I/Q we can link an agent running in a terminal window to our Isabelle session, which it can edit directly. But through I/R, it can also create an Isabelle subprocess that works silently and invisibly to prove theorems and undertake other formalization tasks. Because it doesn’t touch the document, we can work at the same time. The AI agent becomes a partner who works for us and who can advise us but also accepts hints from us. It’s a new type of teamwork, and we still need to figure out how to make it work best. The hardest problems still require human thought, but thinking is hard work, and people get tired. Being able to direct an agent to carry out straightforward but lengthy and tiresome tasks — say, to refactor a working but messy proof development or study a trace to diagnose a problem — leaves us fresh enough to make key decisions when we must. I/R can be run standalone: we can set it up ourselves and direct it to run autonomously for a long time.

title: Introducing Unity Gateway Insights
abstract: When looking to cut AI costs, teams often start with budgets or open-source models. But agent traces can reveal other opportunities to save. At Databricks, trace analysis surfaced several: offline replays showed no performance gain from upgrading from Opus 4.8 to Opus 5, so we stayed on the cheaper 4.8; fixing common MCP errors recovered an estimated $1.2M in costs a year ; and traces showed that simple prompts were going to expensive models, prompting us to adopt Smart Routing . Today, we’re introducing Unity Gateway Insights , which automatically uses Genie to analyze millions of agent traces alongside your business data and ontology. It surfaces where tokens are being wasted: MCP errors that keep recurring, simple tasks running on expensive frontier models, and repeated workflows worth turning into shared skills, all in the context of your business and under the same governance as your other data. If you already have traffic flowing through Unity Gateway, open AI Gateway > Observability > Insights and generate a report for the last day, 7 days, or 30 days. Insights then writes a report on the tokenomics of your coding agent rollout that answers the following questions: Each finding links to example sessions, so you can open the traces behind it. You can add up to 10 questions of your own to a report, such as whether the newest model is worth it for your team's work. To dig further, continue the conversation with Genie. Ask which MCP server wasted the most tokens this month and who owns it, and you have a bug report ready to send. Here's what's behind each kind of waste Insights reports: Finding this kind of waste requires a full record of every step of every agent session: inputs and outputs, tool calls, subagents, intermediate steps, latency, and token cost. A standalone gateway records only the requests that pass through it. Capturing the rest of each session means instrumenting every coding agent yourself, then exporting the traces to a data platform to analyze them. Pointing Claude Code at those traces still leaves you to design the investigation yourself, with no map of your business like the Genie Ontology provides. Insights runs the investigation we developed while rolling out coding agents to thousands of Databricks engineers. It samples sessions and groups them into workstreams by kind of work. Then it checks each workstream for failing MCP tools, bloated context, frontier models on simple tasks, and repeated workflows, and ranks what it finds by the tokens at stake. It depends on four things a standalone gateway can't have: If your developers already run coding agents through Unity Gateway, you can generate your first report today: Subscribe to our blog and get the latest posts delivered to your inbox.

title: What's new for Genie in Microsoft: Copilot Cowork and Chat, Microsoft Teams, and Excel.
abstract: Most AI assistants can read a person's email, files, and calendar, but it can't tell which revenue table is certified or how finance defines net retention. This leads to inconsistent outcomes, low adoption, and a lack of trust among business users. Genie Ontology solves this context problem for Genie by combining the business semantics teams explicitly define with context learned from everyday work, so answers are grounded in a full understanding of the business. Once that context is unified, the next step is putting it to work. As AI assistants and agents spread across the business, organizations need to control data access, spend, and tool usage at scale. Without that control, sensitive data can reach the wrong people, AI spend becomes hard to predict, and agents can connect to tools no one has approved. In Genie, Unity Catalog enforces each user's data permissions, and Unity Gateway gives admins the traces, MCP policies, and budget controls they need to manage AI across the organization. Genie brings both essential context and governance into the Microsoft tools your teams already use with the Azure Databricks Genie plugin, which connects Microsoft Copilot and Copilot Cowork to Genie One. Genie also works in Microsoft Teams, Microsoft Excel, and Microsoft Copilot Studio. The Databricks Genie app for Microsoft Teams is now generally available, bringing Genie into the conversations where teams already make decisions. Users can send Genie a direct message or mention @Databricks Genie in a channel or group chat, and Genie replies in the thread with answers grounded in the organization’s governed business context. With Genie in Teams, users unlock real-time collaboration with knowledge from across their data estate. For example, a sales manager can post in a channel, "Which open leads over $100K haven't had a follow-up this week?" Instead of someone manually pulling the pipeline report, cross-checking it against the CRM, searching meeting notes, and messaging reps one by one, she can now simply tag @Genie. Genie answers in the thread with the matching leads, their latest activity, and links to the sources it used, not only saving the team time and effort, but also allowing the work to happen right where the question was originally asked. Genie in Teams goes beyond answers, enabling users to turn insights into work right from their Teams workspace: The Azure Databricks Genie plugin for Microsoft Copilot Cowork and Copilot Chat brings trusted business answers into the Copilot experience users may already rely on. Instead of Copilot searching for correct answers on its own, it can delegate work to Genie One. Genie leverages Genie Ontology to provide accurate insights based on certified definitions, metric views, and context learned from everyday work, all governed by Unity Catalog. Together, Genie and Copilot can unlock new workflows for teams. For example, imagine an account team preparing for client meetings. An account director asks Copilot Cowork for a briefing ahead of a customer meeting, which delegates to Genie. Genie pulls usage, spend, and account trends from Azure Databricks using certified metric definitions, then reads recent customer email threads in Outlook through its Microsoft 365 connector to flag open escalations. Cowork turns those insights into a Word doc brief, an Excel overview with charts, and a client-ready presentation. Every figure comes from Genie, keeping the deliverables consistent with the numbers finance and the account team already report. Many teams plan, forecast, and report in Excel, but getting trusted data into a workbook often means exporting files, copying numbers, and hoping they match the source. With Genie One in the Azure Databricks Excel Add-in , analysts can ask questions in plain English and get answers from governed Azure Databricks data without hunting for tables or writing SQL. Every answer includes citations that show where the numbers came from, and analysts can refine their analysis with follow-up questions, resume past conversations, and load table results directly into the workbook for further modeling. The Excel Add-in also lets teams: Together, these capabilities bring governed Azure Databricks data into the spreadsheet workflows teams already rely on, without exports or manual data movement. Builders can connect Genie Agents to Microsoft Copilot Studio using the Azure Databricks connector for Power Platform . Adding Genie as a tool lets a Copilot Studio assistant delegate questions about Azure Databricks data to Genie Agents , which answer using curated data and instructions and governance enforced by Unity Catalog. Business questions rarely stay in one tool, so the answers shouldn't either. Together, Microsoft and Genie bring governed business context from Azure Databricks into the tools every employee already uses: Copilot Chat, Copilot Cowork, Teams, and Excel. Genie Ontology makes sure every answer is grounded in your enterprise context, and Unity Catalog and Unity Gateway enforce governance for every answer and action. Now, wherever a question starts, whether in a Teams thread, a Copilot chat, or an Excel workbook, users get the same trusted, governed answer. What is Genie Ontology? Genie Ontology is the enterprise context layer that gives Genie and other AI agents a shared understanding of your business. Agents build it from everyday work, people govern it, and every agent can use it. It combines business semantics that teams define, such as metric views and certified definitions, with context learned from dashboards, queries, and documents. Genie Ontology is now generally available. How does Genie Ontology help Microsoft Copilot give better answers? It gives Copilot the business meaning behind the data. When Copilot or Copilot Cowork asks Genie a question, Genie answers with the certified definition, such as how finance defines net retention, instead of guessing from table names. Teams get consistent answers in every Microsoft tool. How do admins govern Genie across Microsoft tools? Through Unity Gateway. Admins manage AI usage centrally with MCP policies, cost controls, and monitoring. MCP policies decide which MCP servers and tools Genie can use, who can access them, and which actions need human approval. Traces record what Genie did and who asked for it. How do I get started with Genie in Microsoft Teams ? Admins add the Databricks Genie app to Microsoft Teams and choose the default visibility for responses. Users then send Genie a direct message or mention @Databricks Genie in a channel or group chat. The first time, they sign in to Databricks and pick a workspace. Does Genie in Teams support Genie One and Genie Agents? Yes. Genie One is the default. It looks across your entire data estate to answer each question. You can also pin a conversation or channel to a specific Genie Agent. Questions are then sent to that agent through the Genie Agentic API, so answers stay scoped to that agent's curated data and instructions. What can Genie do in Microsoft Teams? Genie in Teams does much more than answer questions. You can: Does Genie in Microsoft Teams support workspaces that use Private Link? Yes. A Databricks account admin needs to create a context-based ingress policy to allow secure connectivity between Teams and your Databricks workspace. Is my data secure for Genie in Microsoft Teams? Yes. Every question runs as the user who asked it, so Genie only uses data that person is allowed to see, based on Unity Catalog and source permissions. Questions are processed inside your Databricks workspace. The service that routes messages between Teams and Databricks doesn't store questions or answers. Should I use the Databricks Genie app in Teams, or publish a Copilot Studio agent to Teams? Use the Databricks Genie app in Microsoft Teams by default. It's a native app that chats directly with Genie One, so users get answers from across their data estate with no extra agent in between.

title: How AUMOVIO centralized AI access with Databricks Unity Gateway
abstract: As AI adoption grew, AUMOVIO teams developed different ways to access large language models. Today, Databricks Unity Gateway provides a shared entry point for our AI workloads. This blog discusses how we brought these approaches together. Teams at AUMOVIO developed different ways to access LLMs, including provider integrations and gateways built for specific use cases. These approaches all addressed real needs, but as AI adoption grew, their variety added complexity to operations, cost attribution and consistent governance. The main opportunities to improve were: Together, these approaches highlighted the value of a shared operating model for managing our AI workloads with a single AI gateway solution AUMOVIO's cross-functional AI taskforce brought together stakeholders from security, data protection, business areas and IT. The taskforce decided on one central AI Gateway as the shared route for LLM access and governance , establishing a common direction for model access across the company. From there, our job was to make the central path useful to teams and their applications. Building an AI gateway is straightforward, but operating one as an enterprise service is a permanent commitment: provider APIs change, dependencies need patching, security requirements evolve, and users need support. Once applications depend on it, a gateway needs a roadmap, an on-call rotation and a support process. Weighing that against buying yet another AI gateway, five arguments decided why Databricks Unity Gateway was the solution for us. 1. Databricks was already our data platform. 1ADP, the One AUMOVIO Data Platform, runs on Databricks. Putting model access next to our governed enterprise data meant no new vendor, no new network path to review and no isolated stack to operate. 2. Corporate identity integration. Databricks is integrated with our corporate Microsoft Entra ID tenant, and other AUMOVIO applications authenticate against that same tenant. An application presents its Entra ID token and gets access to Unity Gateway through token exchange, with no separate account, no API key to distribute and no bespoke integration. Onboarding a new AI-enabled application takes a permission grant, and access to every model ends automatically when the corporate identity does. 3. Governance and usage tracking. Model approvals, access policies, usage tracking and logging sit in one place instead of being reimplemented per application. Payload logging through inference tables is off by default and only enabled with an explicit, approved justification, which is the posture our data protection agreements require. 4. We stayed free to choose providers. This mattered most. We publish a curated catalog of 1adp-* model aliases, and Unity Gateway routes each alias to whichever provider serves it: Databricks-hosted foundation models, Google Vertex AI, Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock or others. Users code against a stable, vendor-neutral name, and we can re-point that name to a different provider or a newer model without a single consumer changing a line of code. The aliases give teams a consistent route to approved models. 5. The setup is infrastructure as code. Terraform expresses everything Unity Gateway does for us: the endpoints behind each 1adp-* alias, the provider each model routes to, the fallback order when a provider degrades, rate limits and the guardrails applied per endpoint. Adding a model, re-pointing an alias or tightening a safety control is a pull request, reviewed, versioned and reproducible across environments. When production misbehaves, our version control explains the configuration that caused it. Because we provision the rest of 1ADP the same way, the Gateway is one more module for the engineers who already run the platform. Centralizing model access was the first step. We then built three capabilities on top of Unity Gateway to support how our teams manage, access, and use AI: Cost attribution and chargeback. Unity Gateway reports on how many tokens were consumed, and every user assigns their consumption to a personal cost center or to one of the projects they work in. Pipelines join that assignment with Databricks system tables and charge usage to the right cost center. We publish the result as dashboards: which models are used, by whom, how consumption develops and what it costs. Budget owners can see their spend and identify changes in consumption. A curated model catalog. Standardized access does not make models interchangeable. The catalog is the single source of truth for which models are approved, what they map to and which consumption tier they run in. Teams still test their application against the model they choose, but they no longer build infrastructure to reach it. An interface for employees. The 1ADP AI App runs in production on the same gateway and gives employees a governed way to use AI without writing code. Developers get an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and can point compatible agentic coding tools at the central models. Same infrastructure, two audiences: we standardize model access and leave the choice of development interface open. Unity Gateway provides a shared route for LLM access. The 1adp-* aliases connect applications to models, guardrails apply centrally, and usage is attributed to cost centers in near real time. The next phase moves up the AI platform stack: sharing agents inside 1ADP projects and connecting knowledge sources, web search and other tools through managed and bring-your-own MCP (Model Context Protocol) connections. Model access stays centralized; what changes is the range of tools an agent can reach. That raises questions about what an agent may retrieve, which tools it may call and whose permissions it acts under. Having one framework to answer them in is why we consolidated in the first place. If you are bringing different model access approaches together, involve security, data protection, business areas and IT in the operating model. Then make the shared service useful to the teams expected to use it. When you compare building to buying, price the decade rather than the prototype. Ask who patches the provider integration, who answers the support ticket, who handles the incident, and who does it again next year. Then decide what is genuinely yours to build. The gateway was not. Cost attribution, the model catalog and the employee-facing AI App were, because they encode how AUMOVIO works and no vendor was going to hand them to us. We remain accountable for our architecture, our security decisions and the quality of our applications. Unity Gateway provides the shared model access service, while teams can continue to choose the applications they build. AUMOVIO chose Databricks Unity Gateway to centralize AI model access without the ongoing maintenance, security updates, and operational overhead of building its own gateway. Because Databricks already powered its enterprise data platform, AUMOVIO could reuse existing infrastructure, Microsoft Entra ID integration, and governance controls. This allowed its teams to focus on building company-specific capabilities such as cost attribution, a curated model catalog, and an employee-facing AI application. Databricks Unity Gateway provides a single, governed entry point for accessing AI models across providers such as Azure OpenAI, Google Vertex AI, AWS Bedrock, and Databricks-hosted models. AUMOVIO uses centralized model approvals, access policies, logging, and guardrails to apply consistent governance across applications. Its curated model aliases also let administrators change the underlying model or provider without requiring application code changes. Unity Gateway provides token usage data that enterprises can use to track AI consumption across models and users. AUMOVIO combines this data from Databricks system tables with project and cost center assignments to attribute AI spending to the appropriate business owners.

title: How we raised Databricks cluster rate limits by 7.5×
abstract: As part of the Compute Platform team at Databricks, we turn cloud infrastructure into clusters ready to run customer workloads. Our day-to-day work includes provisioning virtual machines and coordinating cluster creation across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. Our goal is to keep these systems available while letting customers use as much capacity as we can safely provide. In this post, we'll explore why fixed request-rate limits can fall short for these long-running operations, how adaptive concurrency limits help, and what we learned applying them to cluster creation for Databricks classic compute. You don't need to know any of this to use Databricks, but if you're curious about what happens behind a Databricks Runtime cluster launch, join us for a look inside the kitchen. Historically, we protected the system with fixed request-rate limits, tested against different load patterns and failure scenarios. We scaled our services primarily by adding resources and adjusting per-customer limits. The combination of workloads and dependency failures made these limits increasingly difficult to test and tune. Conservative limits turned away customer requests despite spare capacity, yet kept accepting requests when our services or dependencies, such as cloud providers, slowed down. Engineers manually lowered limits to shed load during incidents and raised them again after recovery. Adaptive concurrency limits account for both unfinished work and changing system health. They let more work start when capacity is available and slow the pace when the system struggles, helping the service make progress with less manual tuning. A fixed API request-rate ceiling remains as a final safety guardrail against exceptionally high incoming traffic. Think of our compute platform as a kitchen, aiming to serve as many orders as its cooks and equipment can handle. The manager posts a fixed rule: accept at most ten new orders per minute, whatever is happening at the stove. Even with spare cooking capacity, the rule turns orders away. When an oven breaks, it keeps accepting orders faster than the remaining cooks and equipment can finish them. The manager has to keep rewriting the sign each time. A better kitchen keeps a short queue and limits how many meals are being prepared at once. If an oven breaks, fewer meals start; as capacity returns, more can begin. Orders can wait briefly, but only while there is still time to serve them. For long-running operations, a fixed request rate is a poor model of capacity. The goal is to let customers run at full throttle when capacity allows, then ease off enough to keep useful work moving during degradation. An API call can launch much more work than the handler performs itself. For cluster creation, the handler validates the request, records a work item, and returns. A background workflow coordinates services, updates state, and provisions resources such as cloud virtual machines. These operations complete asynchronously, and their duration depends on the health and capacity of their dependencies. The API call may take milliseconds; the workflow itself may take minutes. A request-rate limiter at the API entry point caps requests per time window. That is useful for enforcing quotas, preventing abuse, and protecting the resources used to handle API calls. A fixed request-rate limit is easier to tune when available capacity and the work behind each request stay reasonably predictable. Cluster creation makes both difficult: one request may provision a few VMs and another many more, while cloud-provider health changes how long provisioning takes. During a shared slowdown, many workflows take longer at the same time. The same incoming request rate can therefore leave much more work in flight, even as the system’s ability to finish it falls. On the left, arrivals stay fixed at one operation per time unit. Increasing duration from two to six time units triples the work in flight. On the right, processors become slow or unavailable, reducing the capacity available to handle that work. When a dependency degrades, more calls fail or time out. Long-running workflows retry those calls to recover from temporary faults. Across many active workflows, those retries add pressure to the struggling dependency, causing more failures and yet more retries—a retry storm . These internal retries come from work already accepted, so the API request-rate limiter does not see them. They can sustain overload even after incoming traffic returns to normal. Limiting active workflows helps contain that pressure and gives unfinished work a chance to drain. Setting a lower rate does not solve the mismatch. It buys headroom by rejecting more work during healthy periods, and a large enough slowdown can still exhaust that headroom. Raising the rate makes better use of healthy capacity but accepts more work during degradation. One number has to cover both days. “Rate limiting” is sometimes used broadly to include limits on concurrent work. Here, we distinguish the two mechanisms by what they count. Either kind of limit can be fixed or adaptive. Our comparison is between fixed request-rate limits and adaptive concurrency limits for protecting long-running work. The kitchen needs to track meals still being prepared and the capacity available to finish them. In Databricks classic compute, the equivalent is the set of cluster-creation workflows still provisioning infrastructure. We give each active workflow a slot and adjust the number of slots as conditions change. Consider a CreateCluster request for a cluster with a driver and several worker VMs. Once the request is accepted, its provisioning workflow waits for a slot before it starts. We track whether that work is queued, actively processing, or complete. If all slots are occupied, the request stays queued. An active workflow keeps its slot while it provisions VMs and waits for dependencies. Once the workflow finishes, its slot becomes available for another cluster launch. A successfully launched cluster can keep running customer workloads for hours without occupying that provisioning slot. The slot must cover the whole provisioning operation , including background work after the API returns. Tracking a slot does not require holding a thread. This controller counts active provisioning workflows. Running clusters, allocated VMs, and vCPUs are separate measures. One workflow can provision many VMs, so one slot does not imply a fixed resource cost. Now suppose a cloud provider takes longer to provision VMs. Active workflows hold their slots longer, so new cluster launches start less often even if the slot limit stays fixed. Customers see longer launch waits as accepted requests queue. Adaptive control also changes the slot limit. For cluster creation, useful signals include how long provisioning takes and whether critical thread pools are saturated. When these signals indicate congestion, the controller reduces the number of concurrent provisioning workflows. As conditions recover, it cautiously allows more. Capacity pressure changes when accepted work starts; RPC rate-limit rejections are reserved for exceptionally high incoming request rates. Reducing the limit prevents new operations from starting until active work falls below it; existing operations still need time to finish. This response time matters when workflows last minutes. Retries also need backoff and a limit on attempts so active workflows do not keep overwhelming a recovering dependency. Concurrency limiting cannot repair an unavailable dependency, but it can limit the extra pressure while that dependency recovers. The control loop answers how much work to start. Building a useful service also means deciding who waits, how long they wait, and what we tell them. “Too many requests” can hide two very different situations. In the first, a customer sends its usual traffic, but a shared dependency slows down. Capacity has fallen.

title: Branch, sync, serve: What our Lakebase Hackathon taught us about building on Lakebase
abstract: We run these hackathons for a simple reason: the fastest way to learn a product is to build something with it. Each one starts with an enablement session where teams learn the product and where it’s headed on the roadmap. Then the building starts. Teams work together for about a week and submit a project, and the strongest solutions earn prizes. This time, we opened the hackathon to a much wider group of customers than ever before, and the product in the spotlight was Databricks Lakebase . Lakebase is fully managed Postgres, so any developer who has written a SQL query or used an ORM can start building right away. What makes it different is what sits underneath. Storage is separated from compute, and the database lives next to your lakehouse data under the same Unity Catalog governance. That opens up three things a typical Postgres database can’t do as easily: Those map to the two tracks we ran. Track 1 focused on branching and building applications. Track 2 focused on syncing and serving. Underneath both, Unity Catalog governs who can see what, whether the data is being queried in a notebook or read by a production app. Who it’s for: application developers. These are the engineers who build the apps , APIs, and agents that run on operational data, and who have usually had to choose between a slow, shared staging database and an expensive copy for every developer. Branching removes that tradeoff. Every Lakebase project starts with a production branch, and you can create child branches from it for development, testing, or experiments. Because branches use copy-on-write, a branch of a large database is ready in seconds, and only the changes take up new storage. Teams in this track used Genie Code to build their apps and treated branches as cheap, disposable copies of production. Lyft took on a problem that’s growing as AI agents start acting on production data: agents that issue refunds, cancel bookings, or close tickets without knowing the business rules that live inside the database as triggers. Their project, Jevons Search, gives the agent a Lakebase branch to work on. For each batch of support tickets, the agent forks a copy-on-write branch of production in about six seconds, applies its actions, reads back what the database actually did, and adjusts. Instead of using a large LLM to plan, a lightweight classifier built on gte-large embeddings, tracked in MLflow, and served on Model Serving sorts each ticket into one of eight policy categories, with no LLM tokens used at runtime. On a synthetic dataset built from the Wanderbricks sample data, planning up front fully resolved 2 of 11 support backlogs within policy. Testing on branches resolved 10 of 11. The team also tested the idea behind the project’s name: Lakebase forked fast enough to score more than four times as many branches in the same minute, but more branches didn’t lead to more passes. Precise decisions plus real feedback from the database beat brute force. CIBC built Branchflight, a platform that gives every pull request its own preview environment. When a pull request opens, Branchflight creates a zero-copy Lakebase branch from a PII-masked template branch in under five seconds and deploys a preview Databricks App connected to it. Environments scale to zero when no one is using them, expire automatically after a set time, and pass through a schema-diff check before changes merge. The platform’s own state, audit logs, and cost metrics live in Lakebase too. Arbital Health asked a question every team putting text-to-SQL in front of users should think about: how much does the schema itself affect accuracy? Their benchmark, 7NF, keeps the data fixed and changes the schema, with each layout running as its own Lakebase branch. Models are graded only on whether they return the correct rows, so teams can pick the best schema for a customer database or improve their own text-to-SQL models. Branching also showed up in some unexpected places. For their hackathon submission, OneTrust brought Lakebase branching to network security by treating firewall rules like code. To evaluate proposed changes without risk to live infrastructure, they experimented with having a Go app spin up a copy-on-write Lakebase branch with dedicated compute and connect a test instance to run recursive reachability queries and policy checks. In testing, trial runs that expanded the attack surface were discarded instantly, while validated rules merged directly into production. A second CIBC team built BranchCut, a 3D cinematic workspace that brings Git-style branching and merging to creative work. Creators branch from any point in a scene, try different camera moves or lighting, compare versions side by side, and merge the best one back, with Lakebase tracking projects, branches, scene state, and merge history. Reach Mobile built StreetCart, which helps shoppers compare nearby stores on price, distance, and stock instead of walking store to store. Lakebase is the app’s operational database for products, stores, and inventory, and Lakebase search powers product discovery. The team used branching to test new product category attributes before changing the production schema. Markel went after a system most property and casualty insurers run: a separate search index, often Elasticsearch, kept only so claims, underwriting, and call center teams get fast reads. That second copy has its own pipeline, its own schema drift, and its own governance gaps. Markel’s app serves those reads from the same governed gold tables used for analytics, through Lakebase. Claims analysts search for policies by number, name, address, or phone; call center agents identify callers by phone number across policy, claims, and broker data; and underwriters see loss runs for a broker in one place. New claims are scored for risk as they arrive. Building on Lakebase is only half the story. The other half is what happens when the operational database and the lakehouse stop being separate systems. Who it’s for: data and ML engineers. These are the people who build the pipelines and models, and who usually have to build a separate path to get that data into the apps and services that need it in milliseconds. This track was about closing that gap. Synced tables move curated Unity Catalog data into Lakebase Postgres through managed Spark Declarative Pipelines, so apps can join it with their own tables. Lakebase Change Data Feed goes the other way and streams changes made in Postgres back to Delta for analytics. And because Databricks Online Feature Stores run on Lakebase, features defined in the lakehouse can be served to models in real time. Data Axle built PriceWise for vacation rental hosts who set one flat nightly price while demand changes dramatically across the year. Across more than 18,000 listings, the team estimated hosts leave about 64% of potential nightly revenue on the table. PriceWise combines hybrid search (pgvector embeddings plus BM25, merged with Reciprocal Rank Fusion), pricing suggestions broken down into four demand drivers including PostGIS comparisons of listings within 20 miles, and an embedded Genie agent that answers questions like which amenities top competitors have. Every Genie conversation is saved in Lakebase as agent memory, so hosts can pick up where they left off. Search, pricing, agent memory, and feature serving all run from one Lakebase database kept current through synced tables, with pricing responses in as little as 4 milliseconds, and host decisions written back to Lakebase. A team from a transportation company built a real-time flight risk app that turns streaming data into a live operational view. They synced flight, airport, and weather alert tables from Unity Catalog into Lakebase to power a live map in a Databricks App, showing how synced tables let the same pipelines that feed analytics feed an operational app. Another team from an insurance company focused on a gap that comes after a policy is issued.

title: The new Azure Databricks on Azure Government is now in Beta
abstract: Government agencies and their mission-critical partners face a persistent dilemma: adopt the latest data and AI innovations, or meet the stringent security and compliance requirements their missions demand. For too long, these have been competing priorities, forcing public sector organizations to operate on platforms that lag behind their commercial counterparts, sometimes by years. Today, we're excited to announce that Azure Databricks on Azure Government is entering Beta , a major milestone in our commitment to delivering the full power of the Databricks Data + AI Platform to the U.S. public sector. Government agencies and the hundreds of organizations that support them now have access to the modern data foundation already transforming industries across the commercial sector, including Unity Catalog, Databricks SQL, and serverless compute, with the complete suite of AI capabilities to follow, all within an environment working toward FedRAMP Class D (formerly “High”) and DoW IL5 authorization. Databricks recently launched the FedRAMP Class D offering on Azure Commercial. And today we are bringing the best of Databricks to Azure Government, so U.S. public sector customers now have a modern Databricks platform on both Azure clouds. For federal civilian agencies, state and local governments, and partners whose workloads fit FedRAMP Class D, Azure Commercial is available today. For organizations that need a dedicated government cloud and a path to FedRAMP Class D and DoW IL5, the new Azure Government environment is now open for Beta. As a first-party Azure service, Azure Databricks is managed through the Azure portal, integrates natively with Microsoft Entra ID, and counts toward existing Azure commitments, so agencies can adopt it inside the cloud, contracts, and identity systems they already trust. Unlike the legacy environment, the new Azure Databricks on Azure Government runs on the same architecture as commercial Azure Databricks. It is designed to receive the full Databricks platform, with every commercial feature coming to Azure Government through the same ongoing releases. Beta is the first release on that path, and it already gives government teams the core capabilities their commercial peers rely on. Beta lays the governed, secure foundation that AI depends on. Next, we'll bring the full Databricks AI suite to Azure Government, all governed by Unity Catalog, so every model, agent, and answer inherits the same access controls, lineage, and auditing as the underlying data. On the roadmap: Roadmap capabilities and timelines are forward-looking and subject to change. Databricks is actively pursuing FedRAMP Class D (formerly FedRAMP High) and DoW Impact Level 5 (IL5) authorizations for the new Azure Government environment, expected in early 2027. Once authorized, agencies and defense partners will be able to run Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) and mission-critical workloads on the modern Databricks platform, including the defense workloads that require IL5 and are not supported on Azure Commercial. Track our authorization progress on the FedRAMP Marketplace . New to the environment? Opt in with a dedicated Azure Government subscription that has never been used for Azure Databricks. After you register the new-environment preview feature in the Azure portal, every new workspace in that subscription is created in the new environment. During Beta, the environment is intended for non-production workloads. The workspaces you build now will carry forward to production at General Availability. Already on the legacy Azure Government environment? Now is the time to start planning your migration. Your existing workspaces, notebooks, data, and configurations are unaffected, so you can explore the new environment side by side and work out your path forward. We recommend starting with four areas: Our Federal team can help you assess your workloads and plan the move. Ready to get started? Contact your Databricks representative or check out the Azure Databricks documentation for technical details. Subscribe to our blog and get the latest posts delivered to your inbox.

title: Advancing Catalog Interoperability with Unity Catalog and Google Cloud’s Borderless Lakehouse
abstract: The Lakehouse architecture is becoming more open than ever. What started with open table formats – Delta Lake and Iceberg – has evolved into catalog federation for zero-copy access across multiple platforms. Through our partnership and Open Source contributions, Databricks and Google Cloud continue to drive advancements in the Open Lakehouse community. Today, we're proud to announce a significant milestone in catalog interoperability in collaboration with Google: customers can now access a single copy of data from both Unity Catalog and Google Cloud's borderless Lakehouse . The Databricks and Google Cloud partnership continues to thrive, and we're committed to making bi-directional interoperability seamless. Bringing data from Google Cloud into Databricks is simple. With Lakehouse Federation to Google Cloud , now generally available, customers can mount Iceberg tables managed by Google Cloud's Lakehouse runtime catalog in Unity Catalog for analysis in Databricks. These Iceberg tables from Google's Lakehouse runtime catalog can then be queried by Databricks Lakehouse , our serverless data warehouse, or analyzed via Genie , which intelligently answers data questions from natural language – no code or SQL required. Interoperability works in the other direction as well. Data from Databricks can also be brought into Google Cloud's Lakehouse ( learn more ). This allows customers using engines like BigQuery to read Unity Catalog managed tables without data copy. Databricks and Google Cloud are taking major strides to strengthen interoperability by making catalog metadata open. Our belief is that business and governance semantics should be accessible rather than tied to a specific vendor. In the Iceberg community, we helped drive and land catalog labels - a proposal that enables catalogs to share metadata through key-value pairs (a.k.a labels). That way, a table tagged as "domain=finance" and "status=certified" with a column tagged as "pii=ssn" continues to be tagged even as the table is federated from one catalog to another ( learn more ). Shared labels are critical for governance in the era of agents as catalog metadata can be used to flag sensitive data for masking and provide context to agents searching for assets to answer data questions. Through our partnership, Databricks and Google Cloud are committed to advancing the vision of open governance. As data estates grow and AI agents become more embedded in enterprise workflows, that shared commitment becomes increasingly important. We're headed towards a future where governance and business context can travel with data without requiring enterprises to redefine them in every system. Get started with Catalog Federation between Unity Catalog and Google Cloud's borderless Lakehouse by reading our documentation . You can also learn more about Google's catalog federation to Unity Catalog here . If you're interested in sharing your interoperability needs or learning more about our vision for interoperability, please reach out to your Databricks account team.
