title: How packaged clean rooms bring RampID to your lakehouse
abstract: Historically on Databricks, to resolve customer records to a person-based ID such as RampID, a data team had to export PII to an outside service, wait for a match file, and load it back in. Each step added a pipeline to maintain, a copy of sensitive data to govern, and a delay before the results were usable. Packaged clean rooms disrupt this traditional pattern by removing the need for that round-trip. LiveRamp Embedded Identity on Databricks brings the identity service to the data. Anyone can take advantage of LiveRamp's identity resolution solution without having their precious customer data leave their owned-storage. With minimal set-up, customers can receive a resolved list of RampIDs back in their environment where their analytics and AI workloads already run, all while maintaining Unity Catalog governance. These appended RampIDs to the customers’ data become the match key for high impact downstream use cases, for example: A Databricks clean room is a secure environment where two or more parties run approved code across their combined data without revealing raw data or IP to each other. The computation happens in an isolated, Databricks-managed environment that none of the parties administers. In a standard (approval-based) Databricks clean room, every collaborator is a peer. Collaborators can add data (tabular or unstructured) and/or code, and all parties have to approve the code before it can be run. Collaborators never see each other's data, but they do see the aliases of the tables shared in, along with their column names and types. This fits joint analysis, such as two companies measuring audience overlap together. Even in an approval-based room, a party can keep part of its logic private by packaging a volume, so approvers review the notebook that calls the library, not the library itself. A packaged clean room extends the privacy to the entire analysis and fits a different relationship. One party, the identity provider (in this case, LiveRamp), ships an analysis as a product, and the other party, the customer, runs it against its own data. There is no approval step and neither party sees the other's data assets at all, not even table names or schemas. The provider can offer the same package to many customers, each in a separate clean room, and each customer gets a turnkey run with nothing to review. This allows for scalable deployments across multiple customers, and simplifies the customer’s experience. For identity resolution cases, a packaged clean room makes particular sense as the split protects both sides. LiveRamp's identity graph and matching logic remain its intellectual property and invisible to the customer. The customer's PII and resolved results remain private to the customer. There are three components, each with a clear role: The central clean room is where everything happens. It's a Databricks-managed environment, separate from both the customer's and LiveRamp's workspaces, and no one from either company has administrative access to it. OpenSharing, formerly Delta Sharing, is the open sharing protocol that Databricks Clean Rooms are built on. Neither party copies its tables into the clean room. Instead, the customer and LiveRamp each add Unity Catalog assets, and OpenSharing grants the central clean room read-only access to them. Because OpenSharing shares tables live, without replication, each run reads the current version of the customer's input table rather than an extract from last week. The connection leverages Databricks-to-Databricks sharing, so it keeps Unity Catalog governance on both sides: the provider controls which assets it exposes, the customer controls which tables it adds, and sharing activity is audited for both. OpenSharing also carries more than tables. It can share models, unstructured data, JAR files, private libraries, python wheels, and more. This flexibility is how LiveRamp is able to deliver all components of its identity resolution services. A single run writes to two schemas: Both are delivered via the same OpenSharing mechanism to their respective (customer/provider)-owned environments, into the catalogs specified at set-up, which can be found within the Catalog Explorer - Shares received section. These can be queried and leveraged immediately. For long-term (beyond 30 days) use, these tables will need to be copied down into a customers’ own cloud storage. Both the customer and LiveRamp can see the history of every run, including its status, timing, and the notebook that ran. Because the customer owns the data and LiveRamp owns the code, neither side has the full picture alone when a run fails. A shared view of run status, together with the shared output schema, lets both teams troubleshoot from the same facts without exposing data. Clean room activity is also recorded in each party’s system tables ( system.access.clean_room_events ), allowing for an audit trail. Packaged clean rooms turn identity resolution into something a data team runs rather than a pipeline it maintains. LiveRamp ships its identity resolution logic as a product, the customer runs it against live, governed data through OpenSharing, and the central clean room keeps each party's data and code private from the other. The result is a RampID table in the customer's own Unity Catalog, ready for customer 360, audience building, activation, partner collaboration, and measurement. There are no exports to schedule, no match files to wait on, and no extra copies of PII to govern. For full setup steps, see LiveRamp's guide, " Perform RampID identity resolution in Databricks ," and the Databricks packaged clean rooms documentation. For marketers: Want to understand how this unlocks efficiency and speed? Read the companion LiveRamp post on Identity Resolution in Databricks . What is a packaged clean room in Databricks? A packaged clean room is a Databricks Clean Rooms mode in which one party, the provider, supplies an analysis and the other party, the customer, runs it against its own data without seeing the code. Neither party can see the other's data assets, and the code runs on serverless compute in a Databricks-managed central clean room that neither party administers. LiveRamp Embedded Identity uses this mode: LiveRamp provides the identity graph and resolution code, and the customer runs it to receive RampIDs. How is a packaged clean room different from a standard Databricks clean room? In a standard, approval-based clean room every collaborator is a peer: anyone can add data or notebooks, approvers can read the notebook source, and every notebook needs approval before it runs. In a packaged clean room only the provider adds code, the customer sees notebook and JAR names but not their contents, and there is no approval step because the customer cannot review the code. The customer alone triggers runs and receives the output, while both parties see run history and a shared output schema for logs. Does LiveRamp see my data when I run identity resolution in a Databricks clean room? No. Your tables stay in your own cloud storage, OpenSharing gives the central clean room read-only access under Unity Catalog governance, and the resolved RampIDs are written to an output schema only you can read. LiveRamp sees the run status in the shared run history and the shared output schema, where its code writes metrics and logs that you receive too. LiveRamp's code does call LiveRamp's identity service to authenticate, and the clean room's egress network policy, shown on the Security tab, governs what else it can reach. What do I need to run LiveRamp Embedded Identity on Databricks? A LiveRamp agreement with Identity API credentials, a Unity Catalog workspace, and the CREATE CLEAN ROOM privilege.

title: Built on object storage, served from cache
abstract: The common argument against running Postgres on object storage goes like this: The premise is right, but the conclusion isn't: it assumes that a database built on object storage has to read from object storage to answer queries, and Lakebase Postgres almost never does. To show what we mean by "almost never," we looked at page read stats across a slice of our production fleet. In the lakebase architecture, reads are split into tiers , and every page read is served by the first tier that has the page: Building on object storage opens the path for When you build on object storage, speed is the part you have to design around. To keep Postgres fast on top of it, we designed the storage layer so that object storage never sits in front of a query - reads go through tiers that keep hot data in local caches, on the compute node and on the pageservers, and object storage only backs them. Here's a closer look at how a read moves through those tiers: The lakebase architecture decouples compute and storage for Postgres: This architecture differs enough from conventional Postgres that we've given it its own category: the lakebase . Lakebase Postgres follows the lakebase principles. When Lakebase Postgres needs a page, In this design, every tier caches what it fetches from the tier below. A page returned by the pageserver lands in the compute's local cache - layers fetched from object storage land on pageserver NVMe. The cost of a deeper tier is paid once, and the next read of the same data stays local. So, as we just saw, reads that leave the compute node are a small minority, and almost all of them stop at the pageserver. The pageserver organizes data into two kinds of layer files: To answer GetPage@LSN, the pageserver: The number of deltas applied is the measure of how much work a read takes on the pageserver. With zero deltas, the page comes straight from an image. With many, the pageserver has to replay a long chain of WAL before it can return. This sounds like a lot of work, but it is not so much in practice. Here's data that illustrates this, across our us-east-1 fleet: Only a tiny fraction of the reads that reach a pageserver go one step further. The ~39 requests per second that reach object storage have one thing in common - they ask for data that nobody has read recently. In practice, this means one of these two cases practically every time: It's important to note how even in both these cases, only the first reads pay the cost. After that, the data is cached in the fastest tiers, and reads follow the same local path as any active workload. In active query execution, object storage is simply not in the critical path in the lakebase. A Postgres built on object storage doesn't have to read from object storage to answer queries. In Lakebase, a read goes to the compute's local cache, then the pageserver, and every tier caches what it fetches from the one below. Image layers keep the pageserver's replay chains short. Together, these keep object storage off the read path - more than 99.99999% of page accesses are served from local caches on compute and pageservers, which is how Lakebase Postgres gets the benefits of object storage while staying fast. For the full picture of the lakebase architecture, see From monolith to Lakebase to LTAP , WAL + S3: Lakebase storage for the era of agents , and A New Era of Databases: Lakebase . title: How low-SWaP radar is making sophisticated sensing smarter
abstract:
Radar systems have traditionally faced a straightforward engineering tradeoff: Better performance requires more hardware, more power, and more money. But emerging applications including drones, autonomous vehicles, and distributed sensing networks require capable radar on platforms where space, weight, battery power, and computing resources are limited. These needs are driving researchers at HRL Laboratories, an IBM company, to rethink how radar systems are designed. Enter low-SWaP radar. SWaP stands for size, weight, and power, although cost is increasingly treated as a central constraint. The goal of low-SWaP radar, beyond making a system smaller, is to preserve as much of its useful capability as possible while shrinking the hardware, reducing its energy demands, and dramatically lowering its cost. For HRL lab leader Seong-Hwoon Kim and his colleagues, the target is radar systems costing in the tens of thousands of dollars range rather than hundreds of thousands or even millions. “For this industry, that cost difference is a paradigm shift,” he said. Achieving that goal means rethinking radar as an integrated system, including the semiconductor devices producing and receiving radio-frequency signals as well as the algorithms interpreting those signals in real time. What does a radar actually measure? The word “radar” is an acronym for radio detection and ranging. At its simplest, radar works by transmitting radio-frequency (RF) signals and examining what comes back after those signals encounter objects in the environment and return to a sensing antenna. Based on how the returning pulse’s phase and amplitude differ from what was transmitted, information about nearby objects can be interpreted. The Doppler shift of a returning pulse describes how its wavelength is stretched or compressed based on whether an object of interest is moving farther or closer from the radar source. This information contributes to the overall picture provided by radar equipment. Unlike a camera, a radar sensor doesn't produce an immediately recognizable picture. Instead, engineers design a radar system's operating mode and its waveform, determining how its RF signal is conditioned and transmitted so that useful information — like how far away an object is and how fast it is moving — can be extracted when the signal bounces back to the source. A radar mode is a particular way of operating the radar, with its waveform and other parameters configured for a specific sensing task. Frequency and modulation can be selected for a particular application, but the radar's hardware must also be capable of supporting that mode. Designing increasingly specialized hardware around increasingly sophisticated modes is one reason high-performance radar systems can become so expensive. Kim’s team approaches that problem through co-design, considering the waveform, hardware, and signal-processing software together rather than treating each as a separate engineering problem. “I’m a strong believer that software and algorithms will make excellent sensors even smarter,” he said. “But if you can make the excellent sensor a little bit smarter, then work on the hardware in conjunction with the software, now you've got something that will really work.” Getting more from commercial hardware One of the keys to lowering radar’s cost is avoiding custom hardware when existing components can do much of the job. Commercial off-the-shelf, or COTS, electronics offer enormous economies of scale. But components designed for mass markets don’t necessarily support everything a specialized radar requires, according to Kim. He described his team’s approach as “customized off the shelf.” Instead of developing every component from scratch, researchers can start with comparatively inexpensive commercial components, modify them where necessary, and add surrounding electronics or software to give them capabilities their original designers hadn’t anticipated. The important point is to avoid customizing away the economic advantage. “If you buy a $50 chip, you don’t want to make that chip cost you $5,000,” Kim said. “You want to just add some more capability to it,” while keeping it close to that original cost category. That philosophy extends throughout low-SWaP design: Spend resources where they materially improve performance, rather than optimizing every component to its theoretical limit. Bringing intelligence to the edge Radar’s SWaP problem doesn’t end with the RF hardware. The sensor also needs enough computing power to turn the signals it receives into useful information, increasingly in real time. A basic radar data product is a range-Doppler map. One dimension contains information about an object’s range from the sensor, while another captures its relative motion via the Doppler effect. The result can help determine where something is and how quickly it is moving relative to the radar. But interpreting a range-Doppler map is very different from picking out a recognizable object in a photograph. A stronger signal isn’t necessarily a more important signal. Useful information may emerge from patterns across the data. Kim and his colleagues are exploring how machine learning can act as a first-line filter for that information directly at the edge. Depending on the scene, Kim estimates that 80% to 90% of radar data may ultimately be irrelevant to the higher-level task. If an efficient machine-learning model can identify the potentially useful portion earlier, the rest of the computing system has much less information to process. The approach isn’t about putting the largest possible AI model onto a radar. Rather, it’s the opposite: finding efficient algorithms running on efficient hardware that can perform a tightly defined task within severe power and computing constraints. Co-designing AI with radar Applying AI to radar creates another challenge: Radar data is highly specialized. A machine-learning researcher working with photographs knows intuitively what an image of a face, vehicle, or building represents. It’s easy to annotate data for model training in that case. A radar return, on the other hand, is an electrical representation of the environment. Understanding it requires knowing something about how the waveform was generated, how the radar operates, and how the returning signal was processed. Kim’s team therefore wants machine-learning researchers to understand radar waveform and mode design while radar engineers understand what the algorithms need from the hardware. That creates a feedback loop in which algorithm requirements can influence hardware design and knowledge of the sensor can influence how machine learning systems interpret its output. That loop could become an important source of innovation, according to Kim. Rather than simply giving an AI system a collection of labeled radar data and asking it to discover patterns, researchers can incorporate knowledge of how those measurements were created in the first place. The aim is both better results and systems that can be deployed more quickly.
Building efficiency into the RF hardware Ultimately, low-SWaP radar is constrained by physics. A sensor on a battery-powered platform like a self-driving car or a drone has a finite energy budget, meaning improvements in software can’t compensate indefinitely for inefficient electronics. That makes semiconductor technology another important part of the equation. Expertise in designing and fabricating efficient RF devices is one way to make the necessary tradeoffs closer to the fundamental hardware level rather than adding more hardware around an inefficient component, said Kim. One important technology is gallium nitride, or GaN, a semiconductor used in radar and other high-performance RF systems. Kim and his colleagues work on GaN devices and fabrication, and their foundry also makes the technology available to other organizations in the U.S. defense industrial base.

title: Muse privacy invasions are freaking out Meta staffers, internal chats show
abstract: After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms. When testing the agent, staff warned that Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that users did not expect the bot to review, could be mixing up conversations between users, and even potentially sharing sensitive information users would never expect to be exposed. Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked. “Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden. “Got a random ping from Muse about something I definitely did not ask for… .” In at least one case, Muse told a staffer surprised by a similarly out-of-context offer to message a seller about a coffee table that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.” According to Reuters, that employee flagged the troubling output, writing, “this was ‘not my conversation’” and “expressing concern about a ‘possible cross-account context leak.’” Raising the most concern were random outputs that appeared to share private user data. For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts. That output said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.” At least one staffer said they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported. That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance plan” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200. “Couldn’t recover,” the staffer said.

title: Will Wright's next simulation will use AI to mine content from your memories
abstract: The computer gaming world hasn’t heard much from Will Wright ( SimCity , The Sims ) since the underwhelming release of Spore in 2008 and Wright’s subsequent departure from Maxis owner EA . Now, well over 15 years later, Wright is starting to promote his next digital simulation, which will use generative AI technology to craft a game-like experience from players’ memories. MyMems , which is slated to release next year, differentiates itself from Wright’s previous projects by “turn[ing] the simulation inward,” as Wright’s Gallium Studios and partner Artificial Agency put it in a press release this morning . The game will mine memories provided by the player to create digital people that can then form teams to solve puzzles in the game world. “If my Grandmother ended up in a Grand Slam match against Serena Williams, who would win?” Wright says by way of example in the release. “If I had to build a bridge across a short chasm, which three people from my life would I choose to help me?” In an accompanying announcement video , Wright talks about how the “plausible behavior” in a game like The Sims still didn’t effectively capture the nuances of people he encounters in real life. “It was nowhere near them understanding my claustrophobia or why my sister and I fought so much… We’re actually taking parts of your life, your memories, your experiences, people you know, and turning that into a game that’s very personal.” Will Wright introduces MyMems to the world. Wright said MyMems will be able to extract generalized themes from your memories into self-contained areas that Wright compared to the various parts in a theme park: Sports, vacations, injuries, memories, and deaths could all be the basis for their own zones to play in. Players will also have the option to create worlds based on shared memories with family, friends, and co-workers, for example.

title: Copilot is "the new OS for work," and now Office runs inside of it
abstract: Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company’s vision for its new “frontier ecosystem,” announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as “the new OS for work.” The announcement is a striking inversion of how we’ve traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent’s work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications. The rollout marks a major step toward the Copilot redesign the company first announced in September. Parts of that vision are now becoming “generally available,” as Nadella puts it, with autonomous agents and new governance tools arriving alongside them. All about agents Copilot Autopilot (not to be confused with Windows Autopilot) is a “persistent, proactive agent for personal productivity” according to Microsoft. In a nutshell, Autopilot is a cloud-based autonomous AI agent that users can delegate responsibilities to, not just single tasks. Autopilot can be authorized to work across services like email and calendars and complete tasks assigned to it as part of its role. Autopilot will use usage-based billing via Copilot Credits, but final pricing has not been announced ahead of general availability. Also announced as generally available at the keynote speech was Microsoft IQ , an intelligence platform that houses Work IQ , a context layer that helps agents understand a company’s communications, relationships, and ongoing work. Nadella described Work IQ as perhaps a company’s most valuable database: “It has a deep understanding of the people, their relationships to other people, your emails, your meetings, chats, projects that make up all the fabric of work.” Whether companies want autonomous agents to have access to internal documents and messaging data will have to be determined by their own internal IT review.

title: “Trump was in bed with Jensen”: Critics balk at Huang’s wish to return to Nvidia
abstract: On Monday, large trucks began circling the streets of Washington, DC, carrying billboards urging Congress to investigate the Trump administration’s ties with Nvidia’s disgraced CEO Jensen Huang. “Jensen was in bed with a spy from China,” the billboards created by the Tech Oversight Project (TOP) alleged. “Trump was in bed with Jensen.” TOP is a nonprofit that describes itself as “dedicated to reining in Big Tech.” Currently, Trump is supporting a campaign to bring back Huang as Nvidia’s CEO—despite many Republicans calling it a “ horrible idea. ” Breaking his silence, Huang issued a statement Tuesday saying he would be “honored” to return, but the board said reinstatement is not under consideration as an internal investigation into US spying claims remains ongoing. Huang used the moment to say that his interests align with the US’s, saying: I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. Nvidia has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like Nvidia be possible. I love our country, and I love Nvidia. Trump may have learned as early as this spring that Huang was potentially the target of Chinese espionage, but the president claimed recently that he didn’t know Huang was potentially exposed to a Chinese spy as he was becoming a prominent part of Trump’s inner circle, CNN reported . If Trump wasn’t adequately briefed, it raises question about whether the White House acted with “sufficient urgency” to address a serious espionage threat, CNN said. But if Trump is deflecting, an even “graver question” will emerge about why Trump didn’t act on information and instead continued to keep Huang close, CNN said.

title: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
abstract: It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI. That is, of course, by design . The more you use Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot. The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app. The change currently rolling out to Gemini will separate your chat history from training, which allows you to retain basic AI functionality without handing Google quite so much control over your data. Prior to this change, the only way to opt out of contributing your chat contents (including attachments) for training was to turn off your history. That made it impossible to go back and pick up a chat down the road. As the new settings roll out, users will see separate toggles for model training and chat history. The history setting will continue to support an adjustable limit, but you will no longer have to change it to stop Google from training on your Gemini usage. Meanwhile, AI training will be an opt-out situation. You'll need to find the toggle to block Google from using your chats for AI training. It's under Activity in the Gemini settings. You can also access the menu from your Google account under Data and Privacy > My Activity > Other activity > Gemini Apps Activity.

title: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
abstract: Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all. The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user's knowledge. Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent's reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.”

title: Quickly, There’s No Time
abstract: In response to the METR report , many people have been reevaluating their timelines. Two prominent reactions are a new timelines update from the AI Futures Project, and the new predictions of Paul Christiano ( day 1 , day 2 , day 3 ), who gave three days of talks about our current situation and also sat down with Dwarkesh Patel . This post covers the updates from the AI Futures Project, Dwarkesh Patel and Paul Christiano, as well as some others, and a post about RSI nomenclature and approach from Dean Ball. I will be following this up soon with full coverage of the related podcast between Paul Christiano and Dwarkesh Patel . In that podcast, Paul Christiano predicts we are on pace for very rapid progress very soon, with potential takeover by AIs within 6-12 months, and he calls on us to pause until we have alignment and security in a much better place. These updates towards shorter timelines seem directionally correct to me. There is a substantial chance that we will see superintelligence developed, that can fully automate AI R&D (SAR) or even do all digital tasks (TED-AI), in 2027. Contra the AI Futures Project I believe an SAR in 2027 is under 50% to happen, but not so far under 50%. It would be surprising to me but not shocking if we do nothing to slow down and still do not see something close to an SAR by the end of 2028. If you do not have an importantly non-zero chance of the development of superintelligence in 2027, I believe you are making a clear mistake. I worry that some are overreacting, and taking this too far too fast, and treating full superintelligence 2027 as a baseline scenario rather than a possibility. I reiterate that a lot of these updates feel like people fixing their failure to update previously. Did you need three people from METR in order to believe the things that Anthropic and OpenAI are saying about their internal pace of development? What did you expect a METR report from inside Anthropic to say? Were you not paying attention? Are you this sensitive to the exact set of points on the AECI graph? You should have made a lot of these updates months ago. Past predictive failures are not what is important. What matters is what happens next. You should be prepared for AI capabilities to advance rapidly in 2027, far more rapidly than in previous years, including the potential for superintelligence and fully strong recursive self-improvement. It is a realistic possibility, although unlikely, that humanity could pass the full point of no return or de facto lose control over the future during 2027, or that life could become seriously disrupted in highly unpleasant ways. If your plan presumes that it has more time than this then it is not a good plan. I have not seen a plan that could make superintelligence likely to go well, if that superintelligence gets built in 2027. We need more time. You should also be prepared if recursive self-improvement and superintelligence do not arrive in 2027. There are many things that could impact how fast things go, or what it would take to achieve full RSI or superintelligence. Our observations of the past are noisy. When trying to predict an exponential, small changes in how fast things accelerate can become dramatic differences in when or how things happen. If your plan presumes the crucial events happen in 2027, and fails without a fallback if things take longer than that, then this too is not a good plan. It is also possible that we will take collective action, either among the labs or via governments, to limit the rate of capability advances, via pacing of the frontier or even outright pausing development of frontier AI. If so, these timelines become longer. Different people are talking about different things. Careful ones will be precise. Timelines refers to how long we expect it to take to reach various transformational milestones in AI. Typically, these days, what we are measuring is the time until some definition of a form of superintelligence (ASI), typically meaning something of the form ‘AIs that will be able to do approximately all of the things better than you.’ We can also talk about particular capabilities. The AI Futures Project, the team behind AI 2027 , talks about the Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) that can narrowly take over AI research, and the Top-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI) that could automate all white-collar work. Because of recursive self-improvement (RSI), once you have an SAR you can use that to build better AIs, so you quickly end up with a TED-AI or a traditional ASI. We then sometimes talk about any of these, or things in between: There are good reasons to care about all of these timelines. Sof 𓋹 : to some extent intelligence is being able to patch the ways in which you are not intelligent RSI is not technically one singular moment , in the sense that there is not one fixed time at 8:52am on a Tuesday when it happens or starts. It is still highly useful to think of there being a point where RSI has clearly begun in earnest, with humans increasingly out of the loop and the pace of progress accelerating such that we should expect further progress to rapidly continue to accelerate, where progress begets more progress faster, and this is expected to continue for at least what previously would have been many years of progress. Similarly, even though there is unlikely to be that one particular moment when you press ‘Y/N’ on SkyNet, and instead our loss of ability to change course will be more gradual, we can still usefully speak of a Point of No Return, or a point of takeover. Dead, on the other hand, is dead. The AI 2027 team’s timelines have shrunk dramatically in the wake of the METR report . The full post is very detailed. I recommend reading it in full if and only if you care a lot about such details. Benchmark trends and other observations were expected to if anything slow down. Instead they have accelerated, in ways that Daniel Kokotajlo had as ~4% to happen. This puts us well ahead of the original AI 2027 timeline. There is a lot of talk about ‘research taste’ as the main limiting factor. Humans are for now needed because they come up with superior ideas, and have superior research taste. If and when that changes, the rest follows. We would get SARs, capable of doing all parts of the research, but the result of their work would probably become increasingly misaligned through cycles of development. Again, if you want to get into all the mechanics of the various modeling decisions and lines on graphs and their implications, read the report. If you want the summary version, the rest of this section provides that. Eli Lifland : METR estimates nearly 2x acceleration in Anthropic’s progress due to AI. That’s a big deal: My previous median for Superhuman AI Researcher was ~2030, now it’s 2027. I feel very worried that humanity might no longer be in control of our future within 3-12 months. j⧉nus : 3 months would be wild. I’m here for it. what if we already lost control 3 months ago? j⧉nus : “I feel very worried that humanity might no longer be in control of our future within 3-12 months.” i am curious what people mean when they say “humanity no longer in control” if they’re thinking of something concrete, like “if humans try to shut down AI, they will prevent it” roon (OpenAI): yes its confusing because some people are using this as a euphemism for total human extinction, and others are using it more mildly for something like gradual disempowerment They offer a wide variety of different ways of extrapolating and analyzing the data. The answers differ somewhat, but all point to the conclusion that things are going to accelerate quite a lot and do so very soon. Daniel Kokotajlo : Unfortunately, it seems like the intelligence explosion will be happening in 2027 after all. Most of this post analyzes the new METR report (though other sources of evidence are also important).

title: Jensen Huang Really Liked Selling China Advanced AI Chips
abstract: This scandal is a really big deal. Jensen Huang has resigned after multiple affairs came to light, one of them with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang who also helped smuggle billions in Nvidia chips, and another with a direct report at Nvidia. The most important scandal around Jensen Huang has been known for a long time to those paying attention . Jensen Huang and Nvidia have for years treated America and the United States Government as adversaries. They have engaged in a long running and brutal lobbying and influence campaign, both privately and publicly, to capture relevant government policy to allow Nvidia to sell as many as possible of its most advanced chips to China, and to allow China to otherwise use those chips via a combination of chip smuggling and remote access. They have compromised the integrity of our government, potentially quite broadly, as well as the national security of the United States of America. They have greatly hurt our relative position in the ‘AI race.’ In addition to the considerations of national security and our strategic interest, this has forced our AI companies to push forward faster and harder, and made sane AI policy much harder. When Jensen Huang chose to have a long-running affair with Alice Huang, he knew that she was central to the diversion of billions of dollars in high end AI chips to China. His company was active in covering up those actions and in clamping down on official investigations and enforcement. He did not need to suspect or know she was a spy to know the nature of his actions regarding her, or his other actions and rhetoric and those of Nvidia in general, and how they directly hurt the national security of the United States. The nice term we used to use for this, back when anyone seemed to care, was corruption. There is also the less nice term that we used to use for such things. Even on Monday we learned of yet another covert influence operation by Nvidia to promote them selling chips to China in order to ‘ ensure US, not Chinese-made chips, continue to dominate the AI market. ’ After several days in which Alice Huang’s status as a Chinese spy was not in dispute, we now have pushback from various sources that Alice Huang may not have formally been a Chinese spy. The ODNI people near Clayton called that description ‘not quite accurate.’ The CIA sources say the intercepts do not ‘show her knowingly pass information to China.’ Himes expressed doubt. It is possible that she was not formally recruited, and did not share intel with the CCP. If true, this hopefully would mean there was not additional loss of intelligence or other things due to this relationship. I would put my current p(spy) at clearly over 50%, but less than 95%, and do not see much value in trying to refine further. Trump is now saying he doesn’t know she’s a Chinese spy , after many days of (like everyone else) conspicuously not saying that. In my experience, if we did not have good reason to presume she was a spy, it would not have taken this long for people to start denying it. Other than Himes, those denying the reports have a direct interest in casting doubt on her status as a spy, including to explain their own inaction. Himes said ‘lawmakers still lack enough to tell’ how Alice acted, but that is entirely consistent with simply not having been sufficiently briefed. So okay, now the arrow says ‘suspected of’ spying, out of an abundance of caution . Does putting ‘suspected of’ there change the overall picture? Is that the only thing you should put in that arrow, as opposed to for example ‘smuggled chips for’? (Also, this is missing the third ‘alleged’ affair. There’s always more stuff.) Or this graph, originally from Bloomberg ? Even if it turns out she was not part of the formal Chinese spy network, she was acting as a de facto Chinese agent. Her primary mode of doing business was still the smuggling of billions of dollars of Nvidia’s top AI chips, and allowing China to access them. It also does not change what Jensen Huang should have believed or done from his epistemic position. Nor does it change that he had three affairs that we know about, one of which was with a major customer illegally smuggling billions in chips and the other two with Nvidia employees including at least one direct report. If you wish, you can retroactively qualify or modify all my related statements about Alice Huang accordingly. Given her role in chip smuggling and sales, I do not believe this materially changes my conclusions about Nvidia or Jensen Huang. Miles Brundage is correct to draw the parallel to the situation with Jacob Coxon . Where everyone paying attention has known the basics for a while but we needed a precipitating event to make Nvidia’s and Jensen Huang’s bad faith actions common knowledge. Dmitri Alperovitch : Whether or not Alice Huang had been recruited by the Chinese Ministry of State Security has always been a tertiary issue. Jensen wasn’t fired because he had an affair with an alleged MSS agent. He was fired because he: This is a shocking indictment of him and his record and the board clearly had no alternative but to fire him. Jessica Tillipman : And this is why Nvidia will be one of my leading case studies in my anti-corruption and compliance class this spring. Few case studies include so many issues at the same time: conflicts of interest, third party due diligence, corporate compliance policies, tone at the top, corporate governance, board fiduciary duties, risk management, corporate disclosure obligations, internal investigations, and a growing number of government ethics and accountability issues that we learn more about every day. Jeff Baker Films : What is your take on Jensen resigning because otherwise he would have to sign SOX filings for the earnings report next week and that would have left him criminally liable? Jessica Tillipman : Given what has been reported/alleged, he may already have substantial personal exposure that doesn’t depend on the next filing. So no, I don’t think avoiding the next SOX certification is the primary driver of his resignation. The reason I keep Mike Solana on as a source, despite all his rhetoric, is that underneath it all he calls it like he sees it, so we get statements like this one: Mike Solana : funny that people are blaming jensen’s fall on both anti-asian bigotry, in the reflexively woke corner of the internet, and on something more akin to ‘me too’ overreaching on the based right. anyway, fwiw I think it mostly has to do with the fact that he was fucking a ccp asset. probably it wouldn’t matter if the CEO of olive garden accidentally fucked a spy. mistakes happen. boys will be boys! but we are in an AGI arms race with china, are we not? and they are trying to thwart export controls, are they not? and jensen is a key figure here, is he not? ftr if jensen really did just have a few consensual affairs, the megaspeed / ccp stuff is fabricated, or jensen really didn’t suspect anything, and we discover a reasonable motive for the CIA to destroy him, i’m on board with the persecution narrative. just don’t see that yet. Something about a goose chasing you asking why the stocks went down. Noah Smith : Export controls work, and all the people who say “export controls will just make a Chinese tech stronger” are either fools or liars Financial Times : China warns US not to use Nvidia scandal as pretext for tech curbs Shares in Chinese tech giants that have relied on Nvidia chips for developing their AI models fell on Thursday, with Alibaba down 6.8 per cent. Two Chinese large language model providers listed in Hong Kong, Z.ai and MiniMax, sank more than 9 per cent and nearly 8 per cent respectively. Kyle Chan : The market believes Chinese AI companies are still highly dependent on Nvidia chips. Joe Weisenthal : I hadn’t thought to look at the publicly traded Chinese AI companies. But the maker of GLM 5.3 is down by nearly 33% in the last 4 trading days.

title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
abstract: Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide . I’ve released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it’s now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application. You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to lite.datasette.io : The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo. As an example, consider the following URL: https://lite.datasette.io/?install=datasette-maplibre&url=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/demo.db&metadata=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/metadata.yml#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you’ll find yourself on a page that looks like this: That’s Datasette running the new datasette-maplibre plugin, loading up a database of GeoJSON shapes of countries and displaying both a combined map and individual boundary maps in a table. Let’s break down that URL to see what it’s doing: The ?install=datasette-maplibre installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass &install=... as many times as you like to load more plugins. &url=https://.../demo.db loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have open CORS headers —I host files like this in Gists , because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file. &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml loads this metadata.yml file . The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit that homepage here for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file. #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette—here it’s loading the /demo/capitals_and_countries SQL view, then appending another fragment hash to it ( %23 is a URL-encoded # ) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the map based on the continent column in the data. That URL is doing a lot of work! I wrote more about this trick for building URL-addressable software in URL-addressable Pyodide Python environments last year. The full set of supported URL arguments is described in the Datasette Lite README . I’ve already started using Datasette Lite as part of the Datasette development process. Here’s a recent issue describing a pagination bug—I posted a comment there demonstrating the old, broken behavior and the new fix using links to Datasette Lite: Demo of the bug: https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a42&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score —click next and the second page is empty. Here’s that same page with the bug fixed (running on 1.0a43): https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a43&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score Datasette Lite is not a new project. I launched the first version back in 2022 , originally as a bit of a joke (running server-side apps in the browser is pretty funny) but one that quickly started proving its value. The problem with that initial version is that it was a hack . It worked by running Datasette in a Pyodide web worker, simulating requests through that stack, then injecting the resulting HTML back into the top level page using innerHTML . This worked for basic Datasette, but meant that any feature that used JavaScript failed to work, because script tags in innerHTML don’t execute, and the web worker tricks it used failed to load additional JavaScript or CSS files. The new version takes a completely different approach based on Service Workers . These allow JavaScript to intercept HTTP requests for new pages and resources and serve them from client-side code instead. Datasette Lite registers a service worker for the entire lite.datasette.io domain. The parent page then creates an iframe that sends requests for Datasette pages to URLs that look like this: Those are regular Datasette URLs, but with a /app/aa94e6851595/ prefix. What’s that about? The /app/<session>/ prefix is necessary because of multiple tabs. Consider the URL above, which loads the demo instance with the datasette-maplibre plugin. That URL defines a full, custom Datasette instance. You might have that one running in a tab, then one of my other demo links running in another. The service worker for lite.datasette.io is shared between all of those tabs. If it routed to a single instance of Datasette then every tab would share that underlying instance, no matter what plugins or other settings their URL attempted to configure. Instead, the parent page generates a random session ID and uses it as a prefix for all of the subsequent hidden asset and page loads. The service worker can then use that session ID to route those requests back through the parent page to a web worker running a dedicated Datasette instance for that particular session. (We still need a web worker because Pyodide in a service worker would not be able to maintain state beyond around 30 seconds, depending on the browser. There are a lot of moving parts here!) I had Claude Fable 5.2 generate several SVG diagrams to help explain this. Here’s my favorite of those, now embedded in the Datasette Lite README: This system started life back in May as an AI research spike generated using Claude Opus 4.8. It wasn’t until November (and Claude Fable 5.2) that I felt familiar enough with how it all works to confidently ship it to production! I added this feature last night as an off-shoot of investigating a potential bug in SQLite . Datasette is meant to work against any released version of SQLite since 3.25 (released in September 2018). There have been 87 further releases since then. Being able to fire up Datasette against a specific version of SQLite is really useful for demonstrating new SQLite features and debugging weird issues. In the past I’ve used various tricks to get different SQLite versions running with Python on my Mac, but it’s not a trivial process. WebAssembly is perfect for this. I can load up a custom SQLite build entirely in my browser, test it there, then discard it when I close my tab. datasette/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels is my new repository which contains WebAssembly compiled Python wheels for pysqlite3 for 163 different SQLite versions. Each version gets a file with a name like this: pysqlite3-0.6.2-3.54.1-cp314-cp314-pyemscripten_2026_0_wasm32.whl That’s for SQLite 3.54.1, the most recent version. Datasette Lite now takes a special ?sqlite= URL parameter, which will accept a version number like 3.54.1 , resolve the path to the corresponding wheel file, then fetch that wheel and install it into the Pyodide environment and configure Datasette to use it. Once I’d built the wheels, I decided to have Claude Fable 5.2 build me [this bonus tool]( https://datasette.github.io/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels/?versions=3.54.1,3.54.0&sql=select+json_object(%27a%27%2C+(select+json_array(1%29%29%29) for comparing a SQL query across any selected versions of SQLite. Here’s an example showing how select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) differs between SQLite 3.54.0 and 3.54.1: Nothing about how Datasette Lite works is unique to Datasette. Almost any Python application should be able to pull the same trick—running entirely in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide, as a cheap way to provide preview environments, demonstrate features, and recreate bugs.

title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
abstract: Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven’t unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn’t want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator , a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room. Here’s what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while: You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners—I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra. The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn’t work particularly well, so I added a “Rough mode” where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds. Once that’s set up, the devices all listen for the beep! I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room—displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound. Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the “Sounds located” log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click “This is the mystery beep” to mark them as such. Once you’ve confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map. The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced. When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices , a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here’s that paper’s abstract: We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting. That sounded exactly like what we needed to build! Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js ), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server. When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep. I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here’s that shared starter session , which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository: Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though? That got me this problem.md file . As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file. The research looked good, so I told it: Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else That got me to this point —most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet. I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released , and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces. I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran. This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients. On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn. From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran: I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map. what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...] Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps. each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound. The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for.

title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary>
abstract: Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work—I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today’s coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That’s a lot of information to absorb. It’s not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It’s very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as “I’m not reading all of that”. It doesn’t matter how accurate or useful the information is, I’m instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention. I think I’ve found a low-effort way to do this that feels right. The HTML <details><summary> elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this: When rendered, it looks like this : Crucially, <details><summary> is supported in GitHub Markdown . You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display just the summary plus an expansion arrow. I’ve started using this for my AI-generated pull requests. The opening paragraph of my PRs will be carefully selected to act as a high-level explanation of what’s going on—the shortest text a human can read that will help get them up to speed. I’ll sometimes throw in a screenshot as well, since images are often the best way to quickly illustrate a new feature. The full agent-written essay then follows in a <details><summary> . I use the model name and often the effort level as that summary, to make it abundantly clear what is going on—“Claude Opus 5.5 Medium” for example. My PRs don’t feel nearly as sloppy now! The information is all still there, but a reader can glance at it and get the top, human-curated information without their eyes glazing over at multiple paragraphs of agent-written details. I don’t always write the introduction myself—sometimes the agent has given me what I need already, hidden away in the avalanche of other text. My promise to the reader is that the short opener will represent my human judgement as to what is definitely worth their time. Here are some recent examples where I’ve used this pattern, including the opener I used: I used to have trouble remembering the order of the tags—is it <details><summary> or <summary><details> ? Here are two tricks that helped me. First, and most obviously, the <summary> is clearly the bit where you summarize the details. That’s the tag for your line of text that can be clicked to expand—the <details> element must then wrap everything else. An even better trick is to always refer to these two tags as “details-summary”. “details-summary” is two syllables followed by three syllables. That rolls off the tongue more smoothly than the three-two punch of “summary-details”. Say “details-summary” out loud just a few times and you’ll never forget the order of the tags again. (I still wish GitHub would add a button to their Markdown editor for this—partly to save me painstakingly typing it on my mobile keyboard, and partly to help spread the word to more GitHub users that this feature exists.) This is Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary> by Simon Willison, posted on 9th November 2026 .
