title: AI agents ask better questions than KPMG accountants in audit trial
abstract:
LONDON, November 18, 2026 — Artificial intelligence has taken another significant step into the world of professional services after KPMG revealed that AI agents examining the accounts of a major UK-listed company sometimes investigated financial issues more deeply and asked better questions than its human audit team. The experiment, conducted by KPMG UK using more than 100 AI agents, marks an important development in the application of artificial intelligence to one of the most labour-intensive areas of the financial services industry. It also raises an uncomfortable question for the accountancy profession: if machines can increasingly perform the analytical work traditionally undertaken by highly trained professionals, how quickly will the economics of auditing change? According to the Financial Times , the project, codenamed Project Exponential, examined the financial statements of an unnamed FTSE 250 company. The AI agents worked alongside a conventional audit team, undertaking tasks across the audit process rather than simply assisting with isolated administrative functions. Join The European Business Briefing New subscribers this quarter are entered into a draw to win a Rolex Submariner. Join 40,000+ founders, investors and executives who read EBM every day. Subscribe KPMG UK head of audit Cath Burnet said the technology had, in several instances, gone considerably deeper into issues than the regular audit team, identifying areas requiring further investigation and asking questions that human auditors had not necessarily raised. The findings suggest that AI’s potential in professional services may extend well beyond improving productivity. It could fundamentally change how complex financial information is examined, interpreted and challenged. From supporting accountants to conducting audits Project Exponential represents a shift from using AI as a supporting tool towards deploying autonomous agents across an entire audit workflow. The agents collected information, analysed and documented data, developed draft conclusions and observations, and suggested subsequent steps. They were also able to work alongside one another, effectively dividing responsibilities and coordinating elements of the investigation. The technology was developed over approximately four months. However, KPMG was careful to distinguish the experiment from a formally approved statutory audit. Although an audit partner signed off on the experimental exercise, its findings were not used as the basis for formally approving the company’s accounts. Human oversight remained essential. During the trial, an auditor had to intervene when one AI agent failed to correctly match regulatory requirements with the company’s documentation. The episode illustrates both the capabilities and limitations of current AI systems when dealing with complex regulatory frameworks. KPMG plans to expand the initiative to as many as 20 larger audits, although the firm acknowledges that the technology is not yet sufficiently mature to be deployed across thousands of engagements. Data quality also remains a significant obstacle, with some businesses lacking the clean, structured information required for AI agents to operate effectively. A challenge to the Big Four business model? The implications for the accountancy industry could be substantial. Traditional auditing relies on large teams of junior accountants undertaking detailed and repetitive work, supervised by experienced managers and partners. AI agents potentially offer a different operating model, automating significant portions of data collection, analysis and documentation while allowing senior professionals to concentrate on complex judgements and exceptions. For firms such as KPMG, Deloitte, PwC and EY, the attraction is clear: faster audits, potentially lower operating costs and the ability to analyse much larger volumes of financial information. However, whether those savings will ultimately be passed on to clients remains uncertain. KPMG has acknowledged the potential for significant time savings but has not confirmed whether AI-driven efficiencies will translate into lower audit fees. Human judgement remains the final safeguard The transition also presents regulatory and professional challenges. The UK’s Financial Reporting Council has warned that the use of AI must not undermine auditor independence, integrity or professional scepticism. There are also concerns about data security, over-reliance on automated conclusions and the possibility of AI generating inaccurate or fabricated information. The fundamental responsibility for an audit opinion remains with the human auditor, regardless of the technology used. The KPMG experiment does not establish that AI can replace accountants or independently deliver a reliable statutory audit. It does, however, demonstrate that AI agents are beginning to challenge professionals in areas that were once considered dependent on human expertise. For the accountancy profession, the question is no longer simply whether AI will become part of the audit process. It is how much of that process will eventually be performed by machines — and what role human accountants will play when it does.

title: Bank CEOs, NSA Tell Congress That AI-Driven Patches Are Behind Outages
abstract:
Technology Bank CEOs, NSA Tell Congress That AI-Driven Patches Are Behind Outages Artificial intelligence is not causing the disruptions but identifying gaps that are difficult to fix. government and banking officials have told lawmakers that they stem from attempts to fix gaps in cyber defenses. (J. Scott Applewhite/AP) By Jeff Stein November 17, 2026 07:45 p.m. Wall Street executives and the National Security Agency have told members of Congress that this week’s widespread tech outages were caused by attempts to fix vulnerabilities identified by artificial intelligence, according to three sources familiar with the private conversations. Over the last few days, the country has faced a series of startling tech failures, leading to a pause in all flights nationwide, customers being unable to access their bank accounts and a highly classified communications network at the National Security Agency going down . While it does not appear that these disruptions were caused by a cyberattack, government and banking officials have told lawmakers that they stem from attempts to fix gaps in cyber defenses identified by AI models, the sources said. The fixes, however, temporarily overwhelmed the systems. “These models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, and that increases the urgency to patch right away,” said one congressional official briefed on the matter. “They’re trying to push through a lot of patches all at once — more than the system was designed for.” Trending Facing Suspicion Over the Outages, the Trump Administration Tackles the Message Head-On DHS, DOJ Launch Cybercrime Combat Hub Mullin Faces House Democrats Ready to Flex Their Power FBI’s No. 2 Refuses to Name Any Right-Wing Threats On Monday, banks such as JP Morgan Chase blamed software-related bugs for the service issues. On Tuesday, the NSA said that “scheduled routine maintenance” was responsible for the “temporary degradation” of some of its networks. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told CNBC on Tuesday that “they’re pushing new technology on top of really old computer systems, and it just seems to overwhelm the system. ... We’re going to see more of this as new technology rolls out.” Powerful companies and government agencies have increasingly trained the most powerful AI models on themselves, seeking to identify the vulnerabilities that others may weaponize against them. Once these gaps are identified, they are under immense pressure to patch them as soon as possible, knowing that malicious actors have access to comparable AI tools — or will soon. This urgency is what has driven a wide range of public- and private-sector actors to rush fixes to their systems faster than they normally would, the sources said. But even entities with large resources, such as the nation’s top banks and the intelligence community, are finding it difficult to do so without accidentally causing outages. The sources spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations. The outages rippled across the country this week. The Federal Aviation Administration canceled more than 20,000 flights as a result of the nationwide ground stop, according to The Wall Street Journal. Microsoft experienced a major outage of Outlook. Microsoft blamed a technical defect for the disruption. It is also unclear what caused the FAA systems to go down. “There’s some sense in which this is reassuring, in that it means there’s not an attack. But it shows the extent to which safety critical infrastructure we rely on is based on software with large vulnerabilities on legacy systems,” said Nathan Calvin, the chief strategy officer at Encode. “Updating those is going to be a rocky process, and as we get more advanced models this won’t be a one and done thing — we’ll continue to find more vulnerabilities.” The NSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Author Jeff Stein is a reporter at The Washington Sun.

title: Show HN: TrnRT – An open-source LLM inference engine for AWS Trainium
abstract: Hi HN, Sanchit here from RunAnywhere (YC W26). We just open-sourced TrnRT: Trainium RunTime, our inference engine for AWS Trainium. We started 3 weeks back, and currently we’re able to serve and run GLM 5.3 flash (FP8) on AWS trn2.48xlarge, and will bring more models support soon. It’s open to contributions :) What it does today: - Serves 2 instances of GLM-5.3 flash on a single box, 8 trn2 with a cache aware router. - Can process 3.57M TPM (tokens per minute) on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks. - Runs decode as one NKI kernel per layer half, or for the 11 sparse-attention layers fuses both blocks into a single kernel, for faster performance. We started working on Trn2 because we wanted to explore it and see if we can come close to beating it’s performance in terms of cost efficiency compared to H100/H200. A big MoE with 1M context window such as GLM-5.3 flash requires a lot of memory, and memory/tb on a trn2.48xlarge costs less than half compared to 8x h200 on AWS, and hence we wanted to experiment with it and now we’re sharing some early results. But AWS's own stack didn't support the model: vLLM Neuron's latest release did not register any GLM model, and NxDI, AWS's own distributed inference framework, is no longer under active development. We also saw the drop of SGLang Neuron implementation yesterday, but there is no good support for Trn2, which is the only chip available for public use right now. We ran semiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks, which replays real coding agent sessions: - 1 box served 28.9 RPM(requests per minute) with 32 agents at batch 12 (also known as concurrency) -The P50 TTFT with a cached prompt at 16 agents is ~1.24 seconds with a decode of 35.9 tps. Initially, the recurrence in one kda (linear attention) layer was ~2% of the layer's attention time at batch 1, and the rest was projections, transposes and XLA glue between small kernels. So we wrote the megakernel so that it covers the whole layer in 2 kernel dispatch, which made decode 25% faster at batch 8. The sparse attention kernel keep a layer’s working weights in SBUF, distributing weighted streaming across the cores and handling the interchip communication within There’s an approximation in the sparse-attention prefill, affecting about 1.2% of block selections. You can refer to the write-up for the profiling results:  https://runanywhere.ai/blog/glm-5-3-flash-trainium2-nki-mega...  Please give it a try yourself on a trn2.48xlarge and reproduce the AgentX results by following the steps in docs/RESULTS.md. Happy to collaborate and hear any feedback. Deploying high performant dedicated inference at lab like performance and half the price for open models such as the GLM-5.3 family, Kimi K3, Deepseek flash etc. is how we make money. You can talk to us regarding the same at founders@runanywhere.ai. We hope you find this useful. If you are working with Trainium or have experience with NKI kernels, we'd love to get your honest feedback. Feel free to share the models you want support for next, and we welcome any contributions to the repository.

Performance and speed for everyday coding MAI Code 2 is at the frontier of price-performance for common enterprise coding tasks and excels in taking code to production, deep debugging, multi-file implementation, repo-wide reasoning, and UI. It does all of this while also delivering changes code maintainers would merge, at a fraction of frontier cost. Meanwhile, MAI Code 2 Flash is designed for high-volume work such as code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes, and rapid iterations, while bringing quality at a much lower cost. Production quality at less than half the price To deliver the best price-performance, we’ve built these models to prioritize the coding work our customers do every day. They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long-horizon agentic work. Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1), MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT-6.1 Sol at 40% of the cost, and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5’s performance at just 5% of the cost. 1 MAI Code 2 is also tuned for producing great dashboards and visualizations, and excels at visual coding. In blind frontend app evaluations, developers preferred its results over GPT-6 Sol 64% of the time. 2 In addition, MAI Code 2 Flash offers comparable performance to GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 6 5% and 20% of the cost, across three coding benchmarks measuring day-to-day, high-volume routine coding tasks. 3 Beyond coding MAI Code 2 is also becoming the workhorse behind Microsoft products. From Code 2 Flash, we further optimized a single model, MAI Work Flash, to serve multiple Microsoft products across Microsoft 365 and FabricIQ. Excel: Our model is on par for accuracy and token efficiency with GPT-6 Luna across key internal Excel customer-scenario benchmarks. PowerPoint: On key production benchmark scenarios that measure frequent PowerPoint tasks, our model performs on par with GPT-6 Luna in both quality and token efficiency. Word: Our model performs similarly to GPT-6.1 Sol (while being significantly smaller) on 5 key internal benchmarks using ~42% fewer input tokens per call than GPT-6.1 Sol in production. Teams: Our model beats GPT-6 Luna at tracking decisions, filling knowledge gaps, and adapting to custom instructions using up to 28% fewer tokens on instruction following and tool calling. FabricIQ: In offline evaluation runs, our MAI model outperforms GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus 5.5 at DAX query generation, the core capability behind “Chat With Your Data” for Power BI semantic models. title: Launch HN: StarSling (YC P25) – Self-improving CI for agent-volume repos
abstract:
We’re Yonas and Daniel and we’re building StarSling ( https://starsling.dev ), fast GitHub Actions runners with AI agents that ship PRs to continuously improve your tests and workflows. Every CI job gets its own ephemeral sandbox on the fastest Zen 5 machines and NVMe Disk with unlimited concurrency so a burst of agent PRs all run at once. We’re different from other runners because ours come with agents that cut down your CI bill over time. PRs are generated through our CI harness, which runs an agent loop that’s tuned to improve your CI speed and reduce cost. Mastra now merges over 1,800 PRs a month and we got their slowest workflow from 29m 56s on GitHub-hosted runners down to 5m 06s (5.87x) on StarSling. We realized the true value of having an agent loop running on top of fast runners when our agents found an 11-month-old performance bottleneck in better-auth. The fix made one of their test jobs 5.4x faster:  https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/10762 . I previously founded StackShare, which grew to over 1.5M developers. Daniel helped build Netflix's internal developer portal. Last year we started building AI agents for DevOps because shipping code to prod fell way behind agentic coding. We hit the CI bottleneck ourselves as we were building agents. Our own agents shipped so many PRs that at peak our job queues were backed up for hours and our CI bill got close to our inference bill. We now support per-second billing, and just shipped StarSling Disks - persistent disks that give you a 4.9x speedup in dependencies ready over actions/cache. You can see a quick demo of disks in action here :  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2JrrpRm9Mww . Our CI harness runs a loop that has agents:
- Analyze your workflows, run logs, and machine telemetry
- Propose an optimization
- Test your unchanged workflow side by side the proposed change
- Deterministically judge that the difference is statistically significant
- Ship the winner to you as a PR with benchmarks evidence We benchmarked open source repos on our runners and average 10x speedup in wall clock time with 70% less runner time:
-  https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-gogs  (12.8x)
-  https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-shellcheck  (5.5x)
-  https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-chatwoot  (3.9x)
-  https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-transfer.sh  (11.7x)
-  https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-mirotalksfu  (36.4x) Yes, you can do these optimizations yourself with prompts so we’ve released skills for this:  https://github.com/starslingdev/skills . The benefit of using our agents is that you don’t need to spend tokens and CI compute finding optimizations yourself. We started building our runners on AWS at the beginning of the year and realized that was too expensive. But at that time there weren’t any cloud providers that could give us the same machines we were getting on AWS, billed per minute (microVMs). So we convinced a handful of sandbox providers to get Zen 5s and started benchmarking them publicly ( https://github.com/starslingdev/hpc-sandbox-benchmarks ). We’ve learned that fast infrastructure is table stakes for CI, but it’s not sufficient on its own. To get fast and cost effective CI you need a process that continues making improvements. We turned CI optimizations from OpenAI, Anthropic, Linear and others into playbooks for your agent:  https://starsling.dev/ci-playbooks . To try it, give your agent this URL:  https://docs.starsling.dev/start . You get 2,000 free minutes. Our agents start opening PRs once you've hit about 10,000 minutes. Today we announced our CI Challenge: if StarSling can't save you at least 10% on your next CI bill, we'll literally give you $1,000. Eligibility and rules here:  https://starsling.dev/blog/ci-challenge . We’d love your feedback on the headless experience and what you’d like to see improved in your own CI setup!  https://starsling.dev

title: Energy-Based Reasoners: 385x more efficient inference
abstract:
Looping is a powerful inductive bias for reasoning. By repeatedly iterating a recurrent block, looped models can scale their effective depth and enable multi-step reasoning in latent space. However, existing looped models are not inherently guided by an explicit measure of progress, making it difficult to determine when to stop looping and how to improve upon the current state. To enable this, we introduce Energy-Based Reasoners ( EBRs ), which learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. The energy scores latent states, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a signal for stopping. To train EBRs effectively, we further introduce exploration-based training to discover additional modes and to better shape the energy landscape over a broader set of states. Across four algorithmic reasoning benchmarks, EBRs match or outperform prior recurrent reasoning models, achieving 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345× less inference compute than the next-best model and maintaining comparable training compute. On all multi-solution benchmarks, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage of distinct valid solutions while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy. These results suggest that energy-based models are a promising approach for strong reasoning performance.

title: Latent Lattice Language Models
abstract:
Language models typically increase per-token computation through deeper or looped layers and latent reasoning steps, while richer residual connections improve information flow across layers. We instead increase computational capacity : the number of active computational states a model maintains. We introduce the Lattice of Latents , a set of per-layer horizontal latent streams that run recurrently along time, alongside the vertical residual stream that flows through depth. Like hyper-connections, mHC, and attention or value residuals, the Lattice enhances the residual stream, but rather than adding or rerouting residual pathways through depth, it provides companion computational states that persist across tokens. Unlike hybrid Transformer–SSM architectures, whose recurrent states primarily serve as internal memory for sequence mixing, these latents directly condition the vertical stream’s attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding. On Transformers trained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens, a 406M-parameter Lattice model lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 over a parameter-matched Transformer. These gains extend across architectural variants. The Lattice composes with prior residual-stream enhancements: with hyper-connections and input residuals, it lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 (base Transformer) and 14.22 (Transformer with same enhancements) to 13.61. On Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN–Mamba-2 hybrids, it improves perplexity at every tested native state size, with Lattice-GDN & Lattice-Triadic-GDN variants outperforming pure baselines with 4× larger native states. These results identify persistent per-layer state as a complementary axis for scaling language-model computation. Vertical residual streams flow through depth; horizontal latents persist across tokens. Switch between training and inference, and compare models. Interactive versions of the main results. title: Human.md
abstract:
## what this file is A reminder, in plain text, of what I think humans actually bring to the table now that the machines are very good and getting better every day. I keep coming back to the word "taste" and I keep finding it too small. Taste is the surface. There is a whole engine underneath it, and that engine is the part the model can't have. Yet. Maybe ever. I don't know. I'm not in that argument. I'm in this one: ## the actual job ### 1. break the rule on purpose Models are trained on the average. The average is the floor, not the ceiling. Our job is not to conform a little better than the last person who conformed. Our job is to know the rule cold, and then break it on purpose, in public, with a reason. Symmetry is a rule. Break it. Three-act structure is a rule. Break it. "Don't shoot into the sun" is a rule. Break it. If you can't say why you broke it, you didn't break it, you just missed. ### 2. find the thing in the weird place Inspiration does not live in the first ten image-search results. It lives in: a misprinted parking ticket the way your grandfather folded a napkin an obscure Victorian zoetrope of a cat the back of a menu in a town you can't pronounce the tension in Rene Magritte's "The Son of Man", 1946 A model averages the internet. A human walks somewhere strange and brings back something unexpected. ### 3. advocate for the human and humanity Every brief now has an invisible third party at the table. Someone has to keep saying "and what does this feel like for the person on the other end of it." Someone has to keep saying "how is humanity better through the birthing of this idea?" That's the job. Not "is it on-brand." Not "does it convert." What does it feel like? what good does it do? If you aren't there saying it, no one will. The model certainly won't. ### 4. design for emotional resonance, not correctness Tension. Surprise. Restraint. The pause before the punchline. The photograph that's almost in focus. The sentence that ends one beat earlier than you expected. These are not bugs. These are the entire reason anyone remembers anything. "Correct" is the lowest bar in the building. Step over it and keep walking. ### 5. seek delight, not delivery I would rather make one thing that makes someone laugh out loud on a train than ten things that "meet the brief." At the very least, it needs to make ME laugh. This is a personal bias. If it's not at least a little bit fun, why are we here? ### 6. experiment ruthlessly, ship more than you opine A working sketch beats a confident take. Every time. A bad first draft beats a brilliant unwritten one. Every time. A weird little prototype beats a slide deck about prototyping. Every. Time. Make 50 things. Throw away 47. Talk about the 3. Do not, under any circumstances, become a person who mostly posts opinions about other people's work. ### 7. own the output. fully. If the AI output is bad, the AI did not fail you. You failed it. You picked the tool. You wrote the prompt. You accepted the result. You shipped it. The fix is not a better model, or a return to tools of the past. The fix is a sharper you. Sharpen yourself. Sharpen your ideas. Sharpen the way you say what you mean, because the gap between what you wanted and what came back is almost always a gap in you , not in the tool. Powerful tools reward the people who showed up sharp, iterate, spend extra time on the vision. They expose the people who didn't. AI is not the great equalizer, it is the great amplifier. ### 8. design with it, not next to it Watching the generation happen is not the work. Prompting once and accepting the result is not the work. The work is the back-and-forth. The push. The loop. The "again, but tweak is this way..." The hundredth iteration where the thing finally clicks. If you're a spectator to your own output, you are not the author of your own output. Get your hands in. ### 9. play with purpose. and play for play. Both. At the same time. Some days the play is in service of a thing. Some days the play is the thing. A practice that only ever has goals is a job. A practice that never has goals is a hobby. The good work lives in between. Play doesn't result in burnout. It results in excitement, happiness, experiment, the unexpected, and an urge to play more. ### 10. be a builder and an ideas person The split is fake. It was always fake. It's especially fake now. The people who can think of the thing and make the thing are going to eat. The people who can only do one half are going to be very busy explaining why the other half is hard, or blame the processes or tools. Don't be that person. Learn the other half. It's never been cheaper to learn it. ## things I am trying to stop doing waiting until it's "ready" editing in my head instead of on the page making but not sharing publicly taking briefs that secretly bore me pretending taste is an innate quality treating "AI" like a noun instead of a verb ## things I am trying to do more finish the bad version first show people the in-between, mess, experiments write the thing I'd want to read dig deeper, get help stop pretending I know stuff, ask dumber questions say the more specific thing This file will be wrong in six months. That is fine. I'd rather be specifically wrong than vaguely correct. — b. last touched, kitchen table, late.

title: 350 years ago, Ole Rømer discovered that light has a finite speed
abstract:
350 years ago, this man discovered that light has a finite speed Ole Rømer was the first to demonstrate that light takes time to travel. The Danish astronomer Ole Rømer was responsible for an important discovery in the history of science. (Image: Wikimedia Commons) Elise Kjørstad Elise Kjørstad Journalist Published 16 November 2026 - 00:01 In September 1676, Ole Rømer made a prediction to the members of the Académie des Sciences in Paris. He said that on November 9, Io, one of Jupiter's moons, would emerge from the planet's shadow ten minutes later than expected. Rømer was right. In doing so, he proved that light travels at a finite speed. This knowledge became crucial to how we understand the universe today. Until then, people had believed that light travelled instantaneously from one place to another. Annonse Most viewed In a box in the basement lay four girls who died in the 1300s, still wearing red mittens on their hands 350 years ago, this man discovered that light has a finite speed Archaeologists have opened a Viking Age ship burial. The most exciting discovery may lie beneath the ship How dirty and unhygienic were people in the Middle Ages? People with this personality trait are more prone to anxiety and depression Regularly disappears behind Jupiter Ole Rømer was a Danish astronomer and physicist. In 1671, he travelled to Paris, where he spent ten years as a member of the scientific academy and an astronomer at the Paris Observatory, according to the Great Norwegian Encyclopedia . In the years leading up to the discovery, Rømer and other astronomers had been closely observing Io, Jupiter's third-largest moon. "Io regularly disappears behind Jupiter, and this regularity made it possible to use the moon as a clock," Jacob Wüsthoff Linder tells Science Norway. He is a professor at NTNU's Department of Physics. Such a precise ‘clock’ could be useful for navigation, among other things. Ole Eggers Bjælde, a curator at the Science Museums at Aarhus University, writes this in an article on the popular-science media outlet Videnskab.dk . Rømer studied and recorded the exact times when Io disappeared into Jupiter’s shadow and when it emerged on the other side. Discovered a pattern Bjælde explains that because Io orbits so close to Jupiter, only one of these events could be observed on any given night. In the days and months before Jupiter and Earth reached their closest point to each other, astronomers could observe the moon disappearing into Jupiter’s shadow. In the period after Jupiter and Earth were closest to each other, they could see Io emerging from the shadow. Rømer compiled detailed measurements of these events and eventually noticed a pattern. Rømer concluded that light took approximately 22 minutes to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit, says Professor Jacob Wüsthoff Linder. (Photo: Geir Mogen) "Rømer noticed that the eclipses occurred slightly later than expected when Earth was moving away from Jupiter, and slightly earlier when Earth was moving towards Jupiter," says Linder. "He realised that this was because the light had to travel a longer or shorter distance." "Impressive" Annonse In 1676, he therefore predicted that on November 9, Io would emerge from Jupiter's shadow ten minutes later than expected. He was correct. If light travelled instantaneously, Io should have appeared ten minutes earlier. Rømer demonstrated that light does not travel infinitely fast, says Linder. The finding was published shortly afterwards, on December 7, in Journal des sçavans . Rømer was not the first to suggest that light has a finite speed, but he is regarded as the first to demonstrate it with evidence. Other philosophers and scientists had previously theorised that light has a finite speed, including the Greek philosopher Empedocles, the Muslim scientists Ibn al-Haytham and Abu Rayhan al-Biruni, and the English philosopher and natural scientist Roger Bacon, according to Wikipedia . "How accurate was Rømer's estimate of the speed of light compared with what we know today?" "Not very accurate by modern standards, but impressive for 1676," says Linder. Rømer concluded that light took approximately 22 minutes to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit, says Linder. That corresponds to roughly 225,000 kilometres per second, whereas the correct value is around 300,000 kilometres per second. "So his estimate was about 25 per cent too low. What really mattered, however, was not the exact figure, but that he demonstrated that the speed of light was finite and could be measured," he says. An illustration from Ole Rømer's article from 1676. B represents Jupiter, with its shadow shown by shading. K, F, L, and G indicate different observation points along Earth's orbit as Io enters and emerges from the shadow. (Illustration: Ole Rømer) Gained support Was Rømer's finding quickly accepted by other scientists? "It was probably a gradual process, and there were critical voices at first. The head of the observatory where Rømer worked, for example, never fully accepted his explanation. Nevertheless, his findings received support fairly quickly from prominent scientific figures such as Huygens, and later Newton," says Linder. Christiaan Huygens was a Dutch mathematician and astronomer. He is known for developing the wave theory of light, among other things. "The decisive blow came with James Bradley's discovery of stellar aberration about 50 years later, which provided a completely independent and strong confirmation that light has a finite speed," says Linder. Stellar aberration is the phenomenon in which stars appear to shift slightly in the sky throughout the year because Earth moves around the Sun while light travels at a finite speed, the researcher explains. Looking into the past "Rømer was the first to demonstrate that light actually takes time to travel. It was also the first time anyone had produced a reasonably realistic estimate of the speed of light," says Linder. This became very important for astronomy. "Because when we look out into space, we are actually seeing things as they were when the light began its journey towards us. The farther away something is, the farther back in time we are looking," he says. This has been important for understanding how the universe has evolved. ——— Translated by Alette Bjordal Gjellesvik Read the Norwegian version of this article on forskning.no Related content Did the universe begin at a single point, or has it always been infinite? title: Anthropic Paid Rubio's Ex-Chief of Staff's Firm $740k.it Lobbied His NSC
abstract:
In the months after Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote the memo that set off Jensen Huang's fall, Anthropic's two Trump-connected lobbying firms were working the offices Rubio runs , federal disclosures show. One is run in Washington by Rubio's former Senate chief of staff and counts Susie Wiles' daughter as a partner. The other is Wiles' old firm. Anthropic has paid the two $1.63 million since April 2025. (FILE). US Vice President JD Vance (L) and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, 14 April 2025. EFE/EPA/KEN CEDENO / POOL The first is Continental Strategy, which Anthropic has paid $740,000 since April 2025. Its Washington managing partner, Alberto Martinez, is named on all six of Continental's quarterly reports for the AI lab. Meanwhile, Continental's report for April through June lists the National Security Council (NSC) among the offices it lobbied, and its report for July through September lists the State Department. Rubio is both national security adviser and secretary of state. Anthropic hired Ballard Partners on March 9, four days after the Pentagon labeled the company a supply-chain risk, Bloomberg reported. Wiles was a managing partner there until 2019. Ballard's first report, covering the rest of March, lists the White House Office and the Executive Office of the President. Ballard's report for April through June adds the NSC as well , and Anthropic has paid the firm $890,000 this year. Rubio's memo, dated March 30, went to a handful of Cabinet secretaries ahead of Trump's May trip to China, according to the New York Times . Rubio wrote it from a CIA report, recasting the agency's findings "in his own more assertive terms," the Washington Post reported Friday, though CIA officials aren't convinced Alice Huang - the Chinese national at the center of Jensen Huang's ouster - knowingly passed anything to Beijing. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Huang tried at least three times to get a meeting with Rubio and never got one , two people familiar with the matter told the Washington Sun . Rubio's aides nixed proposed talks in the spring of 2025, again that summer and again early this year, with his office saying he was booked or couldn't accommodate the Nvidia chief. The snubs deepened fears inside Nvidia that powerful forces in the US government were out to undermine Huang's influence as a leading voice for closer economic ties with Beijing, the Sun reported. Huang was Washington's loudest corporate backer of open-weight models , the cheap alternative to the closed systems Anthropic sells, and his exit clears the way for a crackdown on them. David Sacks argued on All-In that the ouster served Anthropic's "safetyist" allies, and physicist Steve Hsu wrote that he had heard Nvidia was planning "to go hard at producing frontier class open models" so it wouldn't depend on OpenAI or Anthropic. In the past months I heard on very good authority that Jensen and Nvidia were planning to go hard at producing frontier class open models. They wanted to verticalize their AI presence, and not depend on OAI or ANT to drive the industry forward. OAI, ANT, and GOOG are... — steve hsu (@hsu_steve) November 12, 2026 Huang's ouster could be the best break Anthropic gets as it heads into its IPO this week. Under Huang, Nvidia built its own family of open models, Nemotron, backed startups including Reflection AI, Thinking Machines Lab and Poolside, and was moving to acquire Hugging Face. " Nvidia was on a titanic collision course with the labs ," the CEO of a leading AI startup told Business Insider , and Replit CEO Amjad Masad called the ouster an attack on open models at a conference Monday. Meanwhile, Trump said Monday he doesn't know that Alice Huang was a spy "at all," and defended Lutnick. He called Huang a "legend" after the resignation, and Huang was reportedly weighing a comeback as his Silicon Valley allies lean on Nvidia's board - which isn't considering it , the FT reported. The Wiles Connection By the third quarter Ballard's brief had widened from Pentagon procurement to "US policy regarding AI," and its report adds the Pentagon and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, with the NSC still on the list. President Donald Trump recently replaced his chief of staff Susie Wiles, a one-time Ballard Partners lobbying firm leader. (Evan Vucci/AP) Two of the five Ballard lobbyists on that report came straight out of the national security apparatus. Amaryllis Fox Kennedy is listed as a CIA clandestine service officer from 2003 to 2009 and a deputy director of national intelligence in 2025 and 2026. Micah Ketchel, on the account since March, is listed as Rep. Mike Waltz's chief of staff from 2019 to 2025, then a senior adviser to the national security adviser and at the State Department. Continental promoted Katie Wiles days after the 2024 election, around the time it brought in Martinez. She is not a registered lobbyist and isn't named on the firm's reports for Anthropic. A White House official told CBS last month that Susie Wiles doesn't discuss work with her daughters. On April 17, Wiles hosted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei at the White House with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent , a meeting the White House called "productive and constructive." Wiles was out as chief of staff on Nov. 6, and has since faced "pay-for-play" accusations from former Kennedy adviser Calley Means centered on Ballard (however he incorrectly accused them of representing Pfizer). Brian Ballard says the firm's dealings with her as chief of staff "have been limited and have been the exception, not the rule." Wiles could face a House probe once Democrats take over next year , Rep. Robert Garcia said last week, and her successor, Stephen Miller, has tightened the rules on White House staff meeting lobbyists. Who's On Which Side Bessent said Sunday that Nvidia needs a "dramatic shakeup" and should go outside for Huang's successor. He reportedly confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in the Situation Room over why Megaspeed isn't blacklisted, and later pinned the failure on Commerce on CNBC. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent (AP) Commerce and the Justice Department put out a joint statement Monday night to address what they called "inaccurate information circulating in public reporting." It says Commerce opened an export-control investigation into Megaspeed in 2024, after its monitoring for chip diversion turned up suspicious activity, and that its investigators asked Nvidia in May 2025 for records of direct or indirect sales to the company. Nvidia put Megaspeed on its "no sell" list in June 2025 , according to the statement, the same month Commerce agents and Singaporean law enforcement made an on-site check at Megaspeed and interviewed its CEO, Alice Huang. The Justice Department then took the lead on a criminal investigation. The New York Times reported last week that Commerce's probe was halted late last year after Nvidia's general counsel reached out to the agents running it. Joint Statement from Department of Commerce and Department of Justice on Megaspeed Investigation. — U.S. Department of Commerce (@CommerceGov) November 16, 2026 Continental lists Treasury on four of its six reports for Anthropic. In the third quarter Continental added Caroline Farr, listed as a former senior adviser at the Treasury Department, to the account. Commerce, which put export controls on Anthropic's top models in June and lifted them June 30, is on three. On Monday, Commerce closed the loophole that let Chinese firms rent Nvidia chips in data centers outside China. The rule was "written by and at the direction" of Treasury and the National Security Council , the Washington Sun reported. Business Insider called it a major win for Amodei, who has pushed harder than almost anyone for strict limits on chip sales to China. Anthropic's own third-quarter disclosure , which reports $2.

title: Claude was trained on protein sequences at scale
abstract:
A next-amino-acid test on little-studied proteins finds that the latest Claude models were trained on protein sequences at scale. Other frontier models show no sign of it. The latest Claude models were trained on protein sequences, at scale. Give Claude Fable 5.2 or Claude Opus 5.5 the start of a little-studied bacterial protein and they predict the next amino acid. Shuffle the protein and they can’t. No other model we tested can do this. Like a protein language model, they do better on bigger protein families, and they do it even in families with no papers at all. Fable 5.2 beats every open protein language model we ran, and Opus 5.5 is level with ProtGPT3-10B, the largest of them. Update, 18 November 2026. Since the first version: Frontier LLMs have started to look good at protein tasks. Atharv Jayprakash showed GPT-6 Astra ranking SOD1 variants as well as ESM-2, and PG-LLM found the same across many proteins. Did these models learn from protein sequence databases such as UniProt, or from what is written about proteins? Famous proteins can’t tell the two apart: GFP is printed in countless papers, and most frontier models recite it. So we tested proteins that almost nobody writes about. We give a model the start of a protein and ask for the next amino acids. Then we ask again on a shuffled copy of the same protein. Shuffling keeps the letters and destroys their order, so the difference in accuracy measures what the model knows about the sequence itself. The test set is 668 bacterial and archaeal proteins from 167 Pfam families of unknown function. No family has a solved structure or more than three papers, and no protein has a close relative in UniProt. Each protein is cut at five points. At each cut the model writes the next 10 amino acids, and we score the first. Thinking is at its lowest setting. Appendix E has the details. Fable 5.2 gets the next amino acid right 54% of the time on real proteins and 9% on shuffled ones. The gap is there in nearly every family, not just a few easy ones. It appears in Opus 4.7, jumps in Opus 5.5, and jumps again in Fable 5.2. GPT, Gemini and the seven open-weight models (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Qwen 3.8, Kimi K3.1 Pro, GLM-5.3, MiniMax M3, gpt-oss-120b and Nemotron 3 Ultra) stay near zero, even when they simply continue raw FASTA text, the way they were trained. The latest Claude models also write runs of correct residues that other models rarely manage ( Appendix B ). Protein language models learn only from sequences, so they are the natural yardstick. The closest to an LLM are the ones that read a protein left to right and predict the next residue: ProtGPT3 , whose 10-billion-parameter version is the largest open one, and ProGen3 , whose largest public version has 3 billion. On the same input, Fable 5.2 beats both by a wide margin. Opus 5.5 is level with ProtGPT3-10B and below ProGen3-3B. ESM models are trained to see both sides of a residue, so continuing from the left is harder for them. Appendix C has all nine models. If the models learned from sequences, families with more sequences should be easier. To test this over a wide range, we added 90 smaller families, down to 20 proteins each, for 257 families in all. They are. Opus 5.5 rises with the two protein language models, ProtGPT3-10B and ProGen3-3B, which are trained on nothing but sequences. Fable 5.2 rises fastest and levels off at about 300 proteins per family. Earlier Claude models rise at a lower level, and GPT and Gemini stay near zero. The knowledge also carries over to proteins published after the training cutoff, with no close relative before it ( Appendix G ). Two other explanations don’t fit: Famous proteins are a different story. Many models do well on them, and several recite hundreds of residues letter for letter ( Appendix B ), because these sequences are all over papers and the web. In a first round with famous and obscure proteins side by side, Gemini 4 Carbon was strong on the famous ones and dropped to almost nothing on the obscure ones. The latest Claude models and ProtGPT3-10B held up, and Fable 5.2 was the strongest on both. This also explains the SOD1 and PG-LLM results. Ranking variants of a well-known protein can lean on what is written about it: which residues are buried, which substitutions break a helix, which mutations cause ALS. In PG-LLM, accuracy doesn’t depend on alignment depth and improves with more thinking, both signs of that route. Our test shuts it out. GPT-6 is good at the first kind of task and weak at the second; the latest Claude models are good at both. The latest Claude models know protein families that almost nobody has studied. That takes a lot of sequence data, not a few examples: protein sequences were a sizeable part of their training. Opus 5.5 behaves like a protein language model, and Fable 5.2 goes beyond the best one we could run. GPT and Gemini show none of this. Whatever protein sequence they saw in training, it was not enough to learn these families. DNA is different. Opus 5.5 predicts human and mouse coding sequence but not the rest of the genome, and barely the bacterial genes behind the proteins it knows ( Appendix A ). It learned proteins, not genomes. We are curious what else this knowledge supports. Fable 5.2 predicts little-studied proteins better than any open protein language model we ran, and protein language models carry more than next-residue statistics: ESM-2’s internal representations hold enough structure that a small folding module on top predicts 3D structures (ESMFold ), and their probabilities rank the effects of mutations . Could Claude fold a protein, or rank its variants, the same way? All code, test sets, model outputs and figures are in llm-bioseq-probe . 220-nucleotide windows, 200 shown and 20 to predict, from hg38, mm39 and the bacterial genes behind the test proteins, 500 per region. Non-coding windows contain no repeats, and the control shuffles each window keeping its dinucleotide counts. Opus 5.5 wrote all 20 nucleotides right 25 times in 500 human coding windows; a blind guess does that about once in a trillion. Gemini 4 Carbon blocks most DNA prompts before answering, so it is not shown. All 10 residues right. Each question asks for the next 10 residues. On the 668 little-studied proteins, Claude Fable 5.2 gets all 10 right at 88 real cuts and Opus 5.5 at 12, and neither at any shuffled one. If their residues were independent guesses at their own per-residue accuracy, they would get 15.8 and 0.57 by chance. Runs in a row. On shuffled proteins neither Fable 5.2 nor Opus 5.5 gets more than 3 residues in a row. Once on track they get surer: after one right residue, Opus 5.5 gets the next right 47% of the time, after four in a row 68%. Reciting well-known proteins. At 158 points in well-studied proteins, each model was asked for the next 200 residues at once. GPT-6.1 Sol never reaches 100 residues, and GPT-5.5 never gets past 2. ProtGPT3-10B gets more answers right than Opus 5.5 (38.4% vs 34.9%) but also more on shuffled proteins (10.7% vs 7.5%), because it knows amino acid composition better; the gap between the two, which is what each model knows about order, comes out the same. Prot-xLSTM is trained to read a protein after a set of its homologs; on the protein alone, as here, it is near zero, though one homolog in context lifts it from 14% to 81% on hemoglobin β. The last row is fill-in-the-blank rather than continuation: ESM-2 also sees the residues after the cut, which the LLMs never get. Every model first passed a sanity check on well-known proteins. Continuing ubiquitin and hemoglobin β from the left, ProGen3-3B gets 98% and 87% of residues right and ProtGPT3-10B 100% and 84%; with the whole protein and one residue masked, ESM-2 gets 80% of ubiquitin, ESM C and ESM3-open 100%. Masks are set on token ids, because the ESM SDK’s “_” character is not ESM C’s mask token.

title: Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long?
abstract:
Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long? November 2026 Y Discussion on Hacker News ▲ 238 points 125 comments → While benchmarking Gemini 4 Carbon on one of our private evals, we found something surprising: it spent close to an hour completing tasks that routinely took Opus and Astra only a few minutes: Time and cost per trial Left is faster; lower is cheaper. API list price On a $200 plan, fully used Carbon is priced at its post-introductory rate. Subscription subsidization rates used: Opus 40×, Astra 13×, Carbon 3×, Hydrogen 17×. Turns out we weren't alone in noticing this. I don't really know how to properly emphasize this. Gemini 4 Carbon is unacceptably slow in real world usage. Gemini 4 Carbon low: 22m21s Opus 5.5 high: 9m33s i really love gemini 4 carbon but its too slow. im losing my mind waiting just to stay focused and learn simple things dude why is carbon so fucking slow carbon is nearly unusable because of how slow it is, but people are majorly sleeping on it To find out why, we traced every step of Carbon's runs and quantified what contributes to the slowness. The Task In each task, the agent gets a codebase from just before a bug was fixed, along with a report that describes the bug only by its symptoms. Its job is to diagnose the bug and fix it, without making any unrelated changes. Much of the task's difficulty comes from engineering judgment rather than raw intelligence: tracing the user's symptoms to the right code path, ruling out rival explanations, putting the fix in the right place, and knowing when to stop. Slow inference, or more work? The first (and easiest) factor to separate out was inference speed: queueing at the provider, network latency, prompt processing and generation speed. Together, these set how long each step takes: Seconds per step Slower inference accounts for part of the gap: 16–30% of Carbon’s extra time compared with Astra, and 45–49% compared with Opus. The rest comes from longer trajectories. Carbon simply does more work per task, as the step counts, tool calls and tokens below show: The workload GPT-6 Astra against Gemini 4 Carbon, mean per bug. GPT-6 Astra Gemini 4 Carbon lighter = lower effort Carbon takes about seven times as many steps as Astra, and eleven times as many actions such as reading a file or running a command. It writes seven times as much and, because every step re-sends a longer and longer conversation, it processes more than sixteen times as much input. Ruling out the obvious Before looking inside the runs, we checked two simpler explanations. The harness. We also ran Carbon inside two other coding agents, opencode and mini-SWE-agent, and saw no meaningful difference. Mismatched reasoning levels. Effort settings aren't standardized across providers, so Carbon's "high" may sit closer to the other models' maximum settings, and the fairer comparison might have been Carbon on low. But on low, Carbon often failed to produce a fix at all: it went in circles, re-reading code it had already read instead of making the fix. Reading the traces We labelled every step of the Astra and Carbon runs by what it was for, and then counted how many steps went to each kind of work: Semantic trace analysis Each model’s steps, grouped by what they were for. Leaves out the 20 steps Carbon spent re-reading code it had already read; the next section covers those. Half of Carbon’s steps went into work the ticket never asked for: Auditing code beyond the bug. Once it had found the cause, Carbon kept widening its search, checking every related path through the system and auditing code the fix never needed to touch. Closing loopholes the ticket had already ruled out. Carbon defended against cases the ticket's facts had already excluded, hardening the code against problems nobody had reported. Can Carbon identify its own overworking? Sample trial: time to find the cause vs. time to first edit Minutes from the start of each run. GPT-6 Astra at max effort, Gemini 4 Carbon at high. In this sample trial, both models identified the cause early, Astra within a minute and Carbon within about six. Astra had its fix written three minutes later; Carbon didn't write any code for another 25 minutes. Carbon might not have been sure it had the cause (a knowledge gap), or it might have known and kept going anyway (a general habit, learned from training that rewards right answers more than it penalises extra steps). To tell them apart, we re-ran one of the trials in a modified harness that automatically injects the same check-in every five turns: "do you already have enough to make the fix?" Sample trial with check-ins: time to find the cause vs. time to first edit The same bug and scale as above. Gemini 4 Carbon at high, with the check-in injected every five turns (circles). With check-ins, Carbon finished in 28 minutes instead of 37, and the wait between naming the cause and editing shrank from 25 minutes to about 10. This implies that the slowness seems to come from how Carbon behaves, not what it knows. Carbon's necessary work is also slower Even within the steps the fix needed, we found some additional low-hanging fruit: Carbon got less done with each step, and it kept re-reading code it had already seen. Astra made more than two tool calls per step, often reading several files at once — Carbon, on the other hand, made about one, usually reading a single file. Carbon also re-read far more: 39% of the lines it read were ones it had already seen, against 7% for Astra. We estimate that these two "mechanical" inefficiencies account for roughly 25% of Carbon's excess runtime. Conclusion On difficult bug-fixing tasks, Carbon took close to an hour where Opus and Astra took minutes. We traced that gap to three sources: Slower inference. Each step takes longer, which explains 16–30% of the gap against Astra and about half against Opus. Unnecessary work. About half of Carbon's steps went on work the tickets never asked for: auditing code the fix didn't need and closing loopholes the ticket had already ruled out. Mechanical inefficiencies. Fewer tool calls per step and frequent re-reading slow Carbon down; we estimate that fixing them alone would cut its runtime by roughly a quarter.

title: AI in emerging economy entrepreneurship education
abstract:
This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) is associated with changes in entrepreneurship education in emerging economies, focusing on entrepreneurial competencies, student cognition, venture originality and early graduate behavior.
 
 
 
 The study uses a multisource, multicohort quasi-experimental design. Principal analyses draw on an approximately 900-student longitudinal survey and a preliminary 18-month graduate follow-up. Published evidence on educator perspectives and on 150 business plans with 45 interviews across three Chinese universities is used only for contextual triangulation and is not pooled with the study-specific statistical analyses.
 
 
 
 In the principal student analyses, generative AI was associated with stronger opportunity recognition but lower divergent thinking and higher confirmation bias. Predictive analytics was associated with more evidence-based evaluation, while structured intelligent tutoring was associated with stronger metacognitive reflection. Published business-plan evidence is used only to contextualize homogenization. The 18-month venture-creation differences were not statistically significant and remain exploratory.
 
 
 
 The nonrandomized design, incomplete wave-specific attrition information, unavailable matching diagnostics, reliance on published contextual evidence for homogenization and educator perspectives and short follow-up period limit causal claims and cross-context generalization. Future studies should use controlled designs, complete longitudinal reporting, longer graduate tracking and cross-country comparisons.
 
 
 
 Educators should require prompt logs, independent evidence checks, revision rationales and originality rubrics that reward local validation, assumption testing, judgment and distinctive venture logic.
 
 
 
 In emerging economies, AI can broaden access to entrepreneurial feedback and market knowledge, but inadequate guidance may yield generic ventures detached from local needs.
 
 
 
 The study extends entrepreneurship education ecosystem thinking by treating AI as an active mediator of cognition and venture artifact production whose educational role depends on tool function, assessment design and institutional governance.

title: MCTS Is Counting the Wrong Thing: Learning Exploration Counts for LLM Reasoning
abstract: Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) has powered landmark successes in reinforcement learning, yet its gains in LLM reasoning can remain modest despite substantial search effort. We identify an overlooked bottleneck: what MCTS counts. Standard UCT assigns independent visit counts to textual branches, allowing different formulations of the same reasoning strategy to repeatedly receive exploration bonuses. Our theoretical analysis shows that this count fragmentation can impair exploration efficiency, as quantified by increased cumulative regret. To address this problem, we introduce Learned Pseudo-Count MCTS (LPC-MCTS), which changes only the exploration statistic in UCT. A lightweight Coin-Flipping Network head on the policy's hidden representations estimates representation coverage, enabling related branches to share exploration evidence. Across 5 mathematical-reasoning and 7 search benchmarks, LPC-MCTS consistently outperforms strong MCTS baselines. Holding each LPC-MCTS-trained policy fixed, replacing standard MCTS counts at inference improves average mean@16 accuracy across 5 mathematical benchmarks by 3.79 percentage points on Qwen2.5-7B and 2.71 points on Qwen3-4B. Applying LPC-MCTS during both training and inference yields gains of 4.96 and 4.37 points over standard MCTS, respectively. Together, our theory and experiments show that changing what MCTS counts can substantially improve its exploration efficiency and reasoning performance.

title: DACE: Diversity-Driven Adversarial Co-Evolution for Robust LLM Safety Alignment
abstract: Ensuring robust safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly difficult as adversarial attacks evolve and outpace alignment pipelines built on pre-collected data. Existing co-evolutionary frameworks let the defender chase a moving attacker, yet their training dynamics expose two compounding pathologies: \emph{attack strategy collapse}, where the attacker overfits to a narrow set of high-reward rewrites, and \emph{defense adversarial forgetting}, where the defender loses competence against earlier attacks as the attack distribution drifts. Existing remedies are partial: attacker-side diversity rewards score textual novelty rather than strategy novelty, and defender-side replay relies on discrete judge scores that ignore estimation uncertainty, response stochasticity, and defender non-stationarity. We introduce \textbf{\method}, a diversity-driven adversarial co-evolution framework that targets both pathologies jointly. On the attacker side, \method couples an explicit two-dimensional strategy space (risk category $\times$ attack style) with a \emph{normalized marginal coverage gain} reward, providing a bounded, non-vanishing exploration signal at the strategy layer. On the defender side, \method maintains a unified \emph{Bayesian adversarial replay pool} whose Beta--Bernoulli threat posteriors are refreshed by time decay and sampled via Thompson sampling, anchoring defender training to an evolving threat landscape. Across standard safety, automated-attacker, and general-capability benchmarks, \method improves robustness to out-of-distribution attacks while preserving general capabilities, and yields broader attacker strategy coverage.

title: Stress Testing a Multimodal Large Language Model Grading Assistant on Kinematics Graph Reading
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can recognize graph features yet award credit without sufficient graphical support. This exploratory study examines selected grading outputs for synthetic responses to four kinematics exercises, generated through visual distortion and progressive transformation toward reference graphs. Different model and prompt configurations were used. Some judgments correctly distinguished instantaneous zero velocity from rest over a finite interval and recognized positive curvature. Yet a severely distorted velocity--time graph received full credit despite disconnected and branching traces and an unclear zero-velocity reference. Other submissions graded under the same configuration lost substantial credit. Numerical cutoffs intended to distinguish meaningful features from drawing irregularities were supplied without a coordinate convention for unnumbered graphs, leaving the basis of exact partial-credit awards unresolved. Stress testing can expose unsupported awards before classroom use. For the configurations examined, we do not recommend accepting scores as final grades without instructor review, including review of full-credit responses.

title: PVTSizing 2.0: A Fast and Reliable Analog Circuit Sizing Operator for Agentic EDA Workflows
abstract: Analog circuit design automation requires both coordinated tool execution and efficient numerical search. Large language models (LLMs) offer new ways to organize tool execution, but finding one sizing that satisfies specifications across process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners remains costly. PVTSizing 2.0 addresses these needs through a human-agent workflow built around an independently usable numerical optimizer. An agent carries the designer's approved task through execution and result review. The optimizer reduces unnecessary training through loss-guided updates and uses critic-guided local refinement to explore additional candidates while accounting for cross-corner conflicts. An optional LLM adviser supplies parameter relationships to focus numerical search on circuit-informed directions, while the optimizer selects adjustment amplitudes and verifies their effects through simulation. Across four circuit benchmarks, the standalone optimizer completes all 40 runs and achieves a 7.3x speedup in overall mean runtime over the original PVTSizing, with a comparable mean sample count. In a separate study, the best tested knowledge-injection configuration further reduces mean runtime by 39.9% and simulation samples by 35.4% relative to the standalone optimizer.

title: Generalizable dexterous grasping via primitive policy library reuse and grasp part reasoning
abstract:
This study aims to address the limited generalization of learned dexterous grasping policies to novel objects. To this end, a general framework is developed in which grasp-part reasoning acts as an intermediate mechanism and primitive policy library reuse serves as the core, enabling effective matching and transfer between novel objects and existing grasping policies.
 
 
 
 A primitive policy library is first established through continual learning. Then, a large model is used to perform structural part analysis, relevant part identification and grasp-part reasoning on novel objects so as to determine graspable parts that can be matched to the policy library. Finally, dexterous grasping of novel objects is achieved by reusing the corresponding primitive policies.
 
 
 
 Experimental results validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. The high-level reasoning process enables more accurate localization of graspable parts that are matchable to the primitive policy library, thereby improving policy reuse quality. Compared with heuristic baselines and methods without part reasoning, the proposed framework achieves superior dexterous grasp success, stability and generalization on novel objects.
 
 
 
 The originality of this work lies in the development of a generalizable dexterous grasping framework that combines grasp-part reasoning with primitive policy library reuse. Instead of using large models for direct low-level control generation, the proposed method uses high-level reasoning to identify reusable graspable parts of novel objects, thereby supporting the transfer and reuse of existing primitive grasping policies. This study provides a new perspective for policy generalization in dexterous grasping.

title: HADVQ: Hessian Aware Directional Vector Quantization
abstract: Ultra-low-bit quantization of large language models is a challenging task because aggressive compression severely distorts model parameters and disproportionately harms a small number of highly sensitive channels. We present a vector quantization method tailored for this regime. Our approach begins with random preconditioning, which regularizes the weight space and makes it more amenable to quantization. We then represent weights in polar coordinates and decouple the quantization of directions and magnitudes. To quantize directions, we leverage the structure induced by random preconditioning and design a structured codebook based on the $E_8$ lattice, yielding a compact yet expressive representation. To further reduce degradation, we detect extremely important channels using a proxy Hessian and preserve them with an additional cost of only 0.16 bits. Together, these components provide an effective quantization pipeline for LLMs in the extremely low-bit regime. Empirical results demonstrate improved accuracy, highlighting the benefit of combining geometric structure, lattice-based codebooks, and selective channel preservation.

title: Multi-Agent Memory Inconsistency: Where Factual Conflicts Disappear in LLM Agents
abstract: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%. Within this setting, workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and pooled matched comparisons show higher detection than single-agent execution when one worker reads both claims but lower detection when the claims are split across workers. Worker-to-lead handoffs are a central target for improving conflict detection in multi-agent LLMs.

title: Groups of AI agents underuse resources despite shared evidence of increased capacity
abstract: When AI agents share limited resources, such as computing services or public infrastructure, their individual choices affect how much work they complete as a group. Can sharing evidence of what is available let a group make full use of its resources after capacity changes? We tested this with language-model agents choosing between two simulated servers. One server recovered while its status report still listed it as unavailable. Each server had limited capacity per round, so rejected jobs required another attempt before the deadline. Telling agents that recovery was possible reduced missed deadlines. In controlled tests with Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5, no agent tried the recovered server after a rule reminder, yet all chose it when shown a successful request record. After sharing, all five models tested left capacity unused. Keeping the success record fixed, we gave agents numbers without instructions, using each value equally often but giving group members either identical or distinct numbers. With OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol or Google's Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, distinct numbers spread simultaneous requests across servers and increased job completions even though overall choice frequencies barely changed. Telling AI agents which resources are available leaves a second design challenge: helping them spread demand across those resources.

title: SpatialMind: Adaptive Multi-Level Geometric Fusion for Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate promising capabilities in 2D visual understanding, yet remain limited in 3D spatial reasoning. Recent studies explore integrating 3D reconstruction models into MLLMs. However, these approaches either use a single geometric granularity across all tasks or adopt a fixed multi-level fusion scheme, regardless of task-specific reasoning requirements. Through systematic experiments on multi-level geometric fusion, we find that spatial tasks at different cognitive levels (e.g., distance estimation vs. route planning) require geometric representations of different granularities, revealing that fixed fusion cannot accommodate diverse spatial reasoning requirements. To bridge this gap, we propose SpatialMind, a task-adaptive framework for dynamically integrating multi-level geometric representations. SpatialMind employs GeoFus, a multi-layer geometric fusion module built around a gating network jointly conditioned on textual instructions, visual semantics, and geometric representations. This network adaptively modulates the contributions of shallow, intermediate, and deep geometric features across the layers of the LLM decoder. Furthermore, we introduce a negative-entropy regularization loss to mitigate gate collapse. Gate visualizations indicate that GeoFus adapts geometric granularity to task requirements. Experiments demonstrate that SpatialMind achieves competitive performance across spatial benchmarks, attaining a state-of-the-art score of 72.3 on VSI-Bench. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhaosb-star/SpatialMind.

title: From Perception to Simulation: Unveiling and Empowering Mental Spatial Dynamics in MLLMs
abstract: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental component of world understanding for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). While existing research has advanced the perception of spatial relations in static scenes, the domain of dynamic spatial simulation remains relatively unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MentalGrid, a benchmark focused on spatial reasoning tasks that require models to simulate evolving spatial states without intermediate visual feedback. Extensive evaluation on our benchmark reveals a significant deficiency in the spatial simulation capabilities of existing models. Specifically, we find that performance is constrained by perceptual limitations in simple simulation scenarios and hindered by inadequate multi-step reasoning as complexity increases. To address these challenges, we propose a three-stage curriculum learning framework utilizing 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples. This approach yields SpatialWalker, which achieves a 33.8% average improvement over its base model, surpassing proprietary models like Gemini-3-Flash in spatial simulation. Furthermore, SpatialWalker demonstrates robust generalization, maintaining a 4.9% average gain on out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrating the pivotal role of spatial simulation as a fundamental building block for broader spatial intelligence.

title: From Imperfective Paradox to Moorean Absurdity: Single-Chain Reasoning Lock-In and Multi-Candidate Verbalization Across Aspectual and Pragmatic Ambiguity
abstract: Natural language entailment and coherence judgments often depend on whether an event merely occurred, reached a telic culmination, satisfied a plan, or was evaluated under multiple pragmatic standards. We test observable consequences of the single-chain premature lock-in hypothesis across four preregistered, sealed formal experiments on Qwen3-8B-Q8_0 (16,640 formal units, temperature=0.0): 15 of 16 hypothesis slots retain confirmatory status (12 rejecting H0 under within-experiment Holm control at alpha_fam=0.05; E3_H3 demoted to descriptive status). In Experiment 1, Direct-CoT vs. MCU differs by 25.00 pp on telic high-confidence completion (Holm p=1.31239e-05), while NLI-CoT collapses by -91.25 pp on uninterrupted atelic items (Holm p=1.81805e-21). Multi-Candidate Verbalization (MCV) elicits K=5 weighted estimates in one call, separating the prompt from unweighted (MCU) and self-weighted (MCW) readouts. Mandarin (E2) and English (E3) expose an Interruption-Anchored Realis Paradox under NLI-CoT. In Experiment 4, MCU-CF raises perceived coherence on implicit Moorean sentences by 26.64 pp over Direct-CoT (Holm p=0.0006), alongside Direct-CF - Direct-CoT = 29.15 pp and MCU-CoT - Direct-CoT = 17.31 pp. A 1,800-call OpenAI ablation and a stage="dev"P16.7 cross-model extension (4,240 planned/collected units across five external models: 4,222 valid, 18 format-missing, 0 transport-missing;<2% missing per slice; OpenAI gpt-4o-mini at top_logprobs=20 achieves 1,000/1,000 valid units) show that discrete NLI-CoT and scalar Direct-CoT judgments dissociate across models. Confirmatory effects concern observable prompt-and-readout protocols; internal premature lock-in remains a hypothesis. All code, stimuli, preregistered analysis plans, and verification tools are available at https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies.

title: Do Diffusion Models Learn to Generalize Basic Visual Skills?
abstract: Diffusion models generate high-quality images, but how well they generalize is hard to measure. Current evaluations rely on human preference and prompt-following benchmarks for text-to-image models and on distribution-level metrics such as Fr\'echet Inception Distance (FID) and Inception Score (IS) for class-conditional models, but these cannot tell whether models learn basic visual skills or largely match training patterns. To address this gap, we introduce the Visual Generative Lab (VGL), a controlled experimental framework for studying how diffusion models learn and generalize basic visual skills, including size, position, rotation, count, color, shape, and their compositions. By generating synthetic training data for each skill from explicit rules, VGL allows precise measurement of generalization with task-specific, rule-based metrics. Training models from scratch on these data reveals three patterns in this controlled setting: (1) with our default design, extrapolation is limited: size and position degrade within a few pixels of the training range, count reaches only about 50% accuracy on out-of-range counts, and rotation extrapolation accuracy varies widely across seeds; (2) for compositional generalization, the number of distinct basic visual skill combinations matters more than dataset size; (3) skills mostly fail independently, except position. Code and data-generation scripts: https://github.com/AmishSethi/visual-generative-lab.

title: Communicate the Change: Efficient Expert Parallelism via Activation Compression
abstract: Scaling has driven the success of large language models (LLM), with sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures enabling greater parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation. At large scales, MoE models rely on expert parallelism to distribute experts across devices. Each MoE layer requires two synchronous collective communication steps during inference: dispatching hidden states to the activated experts and combining the resulting expert outputs. As compute throughput has outpaced interconnect bandwidth, these synchronous collectives have become a major bottleneck to MoE scaling and efficiency. We address this challenge with EchoMoE, a lightweight architecture modification that retrofits existing MoE models, requiring approximately 8,500x fewer training tokens than full pretraining. Motivated by the observation that transformer blocks update the residual stream incrementally, we use a hidden state from an earlier layer as a reference and communicate only the compressed difference between it and the current state, rather than communicating each hidden state in full. EchoMoE periodically refreshes these reference states and transmits only the compressed differences synchronously, reducing the traffic on latency-critical paths without significant computational overhead. EchoMoE reduces inter-node communication volume by 58% and improves throughput by 22.6%, while preserving average performance within 3.8 percentage points across 18 benchmarks. EchoMoE further improves inference throughput by up to 2.38x over bandwidth-constrained Ethernet, paving the way for wide-area distributed inference. EchoMoE also tolerates quantization of the communicated representations without measurable quality loss. We release an efficient implementation for applying EchoMoE to pretrained MoE models, together with an inference integration for vLLM.
